## RosettaCodeData popular-title scores 17–16: reviewed candidates (2026-11-20)

The pinned RosettaCodeData title index at
[`1d475861d7141ef2fafff293d9339f56e4b0f5db`](https://github.com/acmeism/RosettaCodeData/blob/1d475861d7141ef2fafff293d9339f56e4b0f5db/popular-tasks)
was used only as a title index. No task pages, solutions, source code, tests,
examples, or prose were consulted or reused. The score-17–16 title slice was
compared against local contracts. Four distinct profiles were confirmed.
Each has a bounded package, independent algorithm references, and ten native
ports, suite registration, and README/catalog entries. Static integration is
complete for the scalar and byte-output suites; no programs or checks were run.

- `json_pointer_evaluation`: resolve RFC 6901 reference tokens against a
  bounded, pre-parsed JSON value tree. This exercises pointer syntax,
  `~1`/`~0` decoding, object-key matching, and array-index selection without
  folding ten unrelated general-purpose JSON parsers into the benchmark.
  Missing members, malformed escapes, duplicate object keys, array `-`, and
  out-of-range indexes have explicit error behavior. Primary specification:
  [RFC 6901](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6901.html). The RFC's
  Simplified BSD requirement applies to extracted code components; none are
  extracted. Only normative behavior is used.
- `ecdsa_signature_verification`: verify a supplied ECDSA signature on a
  bounded toy prime-field curve, including scalar/public-point checks, modular
  inversion, double-scalar multiplication, and the final x-coordinate test.
  It is distinct from ECDH key agreement and hash-based signatures. The small
  curve is for deterministic algorithm benchmarking and makes no security
  claim. Method and curve references: [NIST FIPS 186-5](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/fips/186-5/final)
  and [NIST SP 800-186](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/186/final). Only
  mathematical procedure and standard parameter facts are used; no source
  code, test vectors, or prose are copied.
- `brzozowski_dfa_to_regex`: solve the state-language equations of a bounded
  complete DFA using Arden elimination with deterministic state order and a
  fixed regular-expression serialization. This is distinct from the local
  reverse/determinize DFA minimizer and from regex-to-automaton construction.
  Primary context: Brzozowski and Leiss, “On Equations for Regular Languages,
  Finite Automata, and Sequential Networks” (1980),
  [article PDF](https://im.saske.sk/hospodar/literature/1980_brzozowski_leiss_TCS_equations_for_regular_languages.pdf).
  The paper is copyrighted; only the mathematical method is used, with no
  text, figures, code, examples, or tests copied.

The CP-Algorithms “Flows with demands” article also confirmed
`minimum_bounded_s_t_flow`: binary-search the smallest capacity of the
auxiliary `t -> s` arc, rerunning lower-bound circulation feasibility at each
midpoint. It shares the feasibility reduction with
`lower_bound_circulation_feasibility` but adds a materially distinct
parametric-search workload and differs from the min-cost optimizer in
`minimum_cost_b_flow`. A safe finite search bound is the sum of capacities on
arcs leaving `s`; for the current `n<=6`, `m<=8`, `upper<=2` limits it is at
most 16, so no more than five feasibility calls are needed. The article and
the official repository license both identify CC BY-SA 4.0. The package
attributes the article and uses only its algorithmic idea; it does not copy
code, prose, examples, or fixtures. Source: [article](https://cp-algorithms.com/graph/flow_with_demands.html),
[official repository license](https://github.com/cp-algorithms/cp-algorithms/blob/main/LICENSE).

## Encyclopedia of Algorithms Chapter 322: BGI radio-network broadcast (2026-11-17)

Added [`radio_network_bgi_broadcast`](r/radio_network_bgi_broadcast/README.md) as the complete bounded repeated BGI schedule, distinct from the existing one-call [`radio_network_decay_phase`](d/radio_network_decay_phase/README.md). The profile uses `N=n`, `epsilon=1/2`, `k=2*ceil(log2(Delta))`, and `t=ceil(log2(N/epsilon))`, following original paper §2.2 because the Chapter 322 PDF appears to contain an extra factor two in its displayed `t`. The source's initial message is its first Decay send in slot 0; later activations wait for the next `k`-multiple slot, and recipients cannot retransmit in their receipt slot. Supplied coin tapes make the result a deterministic trace; the profile reports first-informed slots, transmissions, and global Decay phases without claiming probabilistic success or the disputed deterministic lower bound under indistinguishable collisions. The package has ten language ports, direct-simulation and bitmask references, bounded fixtures through the 88-byte maximum output, null/error probes, provenance/rights, and static inventory. Sources: Bar-Yehuda, Goldreich, and Itai, *Encyclopedia of Algorithms*, Chapter 322, [DOI 10.1007/978-1-4939-2864-4_322](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4939-2864-4_322), §§1 and 2.1.1–2.1.3; “On the Time-Complexity of Broadcast in Multi-Hop Radio Networks,” *JCSS* 45(1), 104–126 (1992), [DOI 10.1016/0022-0000(92)90042-H](https://doi.org/10.1016/0022-0000(92)90042-H), §§2.1–2.2; Goldreich's [author errata page](https://www.wisdom.weizmann.ac.il/~oded/p_bgi.html). No source code, prose, or fixtures were reused. The workload and package checker are registered with the `i64_array_bytes_output` runner and verifier, and CATALOG lists the benchmark. No programs, tests, scripts, checkers, builds, compilers, profilers, or benchmarks were run.

Minimum edge-cover *cardinality* on graphs without isolated vertices reduces
to `|V| - |maximum matching|`. The existing maximum-matching kernels therefore
already cover that scalar computation; reconstructing an edge-cover witness
would add an output operation but does not justify a second matching kernel.

All-roots tree distance sums were compared with
[`tree_path_composite_sum`](t/tree_path_composite_sum/README.md). Setting all
vertex values to zero and every edge map to `f(x)=x+1` makes each path value
equal its edge distance, so the existing rerooting message recurrence computes
the same per-vertex sums. The bounded profile's modulus does not alter results
for its `N<=32` tree distances. Treat the distance-sum operation as already
covered; its workload now includes a full-size unit-edge path with distance
sums, without adding a duplicate algorithm package. This comparison uses the
mathematical rerooting idea only; no project code was run.

Static basename comparison of current `c/**/*.c` sources against the Elisa,
C3, V, Zig, and Mojo source trees found a same-named file in each language for

**Static review complete; execution deferred — root:** [`prufer_decode_linear`](p/prufer_decode_linear/README.md)
implements monotone-cursor Prüfer decoding. The existing `prufer_code` package
uses max-leaf selection but its Rust and Mojo drafts scan active labels anew
for each edge and sort the output. This method uses a single monotone cursor,
with an `O(n)` removal-order output contract; the source method is described
by [CP-Algorithms](https://cp-algorithms.com/graph/pruefer_code.html).
Contract, two references, ten language ports, workload, rights note, package
checker, and byte-output suite wiring are present. Only algorithmic ideas are
used. No programs or checks were run.
Static follow-up added a fixture where a newly exposed leaf lies above the
cursor, and linked the profile from the root README and catalog. Harness source
limits cover the specified input and output sizes; no runtime behavior is
established by this inspection.
The workload now also specifies consecutive newly exposed leaves above the
cursor. Static tracing documents why a next leaf exists after every decoded
code symbol; this is not an execution or a substitute for verification.
The timed Prüfer workload now includes 256-vertex star and path sequences,
with directly specified removal-order edge streams. A static audit of all ten
ports found their cursor handling, removal-order output, final edge, error
precedence, byte bounds, and ABI returns consistent with the references and
contract. The package remains uncompiled and unexecuted.

Static duplicate review compared [`ternary`](t/ternary/README.md) and
[`ternary_search_min_max_recursive`](t/ternary_search_min_max_recursive/README.md).
Both recursively optimize a unimodal function, but the former uses binary64,
keeps the left two thirds on an equal-value comparison, and evaluates the
midpoint at termination; the latter uses binary32, keeps the middle third on
ties, and evaluates the left endpoint. The tie branch changes the recurrence
itself, so the two profiles are retained with reciprocal explanations. This is
a source-level comparison; neither profile was executed.

CP-Algorithms follow-up: its [Lyndon-factorization article](https://cp-algorithms.com/string/lyndon_factorization.html)
describes both factorization and a factorization-based least rotation. These
are already represented by [`duval_algorithm`](d/duval_algorithm/README.md)
and [`duval`](d/duval/README.md), respectively. The independent
[`booths_algorithm`](b/booths_algorithm/README.md) and
[`minimum_string_representation`](m/minimum_string_representation/README.md)
retain different least-rotation search methods. The
[Z-function](https://cp-algorithms.com/string/z-function.html),
[Newton root method](https://cp-algorithms.com/num_methods/roots_newton.html),
and [Simpson integration](https://cp-algorithms.com/num_methods/simpson-integration.html)
have existing [`z_algorithm`](z/z_algorithm/README.md),
[`newton_square_root`](n/newton_square_root/README.md), and
[`simpson_integration`](s/simpson_integration/README.md) profiles. These are
algorithm-level comparisons, not claims that every source application or
domain is covered. No aliases were added and no project code was run.

reference drafts, ten language drafts, workload, rights note, package checker,

The sampled category pages report 87 graph-theory, 64 dynamic-programming,
48 combinatorics, 62 number-theory, 97 geometry, and 252 data-structure-tagged
kata. This is a set of visible, high-signal slices, not an exhaustive review of
every entry. The Codewars site supplied public titles and tags only; no kata
statement, examples, tests, submissions, or code were read or reused. The
[authoring guidelines](https://docs.codewars.com/authoring/guidelines/kata/)
discourage blatant duplicates and use of other sites' problem content without
license or permission; this audit respects that boundary by deriving the
reserved contract independently from research literature.

**Implemented — `android_unlock_pattern_count`:** accept
`i64_array_scalar` input `[L]`, with `4 <= L <= 9`, and return the exact number
of valid patterns of exactly `L` points on the canonical 3×3 Android grid.
Number grid points row-major from 0 through 8. A pattern may not repeat a
point; a move is legal when every grid point strictly inside its straight
segment has already been visited. On this lattice the only nonempty interior
segment case is a midpoint. The primary is depth-first enumeration over a
visited 9-bit mask, extending only through legal moves and counting paths at
length `L`; the independent reference scans all length-`L` permutations and
checks each edge against its prior-prefix visited set. At most `9!` candidate
permutations are examined. Malformed input or a length outside 4–9 returns
`-1`. Ten language ports, independent references, fixtures, rights notes, and
`i64_array_scalar` runner/verifier registration are present.
The method contract follows Uellenbeck et al., [“Quantifying the Security of
Graphical Passwords: The Case of Android Unlock Patterns”](https://doi.org/10.1145/2508859.2516700),
and Lee et al., [“A Visibility-Based Lower Bound for Android Unlock Patterns”](https://doi.org/10.1587/transinf.2016EDL8196).
Codewars is title discovery only; no task content is used, and no paper code
or prose is reused. See [`android_unlock_pattern_count`](a/android_unlock_pattern_count/README.md).

## Catalog and suite candidates added during reviews through 2026-11-16

**In progress — root:** `tree_distance_k_dominating_set` reserves unweighted
minimum distance-`k` domination of a tree by repeatedly covering a deepest
uncovered vertex from its `k`-th ancestor. The existing
[`tree_weighted_dominating_set`](t/tree_weighted_dominating_set/README.md)
uses distance one and a weighted three-state DP; the local
[`domination_local_reduction`](d/domination_local_reduction/README.md) performs
a graph reduction rather than solving domination. Static path and README
searches found no equivalent distance-`k` tree package. The [distance-`k`
tree domination paper](https://ftp.gwdg.de/pub/misc/EMIS/journals/JGAA/accepted/2015/TurauKoehler2015.19.1.pdf)
describes this sequential greedy strategy and proves optimality for positive
radii; this independently authored profile does not implement its distributed
protocol. Radius zero selects every vertex. Contract, references,
ten language drafts, workload, package checker and scalar-suite wiring are
present; all remain unverified. Nothing has been executed. Do not duplicate.

**In progress — root:** `tree_weighted_independent_dominating_set` reserves
minimum-weight independent domination on a tree: selected vertices dominate
every vertex and no selected vertices are adjacent. The existing
[`tree_weighted_dominating_set`](t/tree_weighted_dominating_set/README.md)
permits adjacent selected vertices; [`tree_weighted_vertex_cover`](t/tree_weighted_vertex_cover/README.md)
corresponds to maximum-weight independent set without a domination constraint.
Static name and README searches found no equivalent package. The [tree
domination research](https://www.opuscula.agh.edu.pl/vol45/6/art/opuscula_math_4540.pdf)
identifies independent domination and linear tree DP; mathematical ideas only.
Contract, references, ten language drafts, workload, package checker and
scalar-suite wiring are present; all remain unverified. Nothing has been run.
Do not duplicate.

**In progress — root:** `tree_weighted_total_dominating_set` reserves the
minimum-weight total domination problem on a rooted tree: every vertex must
have a selected neighbor, including vertices that are themselves selected.
[`tree_weighted_dominating_set`](t/tree_weighted_dominating_set/README.md)
allows a selected vertex to dominate itself; the general
[`weighted_connected_dominating_set`](w/weighted_connected_dominating_set/README.md)

README searches found no matching total-domination profile. The [total
f-domination paper](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0166218X18306309)
describes a linear weighted tree DP; the profile is the `f=1` specialization.
Only mathematical ideas are used. Contract, references, ten language drafts,
workload, package checker and scalar-suite wiring are present; all remain unverified.
Nothing has run. Do not duplicate this reservation.

The complementary maximum-weight independent-set value can be recovered from
total weight minus this static result, so a second one-shot tree-DP profile
would duplicate the computation. OI Wiki's separate dynamic update method is
reserved below; it maintains HLD chain products after point-weight changes.

**In progress — root:** `tree_min_cost_edge_coloring` reserves the
minimum-cost proper edge coloring of a tree with a shared cost per color.
[`tree_min_cost_proper_coloring`](t/tree_min_cost_proper_coloring/README.md)
colors vertices and enforces a different adjacency relation; the existing
matching and bipartite edge-coloring packages do not optimize costs over a
tree's incident edges. Static README and name searches found no matching
package. [Zhou and Nishizeki](https://doi.org/10.1023/B:JOCO.0000021940.40066.0c)
describe a bottom-up DP with simultaneous matching sensitivity, and
[Ito et al.](https://doi.org/10.1587/transinf.E94.D.190) give a distinct
global matching reduction. Reserve the former fast DP profile; do not replace
its requested matching sensitivity with the exponential reference. A bounded
contract, small independent references, and an unexecuted fast construction
draft, ten language port drafts, workload, package checker and scalar-suite
wiring are present; all remain unverified. Only mathematical ideas are used; no source prose or code
is copied. Nothing has been executed. Do not duplicate this reservation.

**Source distinction:** The [CP-Algorithms Hungarian-algorithm article](https://cp-algorithms.com/graph/hungarian-algorithm.html)
describes a weighted tree coloring with only adjacent vertices required to
differ, then proposes an assignment of distinct colors to all children.
Those are different constraints: siblings can share a color under ordinary
proper coloring. The stronger sibling-distinct problem is tracked separately
below and is not attributed to the article's stated ordinary-coloring contract.

Static comparison of that lead: ordinary vertex-cost coloring is drafted as
`tree_min_cost_proper_coloring`. A rooted variant requiring siblings to have
distinct colors as well can be expressed as edge coloring by assigning each
non-root vertex's color to its incoming edge, with a root-color exclusion on
incident edges. The existing `tree_min_cost_edge_coloring` instead takes one
shared cost per color and has no root-vertex color or root-specific exclusion.
The vertex-specific sibling-distinct contract is therefore distinct from
those two existing profiles and is tracked in the draft immediately below.

**Drafted; validation outstanding:** `tree_sibling_distinct_cost_coloring` covers that
rooted vertex-cost variant. Its bounded contract and independent
subset-assignment drafts in all ten languages, assignment reference, workload,
package checker, scalar-suite wiring, and exhaustive small-tree cross-check
source are drafted; execution remains outstanding. This is not
an implementation of ordinary proper coloring, nor the shared-color-cost
edge-coloring profile. No code has been run.

Source: [CP-Algorithms — Check if point belongs to the convex polygon in O(log N)](https://cp-algorithms.com/geometry/point-in-convex-polygon.html), CC BY-SA 4.0; clean-room algorithm description only. No programs, tests, scripts, checkers, builds, compilers, or benchmarks were run. |

No package uses exact-distance buckets for arbitrary small nonnegative integer weights. Implemented and registered as [`dial_bucket_shortest_paths`](d/dial_bucket_shortest_paths/README.md) across all ten languages. Its bounded directed graph profile has `1<=N<=16`, `0<=M<=64`, source in `0..N-1`, edge weights `0..8`, and allows self-loops, parallel edges, and zero weights. The primary uses a fixed nine-slot cyclic exact-distance bucket ring with stale-entry checks; the independent oracle uses Floyd–Warshall. Input `[N,M,source,(u,v,w)*M]` has maximum valid/parseable lengths 195/196 i64 words; output is one little-endian i64 distance per vertex (`-1` if unreachable), maximum 128 bytes; workspace is 4096 bytes. The bounded maximum finite distance is 120. Candidate distinction: exact integer buckets process one distance at a time in O(M+N*C), unlike the general frontier in Dijkstra or delta-range closure in delta-stepping. Package README/RIGHTS, workload, primary/independent oracles, static inventory checker, and byte-output suite registration are present. ### Newton-doubling formal series reversion (reserved 2026-11-13)

Owner: root. Candidate `newton_compositional_inverse_fps` solves the same mathematical operation as `compositional_inverse_of_formal_power_series` but uses precision-doubling Newton correction of the composition equation, instead of its incremental coefficient recurrence. A repository README/catalog search found no benchmark port using this method. [FLINT's algorithm overview](https://github.com/flintlib/flint/blob/main/doc/src/algorithms/polynomials/composition.md) distinguishes Newton reversion from Lagrange inversion and identifies composition and series division as its core steps. The [Library Checker source repository](https://github.com/yosupo06/library-checker-problems) is Apache-2.0; sources are used for algorithm ideas only, with independent code and fixtures. Contract: `2<=N<=16`, field F_998244353, `f[0]=0`, `f[1]!=0`, and the first N coefficients of the inverse as little-endian i64. No execution is permitted while profiling continues.

The [bounded contract](n/newton_compositional_inverse_fps/README.md), Newton-doubling drafts in all ten languages, workload, Newton primary oracle, reference to the existing independently structured Lagrange oracle, static package inventory, and byte-output suite registration are now written. All remain unexecuted and require further review.

The generated verifier corpus compares the Newton oracle with the Lagrange reference across every supported series length and includes malformed-input precedence and output-capacity cases. This coverage is specified in source only and has not been run.

### Newton-doubling formal series reciprocal (reserved 2026-11-13)

Owner: root. Candidate `newton_reciprocal_fps` computes the same truncated multiplicative inverse as [`inv_of_formal_power_series`](i/inv_of_formal_power_series/README.md), but updates an approximation by `g <- g*(2-f*g)` at doubled precision. The existing package's ten benchmark ports use a coefficient-by-coefficient recurrence; its Newton implementation is an oracle, not a timed language port. [`newton_compositional_inverse_fps`](n/newton_compositional_inverse_fps/README.md) solves a different composition equation and uses a coefficient recurrence for its internal reciprocal. [FLINT's inversion documentation](https://flintlib.org/doc/nmod_poly/inv_series.html) describes both recurrence and Newton approaches. Use the mathematical description only; independently write implementations and fixtures. Contract: `[N,f_0,...,f_(N-1)]`, `1<=N<=64`, F_998244353 coefficients, `f_0!=0`, and N little-endian i64 coefficients; invalid input -1, null/short output -2. All work remains unexecuted.

The [contract](n/newton_reciprocal_fps/README.md), drafts in all ten languages, workload, package inventory checker, byte-output suite registration, and references to the existing local Newton and coefficient-recurrence oracles are written. All remain unexecuted and require further review.

### Reciprocal square root of a formal power series (reserved 2026-11-13)

Owner: root. The [`sqrt_of_formal_power_series`](s/sqrt_of_formal_power_series/README.md) ports compute a square root with a coefficient recurrence; [`newton_reciprocal_fps`](n/newton_reciprocal_fps/README.md) computes a multiplicative reciprocal. A local README and catalog search found no operation returning a series `g` with `f*g²=1`. The [FLINT reciprocal-square-root documentation](https://flintlib.org/doc/acb_poly/index.html) describes a division-free Newton update distinct from computing a square root and then a separate reciprocal. The bounded `newton_inverse_sqrt_fps` profile uses F_998244353, `1<=N<=64`, `f[0]=1`, and outputs the unique `g` with `g[0]=1` and `f*g²=1 mod x^N`. Using unit constant avoids a separate modular-root selection policy and makes the Newton kernel's contract explicit. Source descriptions are used for mathematical ideas only; code and fixtures are independently written.

The [contract](n/newton_inverse_sqrt_fps/README.md), drafts in all ten languages, workload, package checker, suite registration, independently validating Newton and derivative-recurrence oracles, and rights note are now written. All remain unexecuted and require further review.

The verifier source now also includes deterministic maximum-precision alternating-series and highest-degree correction cases. Static review changed the Mojo arrays to explicit zero fills; neither the checks nor the port has been executed.

### Seidel unweighted all-pairs distances (reserved 2026-11-13)

Owner: root. [`floyd_warshall`](f/floyd_warshall/README.md) uses weighted intermediate-vertex relaxation, [`johnson_shortest_paths`](j/johnson_shortest_paths/README.md) combines Bellman–Ford and Dijkstra, and [`apsp_min_plus_repeated_squaring`](a/apsp_min_plus_repeated_squaring/README.md) repeatedly squares a distance matrix over the min-plus semiring. [`all_shortest_paths_unweighted`](a/all_shortest_paths_unweighted/README.md) enumerates shortest paths for one pair rather than a distance matrix. A local README search found no timed Seidel distance algorithm, which instead recursively squares an unweighted undirected adjacency matrix over ordinary integers and recovers original distances by degree-weighted neighbor sums. [Seidel's original paper](https://www.mimuw.edu.pl/~mucha/teaching/alp2006/seidel92.pdf) identifies this method and its connected-graph condition. The bounded `seidel_unweighted_apsp` profile uses schoolbook integer matrix multiplication and does not claim fast-matrix complexity. Source is for mathematical ideas only; contract, fixtures, oracles, and code are independently written. No execution is allowed while profiling continues.

The [bounded contract](s/seidel_unweighted_apsp/README.md), drafts in all ten languages, workload, package checker, suite registration, independently validated Seidel and BFS oracle calculations, and rights note are now written. All remain unexecuted and require further review.

### Karger contraction cut trial (reserved 2026-11-13)

**In progress — root:** `karger_stein_recursive_contraction` reserves the
two-branch recursive contraction algorithm. The existing
[`karger_contraction_trial`](k/karger_contraction_trial/README.md) performs a
single path to two supervertices; [`stoer_wagner`](s/stoer_wagner/README.md)
uses exact maximum-adjacency phases. A deterministic rank tape defines the
recursive choices, and each small leaf solves its remaining graph exactly.
The contract, independent label-based reference, ten language ports, workload,
package checker, and scalar-suite integration are drafted. Mathematical idea:
[MIT recursive contraction notes](https://courses.csail.mit.edu/6.856/21/Notes/n19-mincut.html).
The workload includes a complete seven-vertex graph with different edge ranks
in the two branches, and paired bridge cases that distinguish whether the
second branch can improve on the first. The guide records the cost of repeated edge scanning.
No programs or checks were run.

Owner: root. [`stoer_wagner`](s/stoer_wagner/README.md) computes an exact global cut by deterministic maximum-adjacency phases, and [`randomized_contraction_edge_sampling`](r/randomized_contraction_edge_sampling/README.md) covers only an edge-sampling phase rather than complete contraction to two supervertices. [`karger_contraction_trial`](k/karger_contraction_trial/README.md) is a distinct bounded full contraction trial driven by supplied edge ranks; it does not guarantee a minimum cut. [Karger's original work](https://people.csail.mit.edu/karger/Papers/contract.pdf) supplies the mathematical idea only. Its ports and suite integration remain unexecuted and require verification.

The [CP-Algorithms Stoer–Wagner article](https://cp-algorithms.com/graph/stoer_wagner_mincut.html) describes the same maximum-adjacency contraction method as the existing package, so no duplicate is added. Static review of the Elisa port moved its reused vertex index into the enclosing phase and switched input access to a bounded view; the edit is uncompiled and untested.

The [bounded contract](k/karger_contraction_trial/README.md), drafts in all ten languages, workload, package checker, scalar suite wiring, independently validated disjoint-set and component-label oracle calculations, and rights note are written. All work remains unexecuted and needs verification.

Static review changed the Elisa Karger draft's fixed arrays to the syntax used by neighboring ports. The draft remains uncompiled and untested.
The scalar verifier source now also checks that reversing all undirected edge endpoints preserves each small-graph trial result. This check remains unexecuted.

The two confirmed distinct geometry candidates were assigned to `/root/multipoint_evaluation`. `sort_points_by_argument` and `count_points_in_triangle` now each have ten source ports, workload, docs, independent oracles, and shared byte-output suite registration. The official [`categories.toml`](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/yosupo06/library-checker-problems/master/categories.toml) lists the following 44 Data Structure tasks. This first pass compared every item with local package paths and the relevant README contracts. “Candidate” means the exact operation or algorithm still needs a deeper source and ABI comparison before assignment; a filename search alone is not treated as proof of absence. Two same-algorithm pairs were consolidated under canonical `sparse_table` and `fenwick_tree` benchmarks. The `associative_array` contract received a task-level comparison on 2026-11-11 and was marked already covered by the existing hash-map family. The `segment_add_get_min` and `static_range_mode_query` packages and suite registrations are complete.

### Offline range-distinct Fenwick sweep (reserved 2026-11-13)

After finding two HyperLogLog C3 entry points without `fn`, a static scan of
line-start function declarations found the same omission elsewhere. The first
271 affected C3 files have had `fn` added to those declarations, including
entry points and helpers. This covers the scanned line-start pattern only,
not every possible declaration form, and is not a compilation check. The
edited files have not been compiled or executed.

A follow-up scan for named return types found the C3
`smallest_enclosing_ball_3d` helpers. Their missing function keywords and
C-style local array declarations were corrected; the draft is uncompiled and
unexecuted.

The same static scan found C-style local arrays in the C3 noncommutative
potential union-find draft. Those declarations now use C3 array syntax, and
calls to pointer-taking helpers explicitly pass element addresses. Other C3
array declarations remain to be reviewed; no compiler or benchmark was run.

Static C3 array-syntax review also corrected local buffers in `word_count_julia`,
`word_patterns`, `rail_fence`, `rod_cutting`, and `hill_cipher_mod26_java`.
The word-count helper calls now pass explicit element addresses. These drafts
remain uncompiled and unexecuted.

The C3 Heat-3D and NPB MG V-cycle drafts also now use C3-style fixed-array
declarations. Their stencil helper calls already passed explicit element
addresses. These source edits have not been compiled or executed.

The C3 Heap permutation draft's local array declaration and conditional
expression were also adjusted to C3 syntax; its recursive permutation algorithm
is unchanged and unexecuted.

Further static C3 review converted local array declarations in the ugly-number,
prime-inverse-table, narcissistic-number, NPB EP, and RSA-byte-chunk drafts.
These changes remain uncompiled and unexecuted.

The C3 LCA, list-based queue, and football tie-break drafts now also use
C3-style local arrays; LCA and football helper calls pass explicit element
addresses. These edits have not been compiled or executed.

Static C3 array review also corrected local declarations in the Parboil
stencil, decimal-to-fraction, 2D prefix-sum, optimal-file-merging, and
largest/smallest-words drafts. No code was executed.

The C3 key-priority-queue and Problem 29 drafts now use C3-style local arrays;
the priority-queue helpers receive explicit element addresses. These edits
remain uncompiled and unexecuted.

The C3 mixed-keyword cipher and vertex-connectivity drafts now also use
C3-style local array declarations, as does the bounded `mcoloring` draft.
Their behavior remains unverified, and no compiler or benchmark was run.

The PolyBench LU and Olden Power C3 drafts now likewise use C3-style local
arrays. Olden Power's gradient helper calls already passed element addresses.
Neither draft has been compiled or executed.

Further C3 array-syntax corrections cover concave-gap alignment, largest square
area, largest divisible subset, line sweep, Lorentz transformation, and
Hamming code. The line-sweep and Lorentz drafts now also reject a null input
before dereferencing it. These source edits remain uncompiled and unexecuted.

The large-n first- and second-kind Stirling workloads now explicitly state and
exercise the existing `k<=n` input restriction. Both added cases are invalid
frames under the guides and ports; the fixture changes remain unexecuted.

Static q-binomial fixture review corrected `largest-profile-n-and-q-minus-one`:
its final query formerly used `k=17`, outside the documented bound of 16,
while expecting a successful zero result. The replacement uses `n=15,k=16`,
which exercises the same `k>n` result within the valid bounds. The expected
bytes are unchanged; this fixture has not been executed.

Static Elisa syntax review replaced remaining `InlineArray` declarations in
the q-binomial, discrete-logarithm, and three Stirling-number drafts with
fixed arrays. The discrete-logarithm arrays total 786432 bytes before any
compiler-specific padding, so its stack requirements remain a review item;
its ABI now also checks null before making a bounded input view.
The four q-binomial and Stirling drafts now use bounded input views; static
review also corrected mutable and local-variable declarations in q-binomial
and second-kind matrix exponentiation.
These changes have not been compiled or executed.

The Elisa SA-IS suffix-array draft now uses null checks and bounded input/output
views. The virtual-tree draft's ABI wrapper now uses reference null checks,
the repository export form, and an output view capped at its maximum frame.
Both remain uncompiled and unexecuted.

The Elisa `vertex_set_path_composite` draft's Mojo-style array and export
declarations have been converted to fixed arrays and bounded views. Static
review also initialized every heavy-child entry to its sentinel, including the
root, so a one-vertex tree does not repeatedly follow itself. The port remains
uncompiled and unexecuted and must not be treated as validated. Static review
confirmed the existing workload includes a singleton query and update, and the

Static review aligned `create_maximum_number`'s Elisa view-length calls with

The Elisa Two-Way string-matching draft now uses reference null checks and

An Elisa syntax pass corrected uppercase boolean literals in eight string,
graph, tree, and polynomial drafts. The games-on-graphs ABI wrapper also uses

compiled or executed.

The Elisa persistent range-kth and range-sort-composition drafts now use

set, and packed-bitset predecessor draft now read their validated ABI frames
through bounded views. Noncommutative union-find and predecessor also use

The Elisa persistent union-find, potential union-find, and aggregate queue and
deque drafts now read validated inputs through bounded views. Potential

Static Elisa review also bounded ABI input views in `point_set_range_frequency`

The existing zero-output handling for point frequency is preserved. These

`static_rectangle_add_rectangle_sum`, and
`dynamic_point_set_rectangle_affine_rectangle_sum`. The first now uses a

matching basename somewhere in each of C3, C++, Elisa, Mojo, Nim, Odin, Rust,
V, and Zig. This is only a source-presence comparison: it does not establish
suite registration, matching contracts, compilation, or behavioral correctness,
and it does not detect language-only packages without a C counterpart.
The reverse Mojo-to-C basename comparison found two extra names. The duplicate
`is` Mojo draft was removed in favor of `uint53_is` and its shared
`benchmarks/i/is` workload. The unregistered `job_scheduling_with_release_times`
Mojo draft and its orphaned workload/oracle reproduced the stable profit-first,
latest-free-slot procedure of [`job_scheduling_with_deadline`](j/job_scheduling_with_deadline/README.md),
with narrower bounds and different result encoding; the duplicate files were
removed. The retained README records why this release-time greedy procedure
does not always produce an optimal schedule. No execution was used.

**Implemented, statically reviewed — root:** `unit_job_release_deadline_weighted_matching` is a
distinct exact weighted unit-job scheduler. Unlike the retained deadline
heuristic, it may reassign previously accepted jobs through alternating paths;
unlike generic unweighted Kuhn matching, it orders jobs by weight and uses the
transversal-matroid independence test to maximize total weight. The proposed
scalar frame is `[n,(release,deadline,weight)*n]`, with `0<=n<=32`, inclusive
slots `0..31`, and weights `0..1000000`; invalid frames return `-1` and the
result is maximum total weight. Ten language implementations, a package guide, an
independent min-cost-flow reference, workload, rights note, and scalar runner
and verifier wiring exist. A package checker and a second, exhaustive small
reference are also present. The workload includes a maximum-length frame and
null input at the parser limit. Static review found matching validation,
weight ordering, augmenting-path state, and bounds across all ten ports. The
package remains uncompiled and unexecuted by design.
[Dekel and Sahni's scheduling paper](https://www.cise.ufl.edu/~sahni/papers/convexBipartite.pdf)
describes the weighted unit-job/convex-bipartite relationship; only the
algorithmic idea is used. The implementations are uncompiled and unexecuted by design.

## Encyclopedia of Algorithms Chapter 710: deterministic-threshold spread integrated (2026-11-18)

Reserve `deterministic_linear_threshold_spread` for the deterministic linear-threshold influence-computation procedure from Zaixin Lu, Weili Wu, Bin Fu, and Ding-Zhu Du, “Approximation and Inapproximation for the Influence Maximization Problem in Social Networks under Deterministic Linear Threshold Model,” §II, Algorithm 1, DOI [10.1109/ICDCSW.2011.33](https://doi.org/10.1109/ICDCSW.2011.33). The operation receives a directed weighted graph, fixed positive threshold per vertex, and seed set, then repeatedly adds incoming weight from each newly active vertex and activates a target once its accumulated sum reaches its threshold. The local [`influence_maximization_greedy_linear_threshold`](i/influence_maximization_greedy_linear_threshold/README.md) uses mutually exclusive randomized triggering-parent draws and then greedily selects a seed set; [`influence_maximization_greedy_live_edge`](i/influence_maximization_greedy_live_edge/README.md) replays IC live-edge worlds. Neither computes this deterministic fixed-threshold closure. The bounded profile uses `1<=n<=8`, at most 24 unique directed arcs, nonnegative integer weights and positive integer thresholds scaled to denominator 16, with total incoming weight at most 16 per vertex. It outputs each vertex's synchronous activation round (`-1` if never active), plus the number of nonempty activation waves. Ten clean-room language ports, primary queue reference, independent repeated-scan reference, bounded fixtures, provenance/rights, inventory, and `i64_array_bytes_output` runner/verifier plus catalog registration are complete under `benchmarks/d/deterministic_linear_threshold_spread/`. Sources are used for attribution and method semantics only; no code, prose, or fixtures are reused. No programs, tests, scripts, checkers, builds, compilers, profilers, or benchmarks were run.

## Encyclopedia of Algorithms Chapter 699: hypercube edge monotonicity tester integration (2026-11-18)

Completion status: ten ports, both references, workload, rights/provenance, inventory, and shared `i64_array_bytes_output` runner/verifier plus catalog registration are complete. The input limit is 130 valid words and 131 parseable words, including the trailing-data rejection frame. No executable checks were run.

Reserve `hypercube_edge_monotonicity_tester` for the chapter's hypercube edge tester, whose exact method is specified in Chakrabarty and Seshadhri, “Optimal Bounds for Monotonicity and Lipschitz Testing over Hypercubes and Hypergrids,” §1.1 and §2 ([arXiv:1204.0849](https://arxiv.org/abs/1204.0849); [ACM STOC 2013 paper](https://doi.org/10.1145/2488608.2488661)). It samples a uniformly random hypercube edge and checks the function values in increasing-coordinate order. No local package tests a truth table for coordinatewise monotonicity: [`monotonic_array`](m/monotonic_array/README.md) tests one-dimensional sequences for either nondecreasing or nonincreasing order, while [`monotone_chain`](m/monotone_chain/README.md) builds a geometric hull. The bounded deterministic replay profile accepts a Boolean truth table on `{0,1}^n`, `1<=n<=6`, plus `1<=q<=32` supplied `(vertex,coordinate)` pairs. A pair is interpreted as one uniform vertex and one uniform dimension, which induces the uniform undirected-edge distribution; the endpoints are canonicalized to bit-coordinate zero/one. Query and compare two values per sampled edge, stop at the first violation, and accept only if all q samples pass. Output is `[accept_bit, rounds_executed, oracle_query_calls]`, with two query calls per executed round including coincident/repeated query points. An arbitrary fixed tape and caller-chosen q do not claim the paper's soundness guarantee. Maximum frame is 130 i64 words, output is 24 bytes, and workspace is bounded to 1,024 bytes. Chapter source: Deeparnab Chakrabarty, “Monotonicity Testing,” *Encyclopedia of Algorithms*, Chapter 699, DOI [10.1007/978-1-4939-2864-4_699](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4939-2864-4_699). Ten language ports, references, workload, provenance/rights, inventory, and `i64_array_bytes_output` runner/verifier plus catalog integration are complete under `benchmarks/h/hypercube_edge_monotonicity_tester/`. No code, prose, or fixtures are reused. No programs, tests, scripts, checkers, builds, compilers, profilers, or benchmarks were run.

## Algorithm Archive chapter crosswalk (initial review 2026-10-29; summary rechecked 2026-11-16)

The [official chapter summary](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/algorithm-archivists/algorithm-archive/main/SUMMARY.md) was compared against local package names and README contracts. The Archive is an educational collection and several sections are introductions or incomplete notes rather than executable algorithms; these are marked separately so they do not become speculative benchmark requests.

| Archive chapter / algorithm | Local comparison | Decision / next action |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Iterated Function Systems / Barnsley Fern | [`barnsley_fern`](b/barnsley_fern/README.md) implements the four affine maps with an explicit deterministic sample tape. | Covered; the random source is projected into supplied choices to make the algorithm trace reproducible. |
| Data Structures; Stacks and Queues | The repository has stacks, queues, priority queues, trees, heaps, and persistent/dynamic structures with individual operation contracts. | Covered broadly; the chapter is a topic overview, not one additional data-structure algorithm. |
| Affine Transformations | [`affine_image_rotation`](a/affine_image_rotation/README.md), [`affine_converter`](a/affine_converter/README.md), and other geometry transforms cover selected affine operations. | No standalone named algorithm in the chapter; compare concrete transforms only when they specify a distinct operation. |
| Bit Logic | Bitwise operations and bitset-based algorithms are already represented across local packages. | Excluded as a language/representation tutorial rather than one benchmark procedure. |
| Taylor Series Expansion | [`maclaurin_series`](m/maclaurin_series/README.md) covers fixed-term sine/cosine sums; [`maclaurin`](m/maclaurin/README.md) covers the pinned error-threshold exponential/sine/cosine recurrence; [`exponential_function`](e/exponential_function/README.md) and [`trig_functions`](t/trig_functions/README.md) have their own fixed-term or tolerance-driven contracts. | The Archive page remains incomplete and only gives the generic expansion and a constant-acceleration kinematics illustration. It does not define the supplied function/derivative representation, truncation or stopping rule, numeric domain, or output contract for a general evaluator. With derivative coefficients supplied explicitly, the finite sum is polynomial evaluation after coefficient scaling; otherwise a new benchmark would need a separately specified function family. Classify the general chapter candidate as excluded/underspecified; do not claim that the specialized local series packages implement one universal Taylor evaluator. |
| Convolutions, 1D/2D Convolutions, Convolution Theorem | [`convolution`](c/convolution/README.md), [`convolution_fft`](c/convolution_fft/README.md), [`image_convolution`](i/image_convolution/README.md), [`sobel_filter`](s/sobel_filter/README.md), and related convolution variants cover direct and transform-based workloads, including the 2D chapter's Sobel-gradient operation. | Covered at the operation level; retain direct, FFT, circular, image, and specialized convolution algorithms where their computational behavior differs. |
| Box–Muller Transform: Cartesian form | No normal-sample transform package was found in the name/path inventory. | Confirmed distinct direct transform with no rejection loop; ten language ports, 90-digit Decimal oracle, bounded draw-tape workload, independent verifier oracle, and `float64_slice_io` suite registration are complete. |
| Box–Muller Transform: Marsaglia polar form | No polar or Cartesian normal-sampling transform package was found. | Confirmed distinct rejection-based normal transform; ten language ports, high-precision Decimal oracle, bounded deterministic tape workload, independent verifier oracle, and `float64_slice_io` suite registration are complete. |
| Rejection sampling: finite discrete target with supplied proposal | No general discrete rejection-sampling package or reservation was found. [`marsaglia_polar_normal`](m/marsaglia_polar_normal/README.md) uses a fixed two-dimensional polar proposal and circle test to return Gaussian pairs; [`weighted_random_sampling`](w/weighted_random_sampling/README.md) uses rational priority keys to select a weighted subset; neither samples a caller-supplied finite target distribution through a caller-supplied proposal/envelope. | Implemented and byte-output suite registered as [`discrete_rejection_sampling`](d/discrete_rejection_sampling/README.md): bounded finite-support rejection sampling with integer target/proposal weights, a computed integer envelope, and a fixed supplied draw tape. The Archive chapter motivates rejection/cost but is not a full sampler contract; the general accept/reject construction follows Devroye, *Non-Uniform Random Variate Generation*, Chapter II §3 (1986, DOI [10.1007/978-1-4613-8643-8_2](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4613-8643-8_2)). Ten ports use exact category-specific integer acceptance ranges, so the conditional acceptance law preserves the target probabilities without quantizing the draw threshold. An independent cumulative-table oracle, maximum-input/output fixtures, valid exhaustion case, malformed-tape checks, and capacity probes are included. Its state transition differs from the specialized Marsaglia polar transform and weighted-priority subset selection. Clean-room implementation only. No programs, tests, scripts, checkers, builds, compilers, or benchmarks were run. |
| Probability Distributions | The chapter covers several distribution concepts rather than a single sampling algorithm. | No single benchmark candidate; assess a specific sampler separately, with supplied random tapes where needed. |
| Tree Traversal | Local DFS and BFS packages cover recursive/iterative and queue/stack traversals for binary trees and general graphs. | Covered as a family; retain distinct traversal order and data-structure variants already present. |
| Euclidean Algorithm | Greatest-common-divisor and extended-Euclidean packages are present. | Covered; no duplicate subtraction/division variant unless it has a materially different measured procedure. |
| Monte Carlo | [`monte_carlo_integration`](m/monte_carlo_integration/README.md), [`monte_carlo_simulation`](m/monte_carlo_simulation/README.md), and pi-estimation packages cover bounded random-sample estimators. | Covered by distinct sampling/estimation profiles; a source-specific estimator should be compared before adding another Monte Carlo name. |
| Metropolis Algorithm | [`simulated_annealing`](s/simulated_annealing/README.md) changes temperature while searching for a low-scoring solution; [`metropolis_mcmc`](m/metropolis_mcmc/README.md) is a fixed-temperature trace with symmetric proposals. | The symmetric fixed-temperature sampler remains separate. [`metropolis_hastings_asymmetric_proposal`](m/metropolis_hastings_asymmetric_proposal/README.md) now covers caller-supplied asymmetric finite-state proposals with the Hastings reverse/forward correction, which the symmetric `metropolis_mcmc` contract does not include. It has ten language ports, exact independent references, bounded fixtures, and `i64_array_bytes_output` suite registration. The Algorithm Archive chapter names Metropolis–Hastings as an extension; semantics follow Hastings (1970), DOI [10.1093/biomet/57.1.97](https://doi.org/10.1093/biomet/57.1.97). |
| Matrix Methods; Gaussian Elimination | [`gaussian_elimination`](g/gaussian_elimination/README.md) covers no-pivot elimination on symmetric tridiagonal systems; [`gaussian_elimination_pivoting`](g/gaussian_elimination_pivoting/README.md) covers dense partial-pivot elimination. | The separate `gauss_elimination` package was removed as a duplicate C partial-pivot implementation; its source is cross-referenced to the retained dense pivoting package. The no-pivot and partial-pivot methods remain distinct. |
| Thomas Algorithm (tridiagonal matrix solver) | The existing [`gaussian_elimination`](g/gaussian_elimination/README.md) has a tridiagonal input restriction but uses generic dense elimination and back substitution. | Confirmed distinct: ten ports use the O(N) Thomas recurrence, with exact dense-rational oracle, residual validation, float64 byte-suite integration, and bounded diagonally dominant workloads. |

| Split-Operator Method | [`split_operator_imaginary_time`](s/split_operator_imaginary_time/README.md) already implements the imaginary-time Strang-split position/momentum/position recurrence, with radix-2 FFT ports in all ten supported languages and a direct-DFT oracle. | Covered by the existing package; keep it as the canonical split-operator benchmark and do not add a duplicate. |
| Data Compression; Huffman Encoding | [`nbench_huffman_compression`](n/nbench_huffman_compression/README.md) implements full Huffman tree construction, bitstream encoding, and round-trip decoding. | The weighted-cost-only package was removed as a duplicate projection of this same greedy Huffman construction; no further Huffman implementation is needed. |
| Flood Fill | [`flood_fill`](f/flood_fill/README.md) uses a LIFO stack; [`flood_fill_breadth_first`](f/flood_fill_breadth_first/README.md) uses a FIFO queue for the same eight-connected replacement. The final image is identical, while frontier order and memory traffic differ. | Both DFS and BFS profiles are covered, with separate bounded suite entries. |
| Computus / Gauss's Easter Algorithm | [`easter`](e/easter/README.md) and [`gauss_easter`](g/gauss_easter/README.md) implement Gregorian Easter-date algorithms; [`julian_easter`](j/julian_easter/README.md) uses the Julian calendar formula. | Covered; retain calendar/formula variants as distinct only where the calendar or algorithm actually differs. |
| Approximate Counting Algorithm (Morris counter) | [`morris_approximate_counter`](m/morris_approximate_counter/README.md) implements the base-2 state transition with a supplied uniform draw tape. Exact counters and `morrisinorder` (tree traversal) are different procedures; HyperLogLog uses hash-register maxima rather than the Morris transition. | Covered: ten ports, deterministic draw-tape oracle/workload, strict metadata and fixture validation, boundary/malformed/null/max-tape verifier probes, byte-output runner/verifier registration, and README entry are present. The workload reports compressed state and decoded estimate without a deterministic error guarantee. |
| Plotting, Domain Coloring, Computer Graphics | Plotting is an output/workflow guide; [`domain_coloring`](d/domain_coloring/README.md) covers the named complex-plane rendering kernel. The open Computer Graphics overview mentions Canny edge detection as a planned topic; [`sobel_filter`](s/sobel_filter/README.md) covers a Sobel gradient profile and [`canny`](c/canny/README.md) covers a bounded grayscale Canny pipeline. | The overview remains open-ended and supplies no additional rasterizer or edge-detection contract. Canny is already implemented and is distinct from Sobel's gradient output; mark it implemented rather than a new gap. Exclude plotting/environment behavior and defer any future rendering method until a concrete procedure is specified. |

## Algorithm Archive full-index audit (2026-11-18)

The current [official chapter summary](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/algorithm-archivists/algorithm-archive/main/SUMMARY.md)
was rechecked against the local crosswalk above and repository package
contracts. No defensible new bounded algorithm package emerged. The
[Sierpinski IFS chaos game](https://www.algorithm-archive.org/contents/IFS/IFS.html)
uses a supplied sequence of choices to iterate affine maps, the same update
pattern already represented by [`barnsley_fern`](b/barnsley_fern/README.md);
its exhaustive branching formulation is represented by
[`sierpinski_triangle`](s/sierpinski_triangle/README.md). The
[integer-multiplication-as-convolution page](https://www.algorithm-archive.org/contents/convolutions/multiplication/multiplication.html)
explains grade-school digit products and carry normalization, already covered
by [`big_integer_multiply`](b/big_integer_multiply/README.md), while direct
and transform-based convolution primitives are separately present. The other
complete named procedures map to packages in the crosswalk; overview or
incomplete chapters remain excluded until they provide a distinct bounded
procedure. Only algorithm descriptions were consulted; no source code, prose,
examples, or fixtures were reused. No programs, tests, scripts, checkers,
builds, compilers, profilers, or benchmarks were run.

## PARSEC and SPLASH-2 application crosswalk (updated 2026-11-12)

These are algorithm-level dispositions, not claims that a bounded local kernel reproduces a parallel suite's full application, input set, or score. PARSEC's 13 application names are listed in its [suite characterization](https://www.cs.princeton.edu/techreports/2010/890.pdf); the SPLASH-2 source mirror lists Barnes, Cholesky, FFT, FMM, LU, Ocean, Radiosity, Radix, Raytrace, Water-Nsquared, and Water-Spatial.

| Source candidate | Repository comparison | Decision |
| --- | --- | --- |
| PARSEC `blackscholes` | [`black_scholes_option_price`](b/black_scholes_option_price/README.md) computes the European call/put Black–Scholes formulas. | Already present/duplicate at the algorithm level; no second option-pricing package for the same closed-form formula. |
| PARSEC `bodytrack` | [`rodinia_particlefilter_naive`](r/rodinia_particlefilter_naive/README.md) benchmarks one ordinary likelihood/normalization/resampling transition; PARSEC uses a multi-layer annealed particle filter for articulated 3-D pose tracking. | Confirmed distinct: [`bodytrack_annealed_particle_filter`](b/bodytrack_annealed_particle_filter/README.md) implements bounded likelihood annealing, weighted resampling, supplied pose-shock transitions, and a final weighted estimate in ten languages. Two independently structured oracles, a static package checker, and `i64_array_bytes_output` registration are present; image-feature extraction and parallel scheduling remain outside the profile. See the [PARSEC characterization](https://www.cs.princeton.edu/techreports/2010/890.pdf) and [annealed-particle-filter paper](https://www.robots.ox.ac.uk/~lav/Papers/deutscher_etal_cvpr2000/deutscher_etal_cvpr2000.html). |
| PARSEC `canneal` | [`simulated_annealing`](s/simulated_annealing/README.md) already covers the simulated-annealing search algorithm. | Already present/duplicate at the algorithm level; objective and input graph are profile data. |
| PARSEC `dedup` | No single package represents the complete chunking, hashing, compression, and storage pipeline. The report identifies content-defined fragmentation as a separable kernel. [`rabin_karp`](r/rabin_karp/README.md) searches for a pattern rather than returning fingerprint-selected chunk boundaries; fixed-size chunking and the turnstile singleton fingerprint also perform different operations. | The compound parallel pipeline remains outside the single-call ABI. The distinct bounded profile [`rabin_content_defined_chunking`](r/rabin_content_defined_chunking/README.md) computes chunk boundaries with a four-byte GF(2) sliding fingerprint and low-bit trigger. Its ten ports now remove the outgoing byte contribution before shifting; rolling and independent per-window references, fixtures, provenance, static inventory checking, and byte-output suite wiring are present. Sources: [PARSEC report](https://www.cs.princeton.edu/techreports/2010/890.pdf) and [USENIX sliding-fingerprint study](https://www.usenix.org/legacy/events/usenix04/tech/general/full_papers/policroniades/policroniades_html/index.html). No source code or prose was copied and nothing was executed. |
| PARSEC `facesim` | The source metadata names Verlet position updates and a model-specific Newton solve for quasistatic constraints; local [`verlet`](v/verlet/README.md), [`damped_oscillator`](d/damped_oscillator/README.md), and [`conjugate_gradient`](c/conjugate_gradient/README.md) cover adjacent reusable procedures. | Excluded from implementation for now: the source metadata gives no constraint residual, Jacobian, material law, or element-update contract for a faithful bounded Newton kernel. The Newton system is model-specific, and inventing mechanics equations would not be an honest port. Its source tree has a BSD-style license, but no upstream code is reused. See the [PARSEC characterization](https://www.cs.princeton.edu/techreports/2010/890.pdf), [Facesim metadata](https://github.com/cirosantilli/parsec-benchmark/blob/master/pkgs/apps/facesim/src/README), and [source license](https://github.com/cirosantilli/parsec-benchmark/blob/master/pkgs/apps/facesim/src/LICENSE). |
| PARSEC `ferret` | The application combines image-feature extraction, indexing, similarity search, and query processing. [`intensity_based_segmentation`](i/intensity_based_segmentation/README.md) assigns labels using independent intensity thresholds rather than adjacency-ordered merges. Existing [`min_cost_max_flow`](m/min_cost_max_flow/README.md) and [`minimum_cost_b_flow`](m/minimum_cost_b_flow/README.md) cover general flow methods; earth mover distance is a transport objective, not by itself a separate solver. | The compound pipeline is excluded from the single-call ABI. The distinct kernel [`statistical_region_merging_table`](s/statistical_region_merging_table/README.md) implements ordered grayscale region merging with caller-supplied squared size bounds and a deterministic tie rule. It has ten ports, a sorted-edge DSU primary reference, a flat-relabeling exact-rational independent reference, workload, rights note, static package checking, and byte-output suite wiring. Statistical guarantees are only claimed when the caller supplies bounds from the paper's formula. Sources: [Nock and Nielsen's paper](https://www.lix.polytechnique.fr/~nielsen/pdf/2004-StatisticalRegionMerging-PAMI.pdf) and [PARSEC report](https://www.cs.princeton.edu/techreports/2010/890.pdf). No source code or prose copied; nothing was executed. |
| PARSEC `fluidanimate` | [`splash2_water_nsquared`](s/splash2_water_nsquared/README.md) models a molecular pair potential; it is not smoothed-particle hydrodynamics. | Confirmed distinct: [`fluidanimate_sph`](f/fluidanimate_sph/README.md) adds a bounded one-step SPH density/pressure/viscosity acceleration profile with ten ports, pairwise and target-wise oracles, package rights/checker, and `i64_array_bytes_output` runner/verifier registration. See the [PARSEC characterization](https://www.cs.princeton.edu/techreports/2008/811.pdf) and [source mirror](https://gem5.googlesource.com/public/gem5-resources/+/refs/heads/develop/src/parsec/disk-image/parsec/parsec-benchmark/pkgs/apps/fluidanimate/src/). |
| PARSEC `freqmine` | [`frequent_pattern_growth`](f/frequent_pattern_growth/README.md) implements FP-tree conditional-pattern growth and counts frequent itemsets. | Already present/duplicate at the algorithm level; PARSEC's larger transaction workload and parallel schedule are profile differences. |
| PARSEC `raytrace` | [`freebench_distray`](f/freebench_distray/README.md) already covers ray generation, intersections, shading, shadows, and reflections in a bounded scene. | Already present/duplicate ray-tracing algorithm; PARSEC's full scene and parallel renderer are not a separate algorithm. |
| PARSEC `streamcluster` | [`rodinia_streamcluster_pgain`](s/rodinia_streamcluster_pgain/README.md) implements the same squared-distance facility-opening `pgain` step: evaluate reassignment savings and center-closing costs, then commit only when the objective decreases. | Covered/duplicate: PARSEC's `pgain` is the same measured local-search move. Stream input, initialization, and repeated scheduling change the surrounding application workload, not the benchmarked algorithm, so do not add a second package. See the [PARSEC characterization](https://www.cs.princeton.edu/techreports/2010/890.pdf). |
| PARSEC `swaptions` | [`black_scholes_option_price`](b/black_scholes_option_price/README.md) is a closed-form European-option formula; it does not price a swaption under a simulated LIBOR market model. | Confirmed distinct: [`hjm_forward_path`](m/hjm_forward_path/README.md) implements bounded triangular HJM path generation from explicit shocks in ten languages, with primary and independent drift oracles and `float64_slice_io` runner/verifier wiring. The portfolio scheduler and payoff aggregation remain outside this algorithm profile; see the [PARSEC characterization](https://www.cs.princeton.edu/techreports/2010/890.pdf) and [source mirror](https://github.com/cirosantilli/parsec-benchmark/tree/master/pkgs/apps/swaptions/src). |

### Sparse supernodal Cholesky contract work (2026-11-13)

Reserved candidate: [`sparse_supernodal_cholesky`](s/sparse_supernodal_cholesky/README.md). The bounded contract specifies an SPD matrix, a supplied filled lower-triangular bitmask pattern, and a partition of consecutive columns into supernodes for `n<=8`. It requires update closure, dense diagonal blocks, and rectangular off-diagonal panels. The right-looking block/panel oracle and dense scalar reference now validate frames separately; the primary uses dense scratch for its oracle model. A workload, sparse-storage ports in all ten languages, and byte-output suite registration are present. The supplied pattern must contain every location needed by updates; fill is not silently dropped. All work remains unexecuted and requires further static review.

Static fixture review corrected the Cholesky `partial_panel` mask: it now
passes fill closure while violating rectangular-panel completeness, instead
of being rejected by the earlier fill check. The updated fixture and all
implementations remain unexecuted.

This profile isolates sparse numerical factorization with supplied symbolic analysis. It does not claim to reproduce SPLASH-2's ordering, symbolic analysis, scheduling, or performance results. The published [right-looking supernodal study](https://arxiv.org/html/2409.13090v1) describes these numerical stages and identifies its article as CC BY-NC-ND 4.0; use mathematical ideas only and independently write the contract, fixtures, and code. The [SPLASH-2 repository](https://github.com/staceyson/splash2) is used for suite identification, not as a code or fixture source. Owner: root; other agents should not edit this candidate without coordination.

The suite corpus now also specifies generated positive-definite dense factors under singleton and full-block partitions, sparse chain factors with absent structural slots, comparisons between the two oracle calculations, capacity boundaries, and invalid-input precedence cases. This is source-level coverage only; none of the corpus or ports has been executed.
| SPLASH-2 `Raytrace` | [`freebench_distray`](f/freebench_distray/README.md) covers surface ray tracing at one-pixel scope. | Already present/duplicate surface-ray algorithm; the volume-rendering path is a separate application and is listed below. |
| SPLASH-2 source mirror `Volrend` | Surface-ray tracing in [`freebench_distray`](f/freebench_distray/README.md) is a separate operation. | Confirmed distinct: [`splash2_volrend_raymarch`](s/splash2_volrend_raymarch/README.md) is a bounded clean-room voxel sampler with opacity-support pyramid, trilinear interpolation, front-to-back compositing, and early termination. Ten ports, two independent oracle structures, package metadata, and byte-output suite wiring are present; it is not a reproduction of the protected renderer. |
| SPLASH-2 `Water-Nsquared` | No molecular-water direct all-pairs interaction kernel was found; gravity N-body packages use a different force law. | Confirmed distinct bounded pair-scan profile: ten ports use a clean-room rational potential/force contract, strict cutoff, and signed fixed-point accumulation. It is registered in the byte-output suite with a direct-pair oracle and independent target-wise oracle. This is an algorithmic projection, not a physical force-field or timestep reproduction. See [SPLASH-2](https://github.com/staceyson/splash2) and the [benchmark contract](s/splash2_water_nsquared/README.md). |

### PARSEC and SPLASH-2 kernel-level follow-up (2026-11-20)

This follow-up compares the named stages and operations in the suite descriptions against package contracts, rather than treating application names as kernels. It adds the Facesim element-force coverage and checks Ferret's individual stages, Dedup's five stages, Fluidanimate's numerical and spatial work, VIPS operations, and SPLASH-2's kernel/application split. Sources are the [PARSEC technical report](https://www.cs.princeton.edu/techreports/2010/890.pdf) and the [SPLASH-2 source mirror and suite notes](https://github.com/staceyson/splash2); the published [SPLASH-2 characterization](https://doi.org/10.1145/223982.223990) provides the application-level method descriptions.

## Implementation and attribution rules

- Compare the mathematical operation, input/output contract, and relevant behavior before calling two names duplicates. Keep different algorithms or materially different computational tasks separate.
- Write clean-room implementations from algorithm descriptions. Do not copy submissions, tests, problem statements, or other source text. Link the discovery source and record applicable license or terms before reusing any material.
- Record each new candidate here before assigning it. Mark a candidate implemented only after all ten current language ports and suite registration are present; static presence is not runtime validation.
- While compiler profiling is underway, all work remains static. Do not run programs, tests, builds, compilers, benchmarks, or repository scripts.

The task statements specify factorial, derangement, Bell, binomial-prefix, partition, Stirling, subset-count, subsequence-count, and constrained increasing-sequence outputs; matching a number name alone is not treated as algorithm coverage.

The q-binomial task statement fixes T cases with shared prime m and q, requires 0 <= q < m and 0 <= n,k < min(m,N_MAX), and asks for the Gaussian binomial coefficient modulo m. This local profile caps T at 16, m at 31, and n,k at 16; it retains the prime and range rules while using G(n,k)=G(n-1,k)+q^(n-k)G(n-1,k-1) modulo m. The bounded profile is not a claim to meet the official large-N limits. See [the official q-binomial task](https://github.com/yosupo06/library-checker-problems/blob/master/enumerative_combinatorics/q_binomial_coefficient_prime_mod/task.md) and [its bounds](https://github.com/yosupo06/library-checker-problems/blob/master/enumerative_combinatorics/q_binomial_coefficient_prime_mod/info.toml).

The primary precomputes p-adic factorial valuations and p-free factorial parts, then inverts only p-free units; an independent Pascal recurrence computes the same bounded coefficients without modular division. Maximum valid input is 67 i64 words, maximum parseable input is 68 words, output is 128 bytes, and reserved workspace is 2560 bytes. Ten language ports, workload, package README/RIGHTS, and static inventory checker are present. ## Encyclopedia of Algorithms Chapter 715 package: minimum-weight convex polygon triangulation integrated (2026-11-18)

Implement `convex_polygon_minimum_weight_triangulation` as a bounded package
for the minimum-total-diagonal-weight objective in Chapter 715, restricted to strictly convex
polygons where every chord is legal. The benchmark supplies bounded
nonnegative integer weights for each internal diagonal, isolating the
chapter's additive triangulation DP from coordinate generation and distance
arithmetic. This is distinct from the local
[`convex_polygon_minimax_length_triangulation`](c/convex_polygon_minimax_length_triangulation/README.md),
which minimizes the longest edge, and from the max-min-length, angle, height,
slope, and eccentricity packages listed above. The bounded ABI accepts
`[n,(w_ij for internal diagonals i<j in lexicographic order)]`, `3<=n<=10`,
weights `0..1000`, and returns the minimum sum of the `n-3` selected diagonal
weights as an i64 scalar. The polygon has `n(n-3)/2` internal diagonals, so at
most 36 input words are valid (37 parseable), the
score is at most 7,000, and workspace is bounded to 2,048 bytes. The primary
is the Gilbert–Klincsek interval dynamic program with `O(n^3)` transitions;
the independent reference exhaustively enumerates Catalan triangulations and
scores their diagonal sets. Ten clean-room ports, workload, provenance/rights,
and static inventory are present under
`benchmarks/c/convex_polygon_minimum_weight_triangulation/`; the shared
`i64_array_scalar` runner/verifier and root catalog are integrated. Sources:
Tiow-Seng Tan, *Encyclopedia of Algorithms*,
Chapter 715, [DOI 10.1007/978-1-4939-2864-4_715](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4939-2864-4_715),
and G. T. Klincsek, “Minimal triangulations of polygonal domains,” *Annals of
Discrete Mathematics* 9 (1980), 121–123, [DOI
10.1016/S0167-5060(08)70044-X](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0167-5060(08)70044-X).
Only the mathematical method is used; no source code, prose, or fixtures are
reused. No programs, tests, scripts, checkers, builds, compilers, profilers,
or benchmarks were run.

| --- | --- | --- |
| [Multiple knapsack — monotone queue optimization](https://cp-algorithms.com/dynamic_programming/knapsack.html#monotone-queue-optimization) | [`knapsack_zero_one_tabulation`](k/knapsack_zero_one_tabulation/README.md) permits each item once and updates capacity in descending order. [`unbounded_knapsack`](u/unbounded_knapsack/README.md) permits unlimited reuse and follows an unbounded recurrence. Local FPTAS and greedy packages implement approximation or policy profiles; no bounded-multiplicity exact DP or residue-class monotone queue is present. | Implemented as `bounded_knapsack_monotone_queue` in `i64_array_scalar`, with ten language ports, two oracles, package docs, bounded fixtures, and scalar-suite registration. Input `[capacity,type_count,(weight,value,count)*type_count]`, `0<=capacity<=64`, `0<=type_count<=16`, weights `1..16`, values `0..100`, and multiplicities `0..16`; exact valid/parseable lengths are 50/51 i64 values. Return the maximum value under the capacity limit, or `-1` for malformed input. The primary snapshots the previous capacity DP for each item type and processes each residue class modulo its weight with a sliding maximum deque over `old[r+x*w]-x*value`, expiring candidates older than the multiplicity window; complexity is O(type_count*capacity) time and O(capacity) space. The independent oracle directly enumerates each permitted copy count in a two-row DP. Bounds keep results within signed 64-bit range. Source: CP-Algorithms, “Knapsack Problem,” Multiple Knapsack / Monotone Queue Optimization, CC BY-SA 4.0; algorithm description only, clean-room implementations. |

## CP-Algorithms Pollard p−1 factorization reservation (2026-11-13)

| Algorithm | Local contract comparison | Reservation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [Integer factorization — Pollard's p−1 method](https://cp-algorithms.com/algebra/factorization.html#pollards-p-1-method) | Local [`pollard`](p/pollard/README.md), [`pollard_rho_python`](p/pollard_rho_python/README.md), [`pollard_rho_java`](p/pollard_rho_java/README.md), [`pollard_rho_rust`](p/pollard_rho_rust/README.md), and [`pollards_rho_factorizing`](p/pollards_rho_factorizing/README.md) use polynomial walks and Floyd/Brent cycle detection. Trial division and sieve packages test divisibility directly. No package exploits a prime factor whose predecessor is smooth by modular exponentiation and a gcd. | Implemented as [`pollard_p_minus_one_factorization`](p/pollard_p_minus_one_factorization/README.md) in `i64_array_scalar`, registered in the shared scalar runner and verifier. Input `[N,B,A]` with `2<=N<=1,000,000,000`, `2<=B<=64`, and `1<=A<N`; exact valid length is 3 and parseable length is 4. If `gcd(A,N)>1`, return that proper divisor. Otherwise, for each prime `q<=B` in increasing order, let `e=q^floor(log_q B)`, update `x=x^e mod N`, and compute `g=gcd(|x-1|,N)`: continue for `g=1`, return `g` for `1<g<N`, and return 0 on `g=N` or after all stages. Malformed input returns `-1`; valid failure returns 0. Modular products fit signed 64-bit because `N<=10^9`; workspace is 1024 bytes. Primary uses successive maximal-prime-power modular exponentiation; independent oracle uses a direct big-integer cumulative exponent and Python modular powers at each stage. Ten ports, workload, README/RIGHTS, and package-local static inventory checker are present. Source: [CP-Algorithms — Pollard's p−1 method](https://cp-algorithms.com/algebra/factorization.html#pollards-p-1-method), CC BY-SA 4.0; algorithm description only. Clean-room implementation. |
