## Bitap duplicate audit and BNDM candidate (2026-11-13)

The former `bitap_exact_match_31` and [`bitap_string_match`](b/bitap_string_match/README.md) packages used the same first-match shift-OR recurrence and lowercase-ASCII input format. The latter accepts patterns up to 63 characters, covering the former's 31-character domain. The narrower duplicate was removed, and its C# source remains recorded against the retained package. The 31-character rejection boundary is no longer a separate benchmark contract.

[Backward Nondeterministic DAWG Matching (BNDM)](https://users.dcc.uchile.cl/~gnavarro/abstracts/cpm98.html) is a distinct candidate: it scans each alignment backward with a bit-parallel suffix automaton and skips alignments, unlike the retained forward shift-OR Bitap and the existing Horspool and Two-Way searches. A path and content search found no previous BNDM package. [`backward_nondeterministic_dawg_match`](b/backward_nondeterministic_dawg_match/README.md) has a contract, two references, workload, ten language drafts, source inventory checker, and scalar runner/verifier integration. Verifier source covers exhaustive short binary inputs, 31/32/63-bit boundaries, maximum frame, and null pointers. The drafts and integration remain uncompiled and unexecuted.

## Backward oracle matching reservation (2026-11-13)

The [factor oracle](https://citeseerx.ist.psu.edu/document?doi=4799c88ba0bd0626f9e4916ef3f530e2c8e677bf&repid=rep1&type=pdf) of Allauzen, Crochemore, and Raffinot supplies a compact automaton for backward oracle matching (BOM). It differs from BNDM's bit-parallel nondeterministic suffix automaton and from the bad-character, prefix-function, and critical-factorization matchers already in the catalog. The catalog's Go `bom` source contains only commented-out code and is not an implementation. A local path/content search found no implemented factor-oracle matcher. [`backward_oracle_match`](b/backward_oracle_match/README.md) has a contract, two references, ten language drafts, workload, package inventory checker, and scalar runner/verifier integration. Source-specified cases include exhaustive short binary inputs, long patterns, maximum frames and null pointers. All drafts and integration remain uncompiled and unexecuted; no upstream code or prose was copied.

Static source review corrected the initial suffix-state shifting draft to the factor-oracle BOM rule: when a transition is missing, shift the window past the failed text position. The missing transition proves the examined substring is not a pattern factor, so no skipped window can match. This rule and the distinction from suffix-oracle matching follow Raffinot's [factor-oracle seminar description](https://algo.inria.fr/seminars/sem99-00/raffinot.html). The Go source remains excluded as source code despite the independent algorithm mapping. Verifier source now also specifies exhaustive short ternary inputs and checks long-pattern and maximum-frame agreement between references; those checks remain unexecuted.

## Wavelet matrix reservation (2026-11-13)

The existing [`wavelet_tree`](w/wavelet_tree/README.md) partitions each node's value interval separately and stores node-local prefix counts. Claude and Navarro's [wavelet matrix](https://users.dcc.uchile.cl/~gnavarro/ps/spire12.4.pdf) instead stable-partitions each complete level globally and remaps positions through level-wide zero counts and rank arrays. This is a materially different representation and construction despite supporting the same queries. A local filename/content search found no wavelet-matrix package. [`wavelet_matrix`](w/wavelet_matrix/README.md) has the same bounded rank, quantile, and range-count contract as the existing tree. Ten language drafts, two references, workload, inventory checker, and scalar runner/verifier wiring are present. Verifier source specifies exhaustive small sequences, prefix ranks, maximum frames and null inputs; workload source includes extreme values and ignored fields. The paper supplies algorithmic ideas only; code and fixtures are independently authored. All drafts and checks remain uncompiled and unexecuted.

## XOR filter reservation (2026-11-13)

Graf and Lemire's [XOR filter](https://arxiv.org/abs/1912.08258) builds a static approximate-membership structure by peeling a three-way hash graph and assigning XOR fingerprints in reverse peel order. Local [`bloom_filter`](b/bloom_filter/README.md) sets bits online, while [`hash_map_cuckoo_hashing`](h/hash_map_cuckoo_hashing/README.md) is an exact relocation-based map. A local path/content search found no XOR filter. [`xor_filter_peeling`](x/xor_filter_peeling/README.md) uses caller-supplied slot triples and fingerprints, deterministic queue order, explicit peel failure, and membership queries; supplied hashes isolate construction without claiming randomized error guarantees. Ten language drafts, two references, workload, inventory checker, and scalar runner/verifier wiring are present. Verifier source specifies small graphs, slot permutations, no-false-negative checks, maximum frames, and null inputs. The research description supplies algorithmic ideas only. All drafts and checks remain uncompiled and unexecuted.

## Enumerative bitvector reservation (2026-11-13)

The local [`rank_select_bitstring`](r/rank_select_bitstring/README.md) stores plain 8-bit blocks with prefix counts and scans the bits. The RRR family, described by Raman, Raman and Rao in [succinct indexable dictionaries](https://arxiv.org/abs/0705.0552), represents each block by its one-count class and its rank among same-class bit patterns. [`rrr_class_offset_rank_select`](r/rrr_class_offset_rank_select/README.md) is a bounded class/offset construction and rank/select workload preserving the existing bitstring query contract. Ten language drafts, two references, workload, inventory checker, and byte-output runner/verifier integration are present; verifier source covers all byte patterns, partial blocks, maximum frames, capacity errors, and null pointers. The fixed-size representation and decoding scans do not claim the original succinct-space or constant-time bounds. A local path/content search found no prior RRR profile. Algorithm descriptions only; independently authored code and fixtures. All drafts and checks remain uncompiled and unexecuted.

## Lossy Counting reservation (2026-11-13)

Manku and Motwani's [Lossy Counting](https://www.vldb.org/conf/2002/S10P03.pdf) tracks each retained item's estimated count and bucket-based error and prunes at bucket boundaries. Local [`misra_gries_summaries`](m/misra_gries_summaries/README.md) decrements all counters on overflow, and [`space_saving_frequent_items`](s/space_saving_frequent_items/README.md) replaces a minimum counter; neither uses this bucket pruning. The retained guide now explicitly records empty-input and null-output behavior and lists its Mojo draft alongside the other nine ports. Harness constants statically accommodate the largest specified frame and output; runtime behavior remains unverified.

The [Sticky Sampling](https://www.vldb.org/conf/2002/S10P03.pdf) frequent-item algorithm was identified as a distinct streaming profile. The initial filename and coverage-ledger search found no package by that name; its changing sampling rate and counter thinning differ from deterministic Lossy Counting and from reservoir sampling. The subsequent reservation and current draft coverage are recorded below.

The original paper's section 4.1 describes sampling absent items at a changing rate and, at each rate change, reducing existing counters using independent fair coin tosses until a success or counter deletion. Its phase lengths grow geometrically. A replayable benchmark must specify draw consumption and ordering for both admission and thinning, including deletion and exact phase boundaries; arbitrary supplied draws do not by themselves establish the paper's probabilistic guarantee. The paper's first page permits certain noncommercial copying under conditions and reserves other copying, so use mathematical ideas only and independently author all code, fixtures, and prose.

Reserved [`sticky_sampling_summary`](s/sticky_sampling_summary/README.md): the bounded contract specifies a finite alphabet, an explicit draw tape, ascending-item thinning order, exact draw consumption and a sorted counter snapshot. The current package has two reference drafts, fixtures, ten language drafts, an inventory checker, and byte-output runner/verifier wiring. These are unexecuted drafts; static and runtime verification remain outstanding. Do not duplicate the ports.

The package now also has a phase-oriented independent reference and a C implementation draft. The two references and C port are unexecuted; nine ports, fixtures, inventory checker, and suite integration remain outstanding.

Static review found that `square_free_factor_list` could return a duplicate
result before checking a later invalid element. All ten language drafts now
validate the input first, and the contract and workload record that precedence.
The set-based oracle and scalar runner/verifier wiring are drafted. The Elisa,
V, and Zig drafts also received nonempty-null guards; Elisa uses a bounded view
internally. These changes remain uncompiled and unexecuted.

Draft runner and verifier wiring now checks `square_free_factor_list` against that oracle and includes duplicate-before-invalid and length-boundary cases. It has not been executed; build and harness integration still require validation.

Static tracing confirmed that the shared build selects the workload's declared scalar model and resolves the matching source by name. The verifier now checks fixture metadata and oracle results and defines additional bounded generated cases. All integration remains unexecuted.

Duplicate review compared `square_free_factor_list` with `contains_duplicate`: their results are complementary, but their pairwise-scan and heapsort-and-scan implementations have materially different computational behavior. Both are retained with reciprocal contract links and complexity notes.

Static contract review added complexity descriptions to `sum_of_squares_bin_packing`, `shortest_elapsed_time_first`, `ski_rental_deterministic`, and `sensor_energy_balance_estimator_trace`. No project code was executed.

Static review found a `slicing_floorplan_stockmeyer` orientation tie bug: a dominated child can become dimension-equal at an ancestor, losing a lexicographically better mask. Added a concrete expected-output fixture and documented that the primary oracle and ports require a tie-preserving fix. Also corrected the SPLASH-2 water V source link. No code or tests were run.

The nine existing `slicing_floorplan_stockmeyer` ports and primary oracle now retain dimension-dominated candidates when their orientation mask is lexicographically better. The contract and workload describe this tie-preserving pruning. The change and regression fixture remain uncompiled and untested.

Static review added the transposed floorplan tie case, updated the oracle-method metadata, and documented bounded merge complexity. Neither fixture nor any implementation was executed.

The `slicing_floorplan_stockmeyer` profile now also has a Mojo draft implementing the tie-preserving candidate recurrence. It has not been compiled or run.

Confirmed distinct, implementation drafts unverified: [CP-Algorithms' ascending tree traversal](https://github.com/cp-algorithms/cp-algorithms-aux/blob/7a28ec7ac05eabf2ceeed1778e2b2110a1e1c022/cp-algo/tree/ascending_dfs.hpp)
uses degree-based leaf removal and an XOR of incident edge IDs to recover each
remaining parent edge. Existing `depth_first_search` explores from the root;
`prufer_code` removes leaves in priority order to emit a Prüfer code. The
[`xor_leaf_tree_traversal`](x/xor_leaf_tree_traversal/README.md) package records
this different representation and child-before-parent workload. C, C++, Rust,
Nim, Mojo, Odin, Zig, C3, V, and Elisa drafts, two references,
workload fixtures, and byte-output suite registration are present; none has
been run. The upstream repository publishes
a [CC BY-SA license](https://github.com/cp-algorithms/cp-algorithms-aux/blob/main/LICENSE);
the source was used for the algorithm idea only.

### Library Checker catalog recheck

**Implemented, execution unverified — `effective_resistance_unit_graph`:** an
exact two-terminal effective-resistance calculation on a bounded connected
unit-resistance graph. [`counting_spanning_trees_undirected`](c/counting_spanning_trees_undirected/README.md)
computes only the single Laplacian cofactor, while this profile also computes
the two-terminal forest cofactor and returns their reduced ratio. The

identifies the resistance/cofactor relationship; use mathematical ideas only,
with independent code and fixtures. A static search for resistance names in
the benchmark READMEs and catalog found no matching profile. Reservation does
not claim complete catalog coverage. Do not duplicate this work.
The contract, independent edge-subset reference, workload, ten language
ports, and scalar-suite registration are present. The verifier source covers
all simple graphs through four vertices and a maximum-edge graph. Nothing has
been compiled or run.
The Elisa port uses a bounded input view after its ABI null and length
checks; no compiler or program was run.

## Chazelle–Guibas fractional cascading (2026-11-15)

The [Fractional Cascading Part I paper](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01840440) introduces bridge structures for transferring search positions across related catalogs; Part II applies the technique to geometric search. Existing [`orthogonal_range_reporting_2d`](o/orthogonal_range_reporting_2d/README.md) exposes a different query and independently searches each node's y-catalog. Added [`fractional_cascading_subset_chain`](f/fractional_cascading_subset_chain/README.md) as a bounded nested-catalog path: one lower-bound search in the first catalog followed by parent-to-child bridge lookups. The profile has ten language ports, a bridge primary, independent per-catalog search oracle, workload, README/RIGHTS, a static inventory, and `i64_array_scalar` runner/verifier registration. It does not claim the general catalog-graph construction, geometric range structures, or dynamic updates. Algorithm ideas only.

For the symmetric-group convolution lead, [Maslen and Rockmore's group-FFT
overview](https://library2.msri.org/books/Book46/files/11maslen.pdf) describes
subgroup-chain factorization and partition-indexed representation blocks.
Its orthogonal basis is presented over complex numbers; the proposed finite
field implementation still needs a basis and inverse transform valid in the
specified field, an explicit permutation-composition convention, and a
factorial-scaled workspace plan. The paper is used as mathematical guidance,
not as a source of copied code or fixtures. Direct noncommutative convolution
on small groups can serve as an independent reference once the convention is
fixed. Root now reserves `symmetric_group_convolution_fft` for the full
degree-1-through-9 transform profile. A small direct reference is for
validation only; it must not replace the fast transform. No production kernel
or suite integration is claimed, and nothing has been run.

## PARSEC Facesim kernel crosswalk (2026-11-14)

The [PARSEC technical report](https://www.cs.princeton.edu/techreports/2010/890.pdf)
describes Facesim's update-state, add-forces, and conjugate-gradient kernels
around lines 807–817. The update-state kernel uses Newton–Raphson, and the
linear solve uses conjugate gradient; both method families already have
registered profiles at [`newton_raphson`](n/newton_raphson/README.md) and
[`conjugate_gradient`](c/conjugate_gradient/README.md). The Add Forces kernel
iterates tetrahedra and contributes force to each of four nodes. No local
package was found for linear-elastic tetrahedron element-force integration,
so [`tetrahedral_element_force_kernel`](t/tetrahedral_element_force_kernel/README.md)
has been added as a bounded clean-room element profile, with ten language
drafts, an independent energy-gradient reference, workload, package checker,
and byte-output suite registration. The [FEniCSx
linear-elasticity tutorial](https://jsdokken.com/dolfinx-tutorial/main/chapter2/linearelasticity.html)
and [Physics-Based Simulation elasticity chapter](https://phys-sim-book.github.io/finite-element-method/3d-elastodynamics/elasticity.html)
identify the strain/stress and tetrahedral shape-gradient relations used to
specify it. The profile evaluates independent elements and omits mesh
connectivity and global scatter assembly. No code or prose was copied; static
review only, with no programs, tests, scripts, builds, compilers, checkers, or
benchmarks run.

## Rosetta Code title-only algorithm crosswalk (2026-11-14)

A second comparison used the [RosettaGit task-title index](https://rosettagit.org/tasks/)
and selected algorithmic task pages. Titles were used for discovery; local
contracts and package descriptions were used to assess duplicates. This is a
representative pass, not an exhaustive review of every task.

| Rosetta Code title | Classification and local comparison |
|---|---|
| EKG sequence | Implemented as [`ekg_sequence`](e/ekg_sequence/README.md): greedy least-unused integer sharing a factor with the previous term. Distinct from Mian–Chowla pair-sum uniqueness, Golomb's self-describing recurrence, and Van Eck's last-occurrence recurrence. Ten language ports, incremental-gcd and independent trial-factor references, workload, static inventory, and byte-output suite registration are integrated in source. Sources: Lagarias, Rains, and Sloane, [The EKG Sequence](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0204011), and [OEIS A064413](https://oeis.org/A064413). No executable checks were run. |
| Hofstadter Figure-Figure sequences | Implemented as [`hofstadter_figure_figure_sequences`](h/hofstadter_figure_figure_sequences/README.md): bounded paired prefixes of the greedy complementary Figure and Space recurrences, distinct from Hofstadter Q. Ten language ports, an additive-recurrence oracle, an independent complement-property verifier, workload, static inventory, and `i64_array_bytes_output` suite registration are integrated in source. Sources: Jubin, [Asymptotic Series for Hofstadter’s Figure-Figure Sequences](https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL17/Jubin/jubin2.pdf), and [MathWorld's definition](https://mathworld.wolfram.com/HofstadterFigure-FigureSequence.html). No executable checks were run. |
| Smallest number with exactly `n` divisors | Implemented as [`smallest_number_with_n_divisors`](s/smallest_number_with_n_divisors/README.md): bounded search over nonincreasing prime-exponent profiles, distinct from direct divisor counting and sequence generation. Ten ports, profile-enumeration and independent divisor-sieve references, fixtures, and `i64_array_scalar` suite wiring are integrated in source. Sources: [OEIS A005179](https://oeis.org/A005179) and the [Rosetta Code task](https://rosettacode.org/wiki/Sequence:_smallest_number_with_exactly_n_divisors). |
| A* search algorithm | Present in `a_star_search`, `astar`, and `bidirectional_a_star`; weighted-edge task behavior is a contract variant of the same method. |
| Abelian sandpile model | No local sandpile/chip-firing package existed. This differs from `game_of_life`: sandpile topplings conserve grains except at a dissipative sink and the task is to stabilize an integer-height configuration. Implemented as `abelian_sandpile_stabilization`; bounded profile and source details are recorded below. Discovery used the RosettaGit title only; algorithm semantics come from Dhar's primary paper. |
| Addition chains | Confirmed distinct from [`problem122`](p/problem122/README.md), which searches only Brauer/star chains and sums their minimum lengths, and [`knuth_power_tree`](k/knuth_power_tree/README.md), which returns first discoveries without optimality. Added [`addition_chain_enumeration`](a/addition_chain_enumeration/README.md): bounded unrestricted iterative-deepening enumeration returns the shortest length and counts optimal Brauer and non-Brauer chains. Ten ports, depth-first primary, breadth-first independent verifier, workload, rights note, and byte-output suite wiring are present. Cases are independently derived small targets; the upper-bound profile uses target 31. See the [Rosetta Code task](https://rosettagit.org/tasks/addition-chains/) for the underlying algorithm idea. |
| AKS test for primes | The Rosetta task's title is inaccurate: its predicate checks divisibility of interior binomial coefficients, and its [discussion](https://rosettagit.org/drafts/talk-aks-test-for-primes/) distinguishes this exponential criterion from the polynomial-time [AKS algorithm](https://annals.math.princeton.edu/2004/160-2/p12). Implemented under the accurate name `binomial_divisibility_primality_test`; local trial division, Miller–Rabin, and Fermat testing use different methods. |
| AVL tree | Present in several AVL packages, including `ordered_set_avl_order_statistics` and persistent insert/delete variants. |
| Banker's algorithm | Present as `bankers_algorithm`; the Python printed-sequence demonstration is separately tracked for its duplicate-need behavior. |
| Boids | Rosetta Code's A–C title index includes the “Boids” task. No local flocking or boids package was found. [`particle_swarm_optimization`](p/particle_swarm_optimization/README.md) optimizes an objective through personal/global bests; [`benchmarkgame_nbody`](b/benchmarkgame_nbody/README.md) integrates gravitational pair forces. Neither uses local-neighbor separation, velocity matching, and flock centering. | Implemented as [`boids_flocking_simulation`](b/boids_flocking_simulation/README.md), a bounded deterministic 2D integer profile with ten language ports and `i64_array_bytes_output` suite registration. Its full frozen contract is in `workload.json`: inclusive Euclidean neighborhood with a uniform step-function sensitivity, ascending-ID coincident-position separation tie, exact separation/alignment/cohesion vectors with truncation-toward-zero averaging, ceil-integer-square-root normalization, prioritized collision-avoidance → velocity-matching → flock-centering acceleration allocation with remaining-budget trimming, speed cap, and synchronous snapshot updates. Input is `[N,steps,radius,max_speed,max_acceleration,(x,y,vx,vy)*N]`, with `N<=16`, `steps<=16`, positions `[-256,256]`, speed `<=32`, acceleration `<=8`; final state is emitted as per-boid signed-i32 little-endian tuples. Reynolds's [SIGGRAPH 1987 paper](https://www.red3d.com/cwr/papers/1987/SIGGRAPH87.pdf) supplies the three local behaviors and priority-arbitration model. Rosetta Code is title discovery only; no task text or code is used. Static inventory and dual-reference workload review are included. |
| Carmichael 3 strong pseudoprimes | Implemented as [`three_prime_carmichael_enumerator`](t/three_prime_carmichael_enumerator/README.md), despite the misleading title: the [Rosetta task](https://rosettagit.org/tasks/carmichael-3-strong-pseudoprimes/) enumerates three-prime Carmichael numbers by looping over prime `p1<=61` and parameters `2<=h3<p1`, `1<=d<h3+p1`, applying divisibility/congruence filters, deriving `p2,p3`, and primality-testing the factors. It does not perform a Miller–Rabin strong-pseudoprime test. This differs from [`carmichael_number`](c/carmichael_number/README.md), which classifies one supplied integer by universal Fermat congruences, and from `miller_rabin`, which tests a supplied integer against fixed bases. The package accepts `p1_limit` in `2..61` and returns triples in source-loop order; its 69 triples at 61 require at most 832 output bytes. Ten ports, independent Korselt-criterion oracle, workload, package checker, and byte-output suite registration are present. It is related to, but broader than, the three-factor subfamily found by the Chernick construction below. |
| Chernick's Carmichael numbers | Implemented as [`chernick_carmichael_least_multiplier`](c/chernick_carmichael_least_multiplier/README.md), distinct from [`carmichael_number`](c/carmichael_number/README.md): the [Rosetta task](https://rosettagit.org/tasks/chernicks-carmichael-numbers/) searches the parameterized family `U(n,m)=(6m+1)(12m+1) product(i=1..n-2)(2^i*9m+1)` for the least qualifying multiplier for each `n=3..9`, checking every factor for primality. This restricted universal-form search differs from the general three-prime generator above. The scalar package searches the necessary multiplier progression through the largest reported least multiplier (`m=950560`) and returns `m`, avoiding the full product that exceeds signed 64-bit for larger `n`. Ten ports, independent sieve-based primality reference, workload, package checker, and scalar-suite registration are present. The n=3 Chernick result `(7,13,19)` is one member of the general enumerator's larger result set; the two profiles differ in parameter space, output, and search. |
| Cipolla's algorithm | Confirmed distinct from `tonelli_shanks`; the existing `quadratic_residue` profile covers only Legendre-symbol evaluation, and its source notes Cipolla as excluded. `cipolla_modular_square_root` has contract, primary/independent references, workload, scalar-suite wiring, and ten language ports. |
| Closest-pair problem | Present in divide-and-conquer, sweep-line, and bichromatic profiles. |
| Convex hull | Present in Graham scan, Quickhull, Chan, Melkman, and other method-specific profiles. |
| Cycle detection | Present for linked lists and directed/undirected graphs. |

## Rosetta Code N–R title-index audit (2026-11-17)

This pass compares public task titles in the [RosettaGit task-title
index](https://rosettagit.org/tasks/) from N through R against local package
paths and README method descriptions. The audit uses titles for discovery;
task prose, examples, tests, and submissions are not used.

| Title family | Local comparison and disposition |
|---|---|
| N-Queens, N-body, natural sorting, nonogram solving | Covered by n_queens_solution_count / n_queens_backtracking_csharp, the two distinct n_body_simulation and benchmarkgame_nbody profiles, natural_sort, and nonogram_line_domain_solver. Their README contracts specify the particular bounded methods already represented. |
| N-smooth numbers, numerical integration, perfect shuffle, perlin noise | Covered by hamming_numbers for the canonical 5-smooth sequence; adaptive Simpson, Gauss–Legendre, Simpson, and Romberg integration packages; perfect_shuffle_order; and perlin_noise. These titles add no missing method to the reviewed local profiles. |
| Quickselect, QR decomposition, ray casting, Ramer–Douglas–Peucker, Recamán, runge–kutta, run-length encoding | Covered by quickselect; the distinct classical Gram–Schmidt `qr_decompose`, factorization-property `qr_decomposition`, and PolyBench modified Gram–Schmidt QR profiles; point_in_polygon_ray_casting; ramer_douglas_peucker; recamans_sequence; the explicit Runge–Kutta variants; and run_length_encoding. |
| Range consolidation, reduced row echelon form, Sieve of Eratosthenes, shortest common supersequence | Range consolidation maps to the existing interval-merge contract; reduced row echelon form uses the same Gauss–Jordan pivot normalization and elimination already in gauss_jordan; the sieve and supersequence methods are already represented. |
| Permutation test, Ramsey's theorem, general percolation tasks | Excluded on title-only evidence: each leaves the statistic, stochastic experiment, graph family, or output contract open, so no single deterministic bounded kernel can be reserved from the title alone. |
| Perfect totient numbers | No package or active reservation computes the sum of iterated Euler totients. Local euler_totient computes one φ value, euler_totient_sequence lists φ(n) across n, and totients_linear_sieve builds a table; sum_of_totient_function sums φ(k) over an interval. None computes φ(n)+φ²(n)+…+1 for one n. Implemented as `perfect_totient_number`, scalar ABI `perfect_totient_number(i64)->i64`, conventional input domain 3..65535, return 1 iff the iterated-φ sum equals n, 0 otherwise, and -1 outside the domain. Ten language ports, factorization and coprime-count references, workload, rights/provenance, static inventory, and scalar runner/verifier registration are present; see [package guide](p/perfect_totient_number/README.md). The algorithm definition is independently specified by Douglas E. Iannucci, Deng Moujie, and Graeme L. Cohen, [“On Perfect Totient Numbers”](https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL6/Cohen2/cohen50.pdf), *Journal of Integer Sequences* 6 (2003), article 03.4.5; [OEIS A082897](https://oeis.org/A082897) cross-references the sequence. |

The roster above records the plausible algorithmic titles reviewed in this
alphabetical range; non-algorithm programming-language demonstrations were
not treated as benchmark candidates. No task text or source code was copied.

## Erdős–Gallai graphical-sequence profile (2026-11-14)

The repository inventory had no profile for deciding whether an input degree
sequence is realizable by a simple undirected graph. The cited
[Erdős–Gallai characterization and constructive proof](https://web.iitd.ac.in/~atripath/publications/constructive_Erdos-Gallai.pdf)
is a direct match; [NetworkX documentation](https://networkx.org/documentation/stable/reference/algorithms/generated/networkx.algorithms.graphical.is_graphical.html)
also identifies this test as graphical-sequence membership. It is distinct
from graph construction, coloring, and connectivity algorithms. The new
`erdos_gallai_graphical_sequence` package sorts a bounded degree vector and
uses prefix sums and binary search to check the inequalities. Its independent
Havel–Hakimi oracle provides a different decision procedure. Ten language
ports, scalar workload, static package checker, and `i64_array_scalar` suite
registration are present. Mathematical references only; all package content
is independently authored. No code, programs, tests, checkers, scripts,
builds, compilers, or benchmarks were run.

## Perfect-shuffle order (2026-11-14)

The [Rosetta Code task](https://rosettagit.org/tasks/perfect-shuffle/) asks
for the least positive number of out-shuffles that restores a unique-card
deck, with seven even deck sizes through 10,000 and known counts. The local
[`shuffle_array`](s/shuffle_array/README.md) profile returns one half-interleave
only; it does not measure the permutation order. The new
`perfect_shuffle_order` profile simulates the repeated operation directly,
while an independent reference computes the order of 2 modulo `N-1`. The
classical [`shors_algorithm`](s/shors_algorithm/README.md) has a related
order-finding subroutine but consumes supplied bases and searches for factors,
so the full computation is distinct. Ten language ports, workload, static
package checker, and `i64_array_scalar` suite registration are present. The
task is used as an operation and expected-value reference only; no code,
prose, examples, or tests were copied. All review was static, with no programs,
tests, scripts, checkers, builds, compilers, or benchmarks run.

## Prime-modulus p-free factorial (2026-11-14)

The source crosswalk found no standalone local operation returning the
factorial unit modulo a prime for very large `n`. The nearest profile,
[`binomial_coefficient_prime_power`](b/binomial_coefficient_prime_power/README.md),
computes p-free factorial parts internally but combines them with p-adic
valuations and unit inverses to return binomial coefficients modulo `p^e`;
[`ncr_modulo_p`](n/ncr_modulo_p/README.md) uses an ordinary factorial table.
The directly returned p-free factorial is therefore a distinct scalar profile.

Implemented as `prime_modulus_p_free_factorial` with `[n,p]`,
`0 <= n <= INT64_MAX`, and prime `2 <= p <= 1009`. The primary uses a
precomputed factorial-residue table and Wilson blocks; the independent oracle
forms each complete residue block explicitly. Ten language ports, workload,
package checker, and `i64_array_scalar` suite registration are present. Source:
[CP-Algorithms — Factorial modulo p](https://cp-algorithms.com/algebra/factorial-modulo.html),
CC BY-SA 4.0; algorithm description only, with no source code or prose reused.
The fixture expectations and port logic have only been reviewed statically;
no programs, tests, scripts, checkers, builds, compilers, or benchmarks were run.

## Three-prime Carmichael enumeration (2026-11-14)

The [Rosetta Code task](https://rosettagit.org/tasks/carmichael-3-strong-pseudoprimes/)
is titled “Carmichael 3 strong pseudoprimes,” but its operation enumerates
three-prime Carmichael numbers and does not run a Miller–Rabin test. The bounded
[`three_prime_carmichael_enumerator`](t/three_prime_carmichael_enumerator/README.md)
profile takes `p1_limit` in `2..61`, follows the task's `p1,h3,d` parameter
loops, and emits triples in that order. Its independent reference searches by
prime pairs and applies Korselt's criterion. The 69 outputs at limit 61 fit in
832 bytes. This is distinct from the supplied-integer classifiers
[`carmichael_number`](c/carmichael_number/README.md) and [`miller_rabin`](m/miller_rabin/README.md),
and from the restricted Chernick-family least-multiplier search. Ten language
ports, package workload and static checker, and byte-output suite registration
are present. The task is used for its mathematical enumeration only; no code,
prose, examples, or tests were copied. Review was static only; no programs,
tests, scripts, checkers, builds, compilers, or benchmarks were run.

## Chernick Carmichael least multiplier (2026-11-14)

The [Rosetta Code Chernick task](https://rosettagit.org/tasks/chernicks-carmichael-numbers/)
asks for the smallest multiplier producing an all-prime factorization of
`(6m+1)(12m+1) product(i=1..n-2)(9m*2^i+1)` for `n=3..9`. For `n>4`, the
theorem requires `m` to be a multiple of `2^(n-4)`; for `n>5`, the factors
cover all nonzero coefficient residues modulo five, so a multiplier not
divisible by five makes one factor composite. The new
[`chernick_carmichael_least_multiplier`](c/chernick_carmichael_least_multiplier/README.md)
profile searches only this necessary progression through 950,560 and returns
the least multiplier rather than the much larger product. It complements
[`three_prime_carmichael_enumerator`](t/three_prime_carmichael_enumerator/README.md),
which generates general triples using a different parameterization, and is not
a duplicate of the supplied-integer [`carmichael_number`](c/carmichael_number/README.md)
classifier. Ten language ports, a trial-division primary and sieve-based
independent reference, bounded workload, package checker, and scalar-suite
registration are present. Only the mathematical definition and reported
multipliers from the source were used; all package content is clean-room. Review
was static only, with no programs, tests, scripts, checkers, builds, compilers,
or benchmarks run.

## Lucas binomial coefficient for a small prime (2026-11-14)

The CP-Algorithms binomial-coefficient reference and OI Wiki Lucas theorem
entry describe the base-`p` digit method for computing `C(n,k) mod p` when
`n` may be much larger than `p`. The local exact `combinations` profile is
bounded and returns an integer; `ncr_modulo_p` uses a bounded factorial table;
and [`binomial_coefficient_prime_power`](b/binomial_coefficient_prime_power/README.md)
uses p-adic factorial valuations and p-free units for general prime powers.
Those profiles do not implement Lucas' digit decomposition for signed-64-bit
`n`, so this is a distinct method profile despite sharing the binomial
coefficient operation.

Implemented as [`binomial_coefficient_lucas`](b/binomial_coefficient_lucas/README.md)
with input `[n,k,p]`, `0 <= k <= n <= INT64_MAX`, and prime `2 <= p <= 1009`.
The primary precomputes factorial and inverse-factorial tables below `p` and
processes base-`p` digits; an independent oracle uses exact arbitrary-precision
digit coefficients. Ten ports, a workload, rights/provenance note, static
package checker, and `i64_array_scalar` suite registration are present. Source:
[CP-Algorithms — Binomial coefficients](https://cp-algorithms.com/combinatorics/binomial-coefficients.html)
and [OI Wiki — Lucas theorem](https://en.oi-wiki.org/math/lucas/); algorithm
descriptions only, with no source code, tests, or prose reused. Review was
static only; no programs, tests, scripts, checkers, builds, compilers, or
benchmarks were run.

## Alpha Skip Search (2026-11-14)

Lecroq's [Alpha Skip Search description](https://igm.univ-mlv.fr/~lecroq/string/node33.html)
indexes fixed-length pattern factors in buckets and samples text windows at
an alphabet/pattern-dependent spacing. The repository's KMP, Two-Way,
Apostolico–Crochemore, and suffix-automaton search profiles use different
matching structures; no factor-bucket sample search was present. Drafted as
[`alpha_skip_search`](a/alpha_skip_search/README.md) over a four-symbol
alphabet, with a rolling base-4 factor key and a direct alignment oracle.
The contract uses `max(1,floor(log_4(m)))`; at exact powers of four this
rounding differs from the integer loop in Lecroq's published C routine, while
the shift is derived from the same factor length and therefore retains the
sampled-residue coverage proof. Ten ports, package checker, workload, and suite
registration are present. Only the algorithm description was used. Static
review only; no programs, tests, scripts, checkers, builds, compilers, or
benchmarks were run.

## Persistent leftist heap (2026-11-14)

[OI Wiki's persistent mergeable-heap description](https://oi-wiki.org/ds/persistent-heap/)
copies the nodes along a leftist-heap meld path so earlier versions remain
available. The existing [`leftist_heap`](l/leftist_heap/README.md) benchmark
models destructive mutable merging and does not cover version persistence.
Added as [`persistent_leftist_heap`](p/persistent_leftist_heap/README.md), a
branching versioned workload with insert, meld, pop-min, and peek operations;
its primary oracle uses path-copying nodes and its independent oracle stores
sorted immutable multisets. The bounded contract, fixtures, and suite
registration, all ten language ports, and static package checker are present.
Static audit reconciled the branching fixture and widened result packing to
keep the rank XOR in a separate 15-bit field. Only the algorithm idea was
consulted. No programs, tests, scripts, checkers, builds, compilers, or
benchmarks were run.

## Colussi string search (2026-11-14)

Lecroq's [Colussi description](https://igm.univ-mlv.fr/~lecroq/string/node10.html)
partitions pattern locations into increasing-order noholes and decreasing-order
holes. Its `h`, `next`, and `shift` tables let a mismatch resume without
rechecking a known text prefix; the published bound is linear search with at
most `3n/2` comparisons. Local KMP, Apostolico–Crochemore, Two-Way, and Alpha
Skip Search use different comparison schedules and state. Added as
[`colussi_search`](c/colussi_search/README.md) with bounded four-symbol input,
a table-driven primary reference, and a direct-alignment independent oracle.
The workload and `i64_array_scalar` suite registrations and all ten language
ports are present; a static audit of all ten ports found no actionable issues.
Only algorithm ideas were consulted. No
programs, tests, scripts, checkers, builds, compilers, or benchmarks were run.

The local Min_25, summatory-totient, square-free-count, and Möbius-value

## Burstsort (2026-11-15)

Sinha and Zobel's [Burstsort paper](https://doi.org/10.1145/1005813.1041517)
describes a dynamic trie whose leaves accumulate strings in buckets and burst
into child nodes when their capacity is exceeded. Local
[`american_flag_string_sorter`](a/american_flag_string_sorter/README.md) uses
in-place radix cycles, [`msd_radix_string_sorter`](m/msd_radix_string_sorter/README.md)
uses stable buffered distribution, and `multikey_quick_sort` partitions on
characters; none uses the burst-trie procedure. This bounded profile uses a
fixed threshold of three and insertion-sorts residual buckets of at most three.
Drafted as
[`burstsort`](b/burstsort/README.md) for 0..16 byte strings of length 0..8,
with alphabet 0..3 and threshold three. A host sort independently checks the
primary burst-trie result; ten language ports, the workload, static package
checker, and scalar-suite wiring are present. Static review confirmed the
fixtures and source algorithms; no programs, tests, scripts, checkers, builds,
compilers, or benchmarks were run.

## Ukkonen online suffix tree (2026-11-15)

Ukkonen's [1995 paper](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01206331) builds the suffix
tree online from left to right using active-point updates, suffix links, open
leaf edges, and edge splits. Local [`suffix_tree`](s/suffix_tree/README.md)
inserts suffixes directly, while
[`suffix_tree_from_sa_lcp`](s/suffix_tree_from_sa_lcp/README.md) constructs
from suffix-array and LCP data; neither implements Ukkonen's online method.
Drafted as [`ukkonen_suffix_tree`](u/ukkonen_suffix_tree/README.md), with a
unique terminal, canonical tree-token checksum, distinct-substring count, and
an independent suffix-trie compression reference. Ten language ports, static
package checking, and scalar-suite wiring are present. Static review cleared
the references, fixtures, bounds, and ports. Only algorithm ideas are used. No
programs, tests, scripts, checkers, builds, compilers, or benchmarks were run.

## Johnson elementary circuit enumeration (2026-11-15)

Johnson's [1975 paper](https://doi.org/10.1137/0204007) combines repeated
strongly-connected-component restriction with blocked vertices and
dependency-set unblocking to enumerate elementary directed circuits. The
local [`directed_simple_cycles`](d/directed_simple_cycles/README.md) performs
canonical path search without this output-sensitive pruning, so the method is
distinct. Added as
[`johnson_elementary_circuit_enumeration`](j/johnson_elementary_circuit_enumeration/README.md)
for simple loopless graphs with at most eight vertices and 24 arcs. The
primary reference uses Johnson's SCC/blocked-set procedure; the independent
reference directly searches canonical simple paths. All ten language ports
use Tarjan SCC discovery. Ten ports, workload, rights note, static package
checker, and `i64_array_scalar` suite wiring are present. An independent
static audit found the enumeration and fixtures sound; the documented result
magnitude is a safe upper bound derived from the complete eight-vertex
digraph. Algorithm ideas only.
No programs, tests, scripts, checkers, builds, compilers, or benchmarks were
run.

## Subset Sum bin-packing heuristic (2026-11-15)

Mestre's [2016 Encyclopedia of Algorithms chapter listing, pp. 2126–2129](https://link.springer.com/referencework/10.1007/978-1-4939-2864-4?page=29)
describes repeatedly filling each new bin with a maximum-size subset of the
remaining items that fits its capacity. Existing subset-sum profiles decide,
count, or enumerate target subsets, while local bin-packing profiles place
items by online/decreasing-order rules; this benchmark combines a distinct
repeated subset-sum optimization with a deterministic earliest-item tie rule.
Added as [`subset_sum_bin_packing`](s/subset_sum_bin_packing/README.md), with a
suffix-reachability primary reference and exhaustive-subset independent
reference. Ten language ports, workload, rights note, static package checker,
and `i64_array_scalar` wiring are present; static audit found the ports and
fixtures consistent. The exact maximum valid scalar result is 161,496.
Only the algorithm idea was used.
No programs, tests, scripts, checkers, builds, compilers, or benchmarks were
run.

## Average Rate (AVR) speed scaling (2026-11-15)

The 2016 [Encyclopedia of Algorithms speed-scaling chapter](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4939-2864-4_390)
lists AVR among online policies; Bansal, Bunde, Chan, and Pruhs give its
average-rate rule in [Average Rate Speed Scaling](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00453-009-9379-z).

release/deadline windows, an exact piecewise-rate profile, EDF completion
trace, and cubic-power energy. The primary reference uses integer scaling by
`lcm(1,...,8)`; the independent reference uses rational arithmetic and direct
interval density sums. The workload and byte-output suite registration are
present, as are all ten language ports. Static review found the implementations
consistent with the bounded contract. Only algorithm descriptions were used.
No programs, tests, scripts, checkers, builds, compilers, or benchmarks were
run.

## Top Trading Cycles housing exchange (2026-11-15)

Shapley and Scarf's [1974 paper](https://doi.org/10.1016/0304-4068(74)90033-0)
describes the strict-preference housing exchange whose core allocation is found
by Gale's Top Trading Cycles rule. The local
[`stable_matching`](s/stable_matching/README.md) and
[`stable_roommates`](s/stable_roommates/README.md) solve different pairing
problems without initially owned houses. Added as
[`housing_top_trading_cycles`](h/housing_top_trading_cycles/README.md) for up
to eight agents with strict complete rankings. The primary reference finds all
cycles in each round; the independent reference removes one cycle at a time
with Floyd traversal and checks the no-blocking-coalition core condition. The
workload and `i64_array_scalar` suite registration are present, with all ten

[Stable Partition Problem chapter](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4939-2864-4_397)
mentions TTC for strict B/BW preferences but leaves its procedure to the

## Kruskal reconstruction tree bottleneck queries (2026-11-14)

Local [`kruskal`](k/kruskal/README.md) returns a minimum spanning forest's
total weight, not pairwise minimax bottleneck values. The Kruskal
reconstruction tree adds a merge node on each successful DSU union; its LCA
label records the earliest edge threshold connecting two vertices. Added as
[`kruskal_reconstruction_tree_bottleneck`](k/kruskal_reconstruction_tree_bottleneck/README.md)
with a bounded multigraph/query workload, an LCA primary reference, and an
independent minimax Floyd–Warshall oracle. Workload, rights note, package

## Gao Reed–Solomon decoding (2026-11-14)

The local [`misc_reed_solomon`](m/misc_reed_solomon/README.md) profile
specializes a shortened GF(2^8) encoder and a syndrome decoder; the new
[`berlekamp_welch_rs_decode`](b/berlekamp_welch_rs_decode/README.md) solves a
homogeneous numerator/error-locator system. Gao's method is distinct: it
interpolates the received word, applies partial extended Euclid to its
interpolation polynomial and the vanishing polynomial of the evaluation set,
then divides to recover the message directly. Its proof's partial-EEA bound
stops at degree strictly below `(n+k)/2`. Added as
[`gao_rs_decode`](g/gao_rs_decode/README.md) over GF(7), with `n<=7`, `k<=3`,
and `t<=2` in the unique decoding radius. An exhaustive coefficient oracle is
independent of the primary polynomial-arithmetic decoder. The workload,
rights note, package checker, and scalar-suite registrations are present. All
ten ports passed an independent static audit. Source: Gao's [author-hosted
paper](https://www.math.clemson.edu/~sgao/papers/RS.pdf).
Only algorithm ideas were consulted. No programs, tests, scripts, checkers,
builds, compilers, or benchmarks were run.

## Berlekamp–Welch Reed–Solomon decoding (2026-11-14)

The local [`misc_reed_solomon`](m/misc_reed_solomon/README.md) profile
shortens an RS(255,239) code and specializes its source-compatible decoder to
at most one changed symbol. [`berlekamp_massey`](b/berlekamp_massey/README.md)
infers a linear recurrence from a sequence. Neither solves the evaluation-form
error-locator interpolation system, so Berlekamp–Welch is a distinct decoding
method. Added as [`berlekamp_welch_rs_decode`](b/berlekamp_welch_rs_decode/README.md)
over GF(7), with `n<=7`, `k<=3`, and `t<=2` within the unique decoding radius.
The primary oracle solves for numerator and error-locator polynomials; an
independent exhaustive coefficient enumerator checks the result. The workload,
rights note, scalar-suite registration, and all ten language ports passed
independent static audit. Sources: Welch and Berlekamp's
[patent](https://patents.google.com/patent/US4633470A/en) and the evaluation
equations in [coding-theory lecture notes](https://bpb-us-e1.wpmucdn.com/sites.harvard.edu/dist/7/800/files/2024/10/fall2002-ft02-lect11.pdf).
Only algorithm ideas were consulted. No programs, tests, scripts, checkers,
builds, compilers, or benchmarks were run.

## Howard minimum mean cycle (2026-11-14)

Howard policy iteration is a second method for the existing minimum-cycle-mean
problem, not a second problem definition. It differs from local
[`minimum_mean_cycle_karp`](m/minimum_mean_cycle_karp/README.md): Howard evaluates
a functional graph of selected outgoing edges, assigns exact cycle means and
biases, then improves the policy by lexicographic appraisal, whereas Karp uses
exact-length walk DP and a min-max characterization. Added as
[`minimum_mean_cycle_howard`](m/minimum_mean_cycle_howard/README.md), reusing
Karp's bounded strongly connected graph domain and byte-output ABI. The
independent oracle enumerates simple cycles; workload, rights note, static
package checker, and byte-output suite registration are present. All ten
language ports passed a static audit. Source: Hansen and Zwick,
[“Lower Bounds for Howard's Algorithm for Finding Minimum Mean-Cost Cycles”](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-642-17517-6_37).
The small workload bounds the policy space because the general iteration
bound is not known to be polynomial. Algorithm ideas only; no programs,
tests, scripts, checkers, builds, compilers, or benchmarks were run.

## Goldberg–Tarjan cost-scaling minimum-cost circulation (2026-11-14)

Added [`minimum_cost_circulation_cost_scaling`](m/minimum_cost_circulation_cost_scaling/README.md)
as a bounded integral-circulation profile with a generic epsilon refine loop:
negative reduced-cost arcs are saturated, then excess is routed by admissible
pushes and price relabels. It is distinct from local successive-shortest-path
min-cost flow, tight-edge blocking flow, and the feasibility plus
negative-cycle-cancellation method in
[`minimum_cost_b_flow`](m/minimum_cost_b_flow/README.md). An independent oracle
enumerates bounded edge-flow assignments. Workload, rights note, static package
checker, and `i64_array_scalar` suite registration are present; all ten
language ports passed an independent static audit. Sources: Goldberg and Tarjan's
[1990 paper](https://doi.org/10.1287/moor.15.3.430) and Goldberg's
[network-flow report](https://www.cs.princeton.edu/techreports/1989/216.pdf).
Only algorithm ideas were used. No programs, tests, scripts, checkers, builds,
compilers, or benchmarks were run.

The [Lecroq description](https://www-igm.univ-mlv.fr/~lecroq/string/node12.html)

## Fundamental Pell solution (2026-11-14)

OI Wiki's Pell equation reference gives the continued-fraction method for the
fundamental positive solution of `x^2-D*y^2=1`. The local
[Pell-number sequence](p/pell_number/README.md) generates recurrence terms,
and the generic continued-fraction converter evaluates a finite rational
expansion; neither solves for the least Pell pair. Implemented as
[`pell_fundamental_solution`](p/pell_fundamental_solution/README.md) for
nonsquare `D` in `2..31`. The primary examines convergents of `sqrt(D)` and
packs `(x,y)` as `(x << 32) | y`; an independent bounded oracle scans `y` and
checks exact squares. Ten language ports, workload, static package checker,
and `i64_array_scalar` suite registration are present. Source:
[OI Wiki — Pell equation](https://oi-wiki.org/math/number-theory/pell-equation/);
mathematical algorithm only, with no source code, tests, or prose reused. Review
was static only; no programs, tests, scripts, checkers, builds, compilers, or
benchmarks were run.

## American flag sort (2026-11-14)

NIST defines American flag sort as an in-place radix variant that counts
buckets, computes their start positions, and cyclically permutes elements into
place. The existing [`msd_radix_string_sorter`](m/msd_radix_string_sorter/README.md)
performs stable buffered MSD distribution on the same kind of keys. The two
profiles share lexicographic sorting semantics but exercise different
distribution algorithms and memory behavior, so retain both rather than
merging names.

Implemented as
[`american_flag_string_sorter`](a/american_flag_string_sorter/README.md), with
257 keys per byte position (end sentinel plus all byte values), in-place
permutation of a bounded string-index array, and recursion on byte buckets.
The checksum weights each sorted string's byte content by its rank; an
independent comparison sort checks the output order. Ten language ports,
workload, static package checker, and `i64_array_scalar` suite registration are
present. Source: [NIST — American flag sort](https://xlinux.nist.gov/dads/HTML/americanFlagSort.html)
and its cited *Engineering Radix Sort* paper; algorithm idea only, with no code,
tests, or prose reused. Review was static only; no programs, tests, scripts,
checkers, builds, compilers, or benchmarks were run.

tests, scripts, checkers, builds, compilers, or benchmarks were run.

## Weak-heapsort (2026-11-14)

NIST describes weak-heapsort as building a weak heap and repeatedly extracting
the maximum. The local [`heap_sort`](h/heap_sort/README.md) uses an ordinary
binary heap, while `string_heap_sort` uses the same ordinary-heap structure on

ancestors. Implemented as [`weak_heapsort`](w/weak_heapsort/README.md), using

each extraction. The independent reference uses standard sorting. Ten ports,
workload, static checker, and scalar-suite registration are drafted. See

## Lawler knapsack dyadic profit-scaling FPTAS (2026-11-15)

Lawler's [1979 paper](https://doi.org/10.1287/moor.4.4.339) improves the
Ibarra–Kim approach with a lower bound `P0`, a small/large profit split,
dyadic interval-specific scaling, and grouped large-item transitions. The
local [`knapsack_profit_scaling_fptas`](k/knapsack_profit_scaling_fptas/README.md)
and [`knapsack_profit_scaling_small_large_fptas`](k/knapsack_profit_scaling_small_large_fptas/README.md)
profiles use uniform profit scaling, so the dyadic scales and equal-q groups
are a distinct algorithmic workload. The bounded profile fixes epsilon at
1/2, uses exact ratio ordering and deterministic ties, keeps the lightest
`floor(32/q)` members of each scaled-profit group, and returns the selected
profit and item mask. Added as
[`lawler_knapsack_profit_scaling_fptas`](l/lawler_knapsack_profit_scaling_fptas/README.md)
with grouped-DP and grouped-subset-enumeration references, bounded fixtures,
and scalar-suite wiring; ten language ports are present. The ports use
insertion sorting and bounded grouped frontiers, giving O(n²) time and O(n)
space for the fixed `Q=32` profile. An independent static audit cleared the
contract, references, fixtures, suite hooks, and all ten ports. The Berkeley
[technical report](https://www2.eecs.berkeley.edu/Pubs/TechRpts/1977/Archive/ERL-m-77-45.pdf)
was consulted for algorithm details. Only algorithm ideas were used; no
source code was copied. Static review only; no programs, tests, scripts,
checkers, builds, compilers, or benchmarks were run.

## Irving stable roommates (2026-11-14)

Irving's [1985 paper](https://doi.org/10.1016/0196-6774(85)90033-1) gives an

eliminates all-or-nothing rotation cycles. The local
[`stable_matching`](s/stable_matching/README.md) is the bipartite stable
marriage problem and has a different feasibility guarantee and proposal
structure, so this is a distinct algorithm. Added as
[`stable_roommates`](s/stable_roommates/README.md) with bounded n<=8 input, an
Irving primary oracle, and an exhaustive pairing oracle. The workload and
`i64_array_scalar` suite registrations and all ten language ports are present;
a static audit found the sentinel handling, cycle reductions, and fixtures
consistent with the paper. Only algorithm ideas and published examples were
consulted. No
programs, tests, scripts, checkers, builds, compilers, or benchmarks were run.

## Multi-root hollow heap (2026-11-15)

The heap inventory already contains Fibonacci, binomial, pairing, skew,
leftist, persistent leftist, and monotone radix heaps, but no hollow heap.
These are different structures or priority-queue ordering strategies. Added
the multi-root hollow-heap variant from Hansen, Kaplan, Tarjan, and Zwick:
decrease-key relocates an item and hollows its old node, while delete-min
destroys hollow roots, promotes their children, and consolidates equal ranks.

decrease-key, find-min, delete-min, and arbitrary item deletion, and uses an
independent active-item oracle. The package and `i64_array_scalar` suite hooks
are present; ten language ports have been statically reviewed. See the
[guide](benchmarks/m/multi_root_hollow_heap/README.md), [workload](benchmarks/m/multi_root_hollow_heap/workload.json), and the
[Hollow Heaps paper](https://doi.org/10.1145/3093240). Algorithmic ideas only;
no code or text was copied. No programs, tests, scripts, checkers, builds,
compilers, or benchmarks were run.

## Type-1 rank-pairing heap (2026-11-15)

The local heap inventory includes Fibonacci, binomial, pairing, skew, leftist,
and hollow heaps, but no rank-pairing heap. This is a distinct structure: a
decrease-key cuts one half-tree and repairs ranks along its former ancestor
path, while delete-min disassembles the root's right spine and fairly links
equal-rank roots. Added as
[`rank_pairing_heap`](r/rank_pairing_heap/README.md), based on Haeupler, Sen,
and Tarjan's [2011 paper](https://doi.org/10.1137/100785351). The bounded
operation profile includes independent references, workload cases, a static
package checker, scalar-suite wiring, and ten language ports. The sources,
fixtures, and integrations were reviewed statically only. No programs, tests,
scripts, checkers, builds, compilers, or benchmarks were run.

## Skew binomial queue (2026-11-15)

The local inventory has an ordinary binomial heap and a self-adjusting skew
heap, but no skew-binomial queue or skew links. Added the non-bootstrapped
skew-binomial forest described by Brodal and Okasaki in Section 3 of their
[1996 paper](https://doi.org/10.1017/S095679680000201X). Its insertion checks
the existing two smallest ranks and, when they agree, uses the new singleton
and both existing trees in a type-A or type-B skew link. Delete-min separates
rank-zero singleton children from positive-rank children, melds by simple
equal-rank links, and reinserts the singletons. The bounded trace, independent
references, static package checker, scalar-suite registrations, and all ten
language ports are present; the Type-A rank rule is covered above rank zero.
No programs, tests, scripts, checkers, builds, compilers, or benchmarks were
run.

## DSATUR greedy graph coloring (2026-11-15)

The coloring inventory contains fixed-order degree-first greedy coloring and
several exact search profiles, but no DSATUR saturation-degree heuristic.
Added [`dsatur_greedy_coloring`](d/dsatur_greedy_coloring/README.md), which
selects each uncolored vertex by distinct colored-neighbor count, then
remaining uncolored degree and vertex ID, assigning its lowest available
color. The bounded simple-graph contract pins canonical edges, deterministic
ties, and packed output. Incremental-bitset and adjacency-matrix references,
workload fixtures, a static package checker, scalar-suite wiring, and ten
language ports are present. The ports received static review only. See
Brélaz's [1979 paper](https://doi.org/10.1145/359094.359101) for the algorithm
description; only algorithm ideas were used. No programs, tests, scripts,
checkers, builds, compilers, or benchmarks were run.

## Karger–Klein–Tarjan recursive minimum spanning forest (2026-11-15)

The local `kkt_mst_sampling_filter` implements only the sampled-forest
F-heavy/F-light classification step; it has no Borůvka contractions or
recursive calls. Added [`kkt_recursive_mst`](k/kkt_recursive_mst/README.md)
for the complete KKT structure: two Borůvka contractions, independent
edge sampling, recursive sample-forest construction, F-heavy pruning, and a
second recursive call. The bounded profile pins SplitMix64 seed replay and
`(weight,input_edge_id)` tie-breaking, permits disconnected inputs, and returns
the original-edge-ID mask of the unique minimum spanning forest. A recursive
reference, independent Kruskal oracle, workload, static package checker,
scalar-suite wiring, and ten language ports are present. The original KKT
[1995 paper](https://doi.org/10.1145/201019.201022) supplies algorithm
descriptions only. No programs, tests, scripts, checkers, builds, compilers, or
benchmarks were run.

## Fixed-point HITS hub-authority ranking (2026-11-15)

The local graph-ranking inventory includes PageRank variants, including
GAPBS's in-place binary32 pull update, but no HITS hub-authority recurrence.
HITS alternates incoming-link authority sums and outgoing-link hub sums; this
is a distinct ranking process. Added [`hits_fixed_point`](h/hits_fixed_point/README.md)
with a bounded directed simple graph, fixed iteration count, integer scale
1,000,000, L1 floor normalization, and a weighted scalar checksum. Ten ports,
an edge-list primary oracle, dense-matrix independent oracle, workload,
README/RIGHTS, static package checker, and `i64_array_scalar` runner/verifier
hooks are present. The fixed-point rules are pinned explicitly; no source code
or prose was reused. See Kleinberg's [1999 paper](https://doi.org/10.1145/324133.324140).
No programs, tests, scripts, checkers, builds, compilers, or benchmarks were run.

## Minimum refueling stops with a max-heap (`minimum_refueling_stops_heap`) (2026-11-15)

The local [`gas_station`](g/gas_station/README.md) benchmark finds a feasible
start for a circular gas/cost route. LeetCode 871 describes a separate
one-way route problem that minimizes selected stops. Added a bounded profile
that inserts stations as they become reachable and defers each choice until
reach must increase, then removes the largest available fuel from a max-heap.
The greedy primary and descending-stop dynamic-programming oracle are
independent. Ten language ports, boundary and malformed fixtures, package
inventory, and `i64_array_scalar` runner/verifier wiring are present. Sources:
the official [problem](https://leetcode.com/problems/minimum-number-of-refueling-stops/)
and [editorial](https://leetcode.com/problems/minimum-number-of-refueling-stops/editorial/);
algorithm idea only. No LeetCode code, examples, tests, or problem text were
copied. No programs, tests, scripts, checkers, builds, compilers, or
benchmarks were run.

## Fenwick binary-lifting frequency selection (`fenwick_kth`) (2026-11-15)

The local [`fenwick_tree`](f/fenwick_tree/README.md) package supports point
updates and range sums but does not select by occurrence rank. Added a bounded
frequency multiset profile with point additions/removals and one-based kth
selection. Its primary walks Fenwick blocks from the highest power of two down;
the independent oracle scans the ordered frequencies. Ten language ports,
fixtures, package inventory, and `i64_array_scalar` runner/verifier wiring are
present. This differs from [`ordered_set_avl_order_statistics`](o/ordered_set_avl_order_statistics/README.md),
which uses subtree sizes over unique arbitrary keys, and from
[`segment_tree_max_right`](s/segment_tree_max_right/README.md), which searches

[search-with-powers-of-two](https://cp-algorithms.com/num_methods/binary_search.html#search-with-powers-of-2)
and [Fenwick tree](https://cp-algorithms.com/data_structures/fenwick.html)

## Weighted two-vertex cuts (`two_vertex_cuts_spqr`) (2026-11-15)

The existing [`vertex_connectivity`](v/vertex_connectivity/README.md) computes
minimum separator cardinality but does not count how many components remain
after each vertex-pair deletion. Added a bounded profile for simple biconnected
graphs of three to eight vertices. Its primary uses exhaustive proper split
discovery, paired virtual edges, and reduced S/P/R skeletons to generate
separation-pair candidates; a BFS on the original graph computes exact
component multiplicity. The independent oracle directly scans every pair.
Ten language ports, fixture workload, rights/provenance notes, a static
package inventory, and `i64_array_scalar` suite wiring are present. Sources:
Library Checker proposal [#1427](https://github.com/yosupo06/library-checker-problems/issues/1427),
Gutwenger–Mutzel's SPQR implementation paper, and Hopcroft–Tarjan's classical
triconnected decomposition. The bounded profile does not claim a linear-time
implementation or support general graphs with articulation blocks. See the
[guide](t/two_vertex_cuts_spqr/README.md),
[workload](t/two_vertex_cuts_spqr/workload.json), and
[rights note](t/two_vertex_cuts_spqr/RIGHTS.md).

## GraphAIBench GNNS query profile (`graphai_gnns_hill_climbing`) (2026-11-15)

The local `nearest_neighbour_search` benchmark is exact KD-tree traversal. The
distinct paper algorithm GNNS performs approximate hill climbing over a
prebuilt directed k-NN graph; GraphAIBench's pinned OpenMP file is only an
empty per-vertex stub, so this is a clean-room paper-derived profile rather
than a GraphAIBench source port. The bounded contract supplies the offline
graph and one start (`R=1`), fixes `K=1`, scans at most the first `E` outgoing
neighbors in ascending vertex ID, and performs at most `T` strict-improvement
moves. No visited set is used because distance strictly decreases on every
move. The profile includes ten language ports, mask-based and adjacency-list
oracles, package inventory, fixtures, and scalar-suite wiring. Source:
Hajebi et al., [IJCAI 2011 proceedings page and paper
PDF](https://ijcai.org/proceedings/2011/222); the algorithm idea is cited only,
with no source code or prose reused. See the

## Fiduccia–Mattheyses hypergraph bipartitioning (`fiduccia_mattheyses_hypergraph_bipartitioning`) (2026-11-15)

The repository has a Kernighan–Lin netlist-bisection profile, but it locks and
swaps opposite-side vertex pairs and uses a crossing-pair cost. FM locks one
vertex at a time and minimizes the number of cut nets with gain buckets, so it
is a distinct partition algorithm. Added a bounded half-split hypergraph
profile with deterministic bucket ties, a one-vertex balance window, and
earliest-best-prefix acceptance. The direct gain-rescoring oracle is checked
against an independent oracle that recounts each candidate cut; bounded
fixtures, a static package checker, scalar-suite wiring, and ten ports are
present. See Fiduccia and Mattheyses's [1982 paper](https://doi.org/10.1109/DAC.1982.1585498);
algorithm idea only. See the [guide](f/fiduccia_mattheyses_hypergraph_bipartitioning/README.md),

[rights note](f/fiduccia_mattheyses_hypergraph_bipartitioning/RIGHTS.md).

## Random_Mate weighted list ranking (`list_ranking_random_mate`) (2026-11-15)

The existing list-ranking package covers deterministic 3-color/popular-class
contraction. Added the distinct parallel-list-ranking Random_Mate rule:
synchronously read supplied per-round male/female bits, splice successors on

- **KACTL `IntervalCover` (`interval_cover`):** This is a separate greedy
  problem: choose the fewest supplied half-open intervals that cover a target,

  maintain a union under updates like `interval_container`, and it does not
  merely merge a batch like `merge_intervals`. The clean-room
  [ten-language implementation](i/interval_cover/README.md) uses KACTL's

## RosettaCodeData popular-title range 59–57: Yellowstone permutation integrated (2026-11-18)

The title-only audit compared the count bands 59 through 57 in the
[RosettaCodeData popular-tasks index](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/acmeism/RosettaCodeData/main/popular-tasks)
against local package names, README contracts, and active ledger entries.
Existing matches in this range include adaptive Simpson integration,
Hofstadter Figure–Figure sequences, square-free classification, Gaussian
elimination, convex hull, and digital-root packages. Runtime,
service, graphics, audio, and language-feature titles were excluded as
non-algorithm benchmarks; Heronian-triangle and named-number titles do not
alone pin one deterministic bounded operation. The `Chebyshev coefficients`
title does not identify its sample-node or normalization convention, so it was
not reserved from title-only evidence; local Clenshaw evaluation is a different
operation. `Yellowstone sequence` (A098550) had no matching local
package or reservation. It is materially distinct from EKG, Mian–Chowla,
Van Eck, and Hofstadter sequence packages: each new term depends on the prior
two values and is the least unused positive integer sharing a factor with
`a(n-2)` while coprime to `a(n-1)`.

Reserve `yellowstone_permutation_prefix` for this clean-room bounded profile.
Its scalar input is `[N,candidate_cap]`, with `1<=N<=64` and
`3<=candidate_cap<=256`. Indexing is 1-based and `a(1)=1`, `a(2)=2`,
`a(3)=3`; those base requests return directly. For each requested `n>=4`,
scan candidate values from 1 upward through the inclusive cap, skipping any
value already in the generated prefix and selecting the first `x` satisfying
`gcd(x,a(n-2))>1` and `gcd(x,a(n-1))=1`. If any requested step has no candidate
within the cap, the input is invalid and the scalar result is `-1`; the profile
makes no claim that every cap suffices. The workload uses successful terms
whose published prefix values fit the cap, plus a small-cap exhaustion case.
The primary uses Euclid GCD and a used-value table; the independent reference
uses trial prime-factor extraction, set intersection for common-factor tests,
and a linear scan of the prefix for membership. The 256-entry candidate bound
and 64-term prefix fit fixed bounded storage; values remain positive i64s.
Primary algorithm source: Applegate, Havermann, Selcoe, Shevelev, Sloane, and
Zumkeller, “The Yellowstone Permutation,” *Journal of Integer Sequences* 18
(2015), Article 15.6.7, [paper](https://www.maths.tcd.ie/EMIS/journals/JIS/VOL18/Sloane/sloane9.pdf).
The ten language ports, two Python references, workload, provenance/rights,
README, inventory, static inventory source, and `i64_array_scalar`
runner/verifier plus catalog integration are complete under
`benchmarks/y/yellowstone_permutation_prefix/`. The popular-title index is
discovery only. No Rosetta task text, code, or fixtures are used. All project
execution remains disabled for this package.

## RosettaCodeData popular-title range 56–54: arithmetic derivative integrated (2026-11-18)

The next title-only pass compared count bands 56 through 54 in the
[RosettaCodeData popular-tasks index](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/acmeism/RosettaCodeData/main/popular-tasks)
with local paths, package contracts, and ledger reservations. The shunting-yard
title maps to existing infix-to-postfix packages; bounded knapsack maps to the
monotone-queue and binary-grouping profiles. Wireworld is a cellular-automaton
rule variant of the local synchronous grid simulators; the title alone does not
pin a benchmark's grid, boundary, or output convention. Ulam-spiral, GUI,
format, and animation titles were excluded as visualization/representation
profiles or underspecified from title-only evidence. Exact package and ledger
search found no arithmetic-derivative implementation or reservation. This
operation differs from [`mobius_function`](m/mobius_function/README.md),
[`liouville_lambda`](l/liouville_lambda/README.md), and factorization packages:
it is the unique product-rule derivation with `D(1)=0`, `D(p)=1` for primes,
and `D(ab)=aD(b)+bD(a)`.

Profile `arithmetic_derivative` for scalar input `[n]`, `0<=n<=10^12`, returning
`D(n)` with `-1` for malformed/out-of-domain input. The primary groups the
prime factorization `n=∏p^e` and accumulates `(n/p)*e` for each distinct prime.
An independent recursive reference applies the product rule one prime factor
at a time, `D(pq)=pD(q)+q`, with `D(1)=0`. Trial division performs at most
500,000 candidate-divisor checks through `sqrt(n)` plus at most 39 factor
removals at the domain cap; its explicit scalar state is under 64 bytes and
the workspace cap is 256 bytes. The reference makes at most 39 recursive
product-rule steps, each testing at most 500,000 least-factor candidates
(at most 19.5 million total), with 40 stack frames including its base call.
For n>=1, `D(n)=n∑e_p/p <= n*floor(log2(n))/2`; with D(0)=0 separately,
valid output is at most 1.95e13 and safely fits i64. Primary source: E. J. Barbeau, “Remarks on
an Arithmetic Derivative,” *Canadian Mathematical Bulletin* 4(2) (1961),
117–122, [DOI 10.4153/CMB-1961-013-0](https://doi.org/10.4153/CMB-1961-013-0).
The ten language ports, primary factorization oracle, independent product-rule
reference, workload, provenance/rights, README, static inventory/checker
source, and `i64_array_scalar` runner/verifier plus catalog integration are
complete under `benchmarks/a/arithmetic_derivative/`. The title index is
discovery only; no Rosetta task text or code is used. No programs, tests, scripts, checkers,
builds, compilers, profilers, or benchmarks were run.

## Wilson loop-erased uniform spanning tree integrated (2026-11-18)

Reserve `wilson_uniform_spanning_tree` for Wilson's `RandomTreeWithRoot`
procedure: grow a rooted tree by simple random walks from vertices in a fixed
order, overwrite successor links to erase loops chronologically, and add each
walk's final loop-erased path when it reaches the current tree. This is
distinct from local MST/forest algorithms, which optimize deterministic edge
weights; [`counting_spanning_trees_undirected`](c/counting_spanning_trees_undirected/README.md),
which counts trees; and [`tree_random_walk_edge_hitting_cost`](t/tree_random_walk_edge_hitting_cost/README.md),
which computes expected traversal costs on a supplied tree. The bounded
replay frame is `[n,m,root,sorted_simple_edges(2m),q,draws(q)]`, with
`1<=n<=8`, a connected undirected simple graph, and `0<=q<=64*(n-1)`.
Each draw is an ordinal `0..6` into the current vertex's sorted neighbor list
and must be less than that vertex's degree when consumed. Visit non-root
starts in ascending ID order. Each walk may consume at most 64 draws; reject
an incomplete walk, invalid consumed choice, or leftover tape word. The
`n=1`, `q=0` case is valid and has empty output. Emit `(child,parent)` pairs
for non-root children in ascending ID order, serialized as little-endian
i64s; output is at most 112 bytes. Valid and one-extra-word parse bounds are
508 and 509 i64 words, and workspace is capped at 2,048 bytes. Caller-supplied
draws make the workload deterministic; it claims no uniformity or randomness
for a fixed tape. The primary follows the paper's successor-pointer process;
the independent reference buffers each walk and applies a last-occurrence
chronological loop erasure afterward. The package, ten ports, references,
workload, provenance/rights, static inventory, and `i64_array_bytes_output`
runner/verifier plus catalog integration are complete under
`benchmarks/w/wilson_uniform_spanning_tree/`. Primary source: David B. Wilson, “Generating Random Spanning
Trees More Quickly than the Cover Time,” STOC 1996, DOI
[10.1145/237814.237880](https://doi.org/10.1145/237814.237880), Figure 1
and `RandomTreeWithRoot` in the [author-hosted paper](https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~15859n/RelatedWork/RandomTrees-Wilson.pdf).
Only the algorithm description is used; no code, prose, or fixtures are
reused. No programs, tests, scripts, checkers, builds, compilers, profilers,
or benchmarks were run.

## RosettaCodeData popular-title range 53–51: taxicab minimum representations integrated (2026-11-18)

The title-only audit compared count bands 53 through 51 in the
[RosettaCodeData popular-tasks index](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/acmeism/RosettaCodeData/main/popular-tasks)
with local package paths, catalog contracts, and reservations. The safe/Sophie–Germain
prime titles overlap the existing [`germain_prime_and_safe_prime`](g/germain_prime_and_safe_prime/README.md)
profile; Mersenne primes and Doomsday are already represented, and the Pascal
triangle titles map to existing Pascal-row packages. Display, GUI, file, and
language-feature titles were excluded as non-kernel or representation tasks.
The pre-audit local inventory and ledger contained no Taxicab or
two-positive-cube sum enumerator. `taxicab_number_minimum_representations`
implements the least
positive integer expressible as a sum of two positive cubes in `k` distinct
unordered ways, with `k∈{2,3}`. The bounded scalar ABI is `[k]`, returning the
least value and `-1` for malformed/out-of-domain input. The row-wise min-heap
merge initializes the monotone rows `a^3+b^3` for `1<=a<=b<=444`, removes
globally smallest pairs, counts equal sums, and advances each removed row.
Christian Boyer’s primary paper defines Taxicab(n) as the least such value and
gives Taxicab(2)=1,729 and Taxicab(3)=87,539,319. Since `445^3` exceeds the
largest result, every positive root in a representation of either result is
at most 444. The search has at most 98,790 unordered pairs, O(P log 444) time,
and a fixed 444-entry heap of 12-byte nodes (5,328 bytes); workspace is capped
at 8,192 bytes. An independent oracle materializes and sorts all pair sums.
The ten-port package and shared scalar runner/verifier plus catalog are
integrated under `benchmarks/t/taxicab_number_minimum_representations/`.
Primary source: Boyer, “New Upper Bounds for Taxicab and Cabtaxi Numbers,”
*Journal of Integer Sequences* 11 (2008), [Article 08.1.6](https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL11/Boyer/boyer.html).

examples, or fixtures are copied. No programs, tests, scripts, checkers,
