## NIST DADS keys-only IBLT set reconciliation integrated (2026-11-18)

`invertible_bloom_lookup_table_reconciliation` profiles the keys-only
set-difference form of an invertible Bloom lookup table. The local
[`bloom_filter`](b/bloom_filter/README.md) answers approximate membership
queries, while [`xor_filter_peeling`](x/xor_filter_peeling/README.md) peels a
three-uniform hash graph to assign fingerprints for membership. Neither
recovers which keys occur in one supplied set but not another. The bounded
profile accepts two sorted, unique key sets, each of size at most eight, with
keys in `0..63`; it adds the first set to a fixed table and subtracts the
second. The table has three 16-cell subtables and deterministic locations
`h0(x)=x mod 16`, `h1(x)=16+((3x+5) mod 16)`,
`h2(x)=32+((5x+9) mod 16)`. Each cell stores a signed count, key sum, and
checksum sum using `g(x)=x^2+3x+7`. Repeatedly peel the lowest-index cell
whose count is `+1` or `-1` and whose signed key/checksum agree; emit the key
as first-set-only or second-set-only and undo its contribution at all three
locations. Output also records whether every cell reached zero; a nonempty
2-core is a valid incomplete decode. This fixed-hash replay makes no
probability or random-hash guarantee. The independent oracle rebuilds the
residual table from the original difference terms and prior peel corrections,
then rescan it from slot zero, rather than mutating the table in place. The
NIST DADS [IBLT entry](https://xlinux.nist.gov/dads/HTML/invertibleBloomTable.html)
points to Goodrich and Mitzenmacher, “Invertible Bloom Lookup Tables,”
[arXiv:1101.2245](https://arxiv.org/abs/1101.2245), especially §§2.2–2.4
and §3, Figure 3. The package is ready under
`benchmarks/i/invertible_bloom_lookup_table_reconciliation/`: ten ports, the
mutating-table primary and residual-rebuild independent references, workload,
provenance/rights, and static inventory. Its suite ABI is
`i64_array_bytes_output`; valid inputs contain at most 18 i64 words (19-word
parser boundary), output is at most 152 bytes, and workspace is capped at
2,048 bytes. The shared byte-output runner/verifier and catalog registration
are integrated. Only the mathematical method is used; no code, prose, or
fixtures are reused. No
programs, tests, scripts, checkers, builds, compilers, profilers, or benchmarks
were run.

## Zeckendorf arithmetic: direct addition (2026-11-18)

Added [`zeckendorf_addition`](z/zeckendorf_addition/README.md), a bounded
three-pass normalizer that adds canonical Fibonacci-weight bit vectors without
decoding them to ordinary integers. This is separate from
[`fibonacci_integer_code`](f/fibonacci_integer_code/README.md), which encodes
each integer independently. The primary follows Ahlbach, Usatine, Frougny, and
Pippenger's four-position left-to-right rules, then applies a right-to-left and
left-to-right `011→100` pass. The finite-width cleanup includes `021→110`, the
three-digit specialization of the paper's `021x→110x` rule; the paper's
enumerated terminal cleanup omits this case, which the `6+7` regression fixture
exposes. A high-order zero is retained before stage two so output expansion is
not truncated. The independent reference decodes by Fibonacci weights and
greedily re-encodes.

The profile accepts two canonical vectors of up to 64 bits, returns up to 66
ASCII bytes, and uses a 256-byte fixed workspace. Ten language ports, 21 fixture
cases, provenance/rights, static inventory, and shared `i64_array_bytes_output`
runner/verifier integration are included. Discovery used the pinned
RosettaCodeData task title only; algorithm details come from Ahlbach et al.,
[“Efficient Algorithms for Zeckendorf Arithmetic”](https://www.fq.math.ca/Papers1/51-3/AhlbachUsatineFrougnyPippenger.pdf).

## Vogel approximation method (`vogel_approximation_transportation`) — complete

Shore, [“The Transportation Problem and the Vogel Approximation Method”](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1540-5915.1970.tb00792.x), describes VAM as a shortcut for constructing an initial transportation solution and notes that it need not be optimal. The RosettaGit [Vogel task](https://rosettagit.org/tasks/vogels-approximation-method/) is a discovery reference only. The deterministic penalty and allocation steps are cross-checked against the Open University [VAM course chapter](https://egyankosh.ac.in/bitstream/123456789/28668/1/Unit-7.pdf).

The bounded `vogel_approximation_transportation` profile accepts balanced
transportation tables with input `[R,C,costs row-major,supply[R],demand[C]]`,
`1<=R,C<=3`, unit
costs in `0..9`, and positive supply/demand values in `1..3`. The exact frame
length is `2+R*C+R+C`; the maximum valid frame is 17 words and the maximum
parseable frame is 18. At each iteration compute each active row/column's
penalty as the second-smallest active cell cost minus the smallest. A lone
active cell receives penalty 10, which exceeds every possible finite penalty
and makes the forced allocation explicit. Select the largest penalty, with
row candidates scanned before columns and increasing index within each group;
ties retain the earlier candidate. In the selected line choose the cheapest
cell, breaking equal costs by the lowest partner index, and allocate
`min(remaining supply,remaining demand)`. Remove all exhausted rows and
columns. Continue until balanced supply and demand are exhausted.

Return `total_cost*4^9 + allocation_signature`, where the low nine base-4
digits hold the allocation matrix in fixed 3x3 row-major positions, including
zero digits for absent rows/columns. Every allocation fits one digit because
each supplied or demanded amount is at most three. The maximum valid encoded
result is `81*4^9+(4^9-1)=21,495,807`; invalid/null input returns `-1`. The
algorithm is distinct from the exact `minimum_cost_b_flow` package: the output
is a deterministic VAM initial feasible allocation, not a minimum-cost flow.
The package includes all ten language ports, a penalty-scan primary reference,
an independently structured sorted-candidate reference, bounded workload
fixtures, rights/provenance notes, and a package-local static inventory. The
scalar runner/verifier, CATALOG entry, and root README are wired. Only algorithm
descriptions are used; no task prose, examples, tests, or code are copied.
Static-only work; no programs, tests, scripts, checkers, builds, compilers,
profilers, or benchmarks were run.

## OI Wiki Entringer number (2026-11-18)

Added [`entringer_number`](e/entringer_number/README.md) from [OI Wiki's
Entringer Number article](https://oi-wiki.org/math/combinatorics/entringer/),
which defines `E(0,0)=1`, `E(n,0)=0` for `n>0`, and
`E(n,k)=E(n,k-1)+E(n-1,n-k)`. `E(n,k)` counts down-up alternating
permutations of `{0,...,n}` whose first element is `k`. Static package,
CATALOG, ledger, and reservation searches found no Entringer profile; the
nearby `zigzag_conversion` is a string layout operation, and Eulerian-number
counts by descents are a different statistic. Its `i64_array_scalar` input is
`[n,k]`, `0<=n<=12`, `0<=k<=n`; invalid input returns `-1`. The primary builds
one row at a time; an independent subset-state permutation count and tiny
direct enumeration provide separate references. The values fit signed i64:
each row entry is at most `(n+1)!<=13!`. Ten clean-room ports, workload,
provenance/rights, and package-local static inventory are present under
`benchmarks/e/entringer_number/`. Scalar runner/verifier, CATALOG, and README
registrations are integrated. No programs, tests, scripts, checkers, builds,
compilers, profilers, or benchmarks were run.

## Encyclopedia of Algorithms Chapter 274: Random Schedule — package and suite integrated (2026-11-17)

Implemented `packet_switching_random_schedule` as a bounded replay of the
Random Schedule policy specified in Albers and Jacobs, §3.2, “An Experimental
Study of New and Known Online Packet Buffering Algorithms,” DOI
[10.1007/s00453-008-9230-y](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00453-008-9230-y), in
the Chapter 274 multi-queue-switch setting. The profile bounds the switch to
2–4 queues, capacity 1–4, 1–8 slots, and at most one arrival per queue per
slot. Each arrival has a caller-supplied 32-bit priority word mapped into the
open interval `(0,1)`; the input tape replaces random draws and carries no
probabilistic guarantee. Each queue keeps at most `B` arrival tags, evicting
its oldest tag on overflow. Per slot, the policy marks and chooses the largest
unmarked priority globally and serves that tag's queue; when no unmarked tags
remain, it serves the smallest-index nonempty queue. Priority ties use the
smallest queue index and then oldest tag as deterministic refinements of the
source's arbitrary tie choices. It emits one queue index or `-1` per slot as
little-endian i64 bytes. This differs from local deterministic
[`packet_switching_sgr_multi_queue`](p/packet_switching_sgr_multi_queue/README.md)
and work-conserving packet-route replay. Ten language ports, two structurally
independent references, bounded workload fixtures, README/RIGHTS, static
inventory, and a package-local inventory checker are present. Static review
found the ten source paths and the hand-derived fixtures consistent with the
contract. The `i64_array_bytes_output` runner/verifier and CATALOG entry are now
integrated. No source code or protected text is reused; no executable checks
are run.

Charras–Lecroq's [Simon algorithm description](https://igm.univ-mlv.fr/~lecroq/string/node9.html) identifies the compact minimal prefix automaton: the forward edges are implied by the pattern, while only significant backward transitions are stored. ## Encyclopedia of Algorithms entry 331: maximum-cardinality popular matching (package complete)

The chapter crosswalk's [`ranked_matching_popular_matching`](r/ranked_matching_popular_matching/README.md) covers popular matching on one-sided ranked lists with ties and incomplete lists, but does not optimize the number of real posts assigned. ## Encyclopedia of Algorithms entry 331: tied-list maximum-cardinality popular matching (package complete)

completion times. All ten clean-room ports, an independent direct schedule

runner/verifier registration are present. Hand-derived workload cases include

## Abelian sandpile stabilization (`abelian_sandpile_stabilization`) (2026-11-16)

Dhar's primary paper, [“Self-Organized Critical State of Sandpile Automaton
Models”](https://repository.ias.ac.in/9280/1/311.pdf), defines integer site
heights and topplings by a dissipative toppling matrix. The
[RosettaGit task title](https://rosettagit.org/tasks/abelian-sandpile-model/)
was used only for discovery. Static package and reservation searches found no
existing sandpile/chip-firing profile; `game_of_life` is a neighboring but
different finite-state cellular automaton.

Added `abelian_sandpile_stabilization` as a bounded open-boundary square-grid
stabilization kernel with input `[rows,cols,cells...]`, `1<=rows,cols<=4`,
each initial height in `0..31`, and exact length `2+rows*cols`. Every site has
threshold four and sends one grain to each in-bounds orthogonal neighbor when
toppled; grains sent toward missing neighbors leave through the sink. Return
the stable row-major height vector packed in base four, `sum(height[i]*4^i)`;
malformed frames return `-1`. The primary uses a deterministic legal-toppling
queue, while an independent reference applies all currently enabled
topplings in synchronous batches. For coordinates `x=1..cols`, `y=1..rows`,
the nonnegative potential `phi=x(cols+1-x)/2+y(rows+1-y)/2` drops by two for
each legal toppling and is at most six per grain, so no valid frame requires
more than 1488 topplings. The maximum valid packed result is `4^16-1`. All ten
language ports, primary and independent references, hand-derived workload,
rights/provenance note, and package-local static inventory are present. The
scalar runner/verifier, README, CATALOG, and coverage crosswalk are wired.
Only algorithm descriptions are used; no task prose, examples, tests, or code
are copied. Static-only work; no programs, tests, scripts, checkers, builds,
compilers, profilers, or benchmarks were run.

## KACTL graph algorithms: Misra–Gries general edge coloring (`misra_gries_edge_coloring`) — complete

The current KACTL graph chapter imports [`EdgeColoring.h`](https://github.com/kth-competitive-programming/kactl/blob/main/content/graph/EdgeColoring.h), which specifies a proper `Delta+1` edge coloring of simple undirected graphs using the Misra–Gries/Vizing fan procedure. The primary source is Misra and Gries, [“A Constructive Proof of Vizing’s Theorem”](https://doi.org/10.1016/0020-0190(92)90041-S), with the [author-hosted paper](https://www.cs.utexas.edu/~misra/psp.dir/vizing.pdf). Static searches of benchmark paths, `CATALOG.md`, and active reservations found only [`bipartite_edge_coloring`](b/bipartite_edge_coloring/README.md), which decomposes bipartite multigraphs into the optimal `Delta` matchings, and [`tree_min_cost_proper_coloring`](t/tree_min_cost_edge_coloring/README.md), which optimizes shared color costs on trees. Neither handles proper `Delta+1` coloring of general simple graphs.

The package `misra_gries_edge_coloring` accepts loopless simple undirected graphs with
`1<=N<=6`, `0<=M<=6`, and input `[N,M,(u,v)*M]`. Edge endpoints are in
`0..N-1`; duplicate unordered edges and self-loops are invalid. The exact
frame length is `2+2*M` (maximum valid 14, maximum parseable 15); null or
malformed input returns `-1`. Process uncolored edges in input order. For
each, extend a maximal fan at its lower-index endpoint by scanning neighbor
IDs upward and adding the first unused neighbor whose edge color is free at
the current fan tail. Choose the smallest free color at the center and the
smallest free color at the tail, invert their maximal alternating path from
the center, choose the smallest fan-prefix endpoint where the tail color is
free, rotate that fan prefix, and assign the freed color to the newly
uncolored edge. These scan/tie choices are deterministic profile rules; the
paper leaves the choices nondeterministic. Use palette `0..Delta` for a
nonempty graph and palette size zero when `M=0`. Pack the palette size in the
high field and each edge's color in input order in six fixed 3-bit fields:
`palette_size*8^6 + sum(color[i]*8^i)`. The valid result range is
`0..1,760,109`. This observable coloring is
distinct from the existing optimal bipartite edge-coloring and tree-only
costed edge coloring. Ten language ports, a primary Misra–Gries reference, an
independent coloring certificate verifier, workload, README/RIGHTS, static
inventory checker, scalar runner/verifier registration, CATALOG, and root
README are wired. Only algorithm descriptions are used; no code or prose is
copied. No programs, tests, scripts, checkers, builds, compilers, profilers,
or benchmarks have been run.

## Encyclopedia of Algorithms 212: randomized uncapacitated facility-location add-one/delete-many (`facility_location_randomized_add_delete_many`) — package complete

The supplied Encyclopedia chapter's Facility Location section describes the
Charikar–Guha randomized neighborhood: sample a facility candidate, mark
clients strictly closer to it than their currently assigned facility, then
consider deleting each open facility whose fee plus the remaining assigned
service cost exceeds assigning those clients to the sampled candidate. The
chapter's equation defines this as uncapacitated facility location; this is
not the capacitated T-Hunt procedure in §5 of Arya et al. The original
Charikar–Guha SIAM paper describes a random candidate draw at each iteration
and accepts only positive-gain updates. The current deterministic
`facility_location_add_delete_swap` tests one-copy add/delete/swap neighbors
and does not implement this multi-delete rule. Implemented
`facility_location_randomized_add_delete_many` as a bounded replay profile:
input `[n,F,Q,initial_mask,assignment[n],demand[n],D[(n+F)^2 row-major],fee[F],draw[Q]]`, with `1<=n,F<=5`, `1<=Q<=8`, integer demands `1..10`, integer metric distances `0..1000`, opening fees `0..1000`, a nonempty feasible supplied start assignment, and facility-index draws in `0..F-1`. Every supplied draw is an explicit random-choice tape value so workloads are reproducible; this profile makes no probabilistic guarantee. An already-open draw is a no-op. For a closed candidate, use strict distance comparison for the reassignment set and strict positive local drop savings, then accept the combined add/drop move only if total cost strictly decreases. The max frame is 127 valid/128 parseable words; output is a little-endian per-draw cost/acceptance trace plus the final cost, open mask, assignment, and accepted-step count. Ten language ports, independent direct subset-enumeration reference, workload, README/RIGHTS, static inventory checker, byte-output runner/verifier registration, and CATALOG/root README entries are complete. The entry 212 crosswalk remains partial because additional capacitated facility-location coverage is needed. Only the chapter and paper descriptions are used; no source code or prose is copied. No programs, tests, scripts, checkers, builds, compilers, profilers, or benchmarks have been run.

## Encyclopedia of Algorithms 634: suffix-array/PSV/NSV LPF factorization (`lz77_lpf_suffix_array`) — package complete

Simon J. Puglisi's [Lempel-Ziv Compression entry](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4939-2864-4_634) cites the suffix-array longest-previous-factor parser; the method is specified in Kärkkäinen, Kempa, and Puglisi, [“Linear Time Lempel-Ziv Factorization: Simple, Fast, Small”](https://cpm.cs.helsinki.fi/cpm13/16_kempa.pdf). For each parse position, the method obtains previous- and next-smaller suffix starts from PSV/NSV arrays over the suffix array, compares their LCP lengths, chooses NSV only when its LCP is strictly larger (PSV on a tie), emits the selected longest previous factor, and advances by `max(match_length,1)`. A zero length is a one-symbol literal. The output preserves each factor as `(source_position, match_length)`, using source `-1` for literals; it is distinct from [`lz77_infinite_rightmost`](l/lz77_infinite_rightmost/README.md), which emits a following character and consumes it in each nonterminal token. For example, on `ababc`, the LPF-only profile emits `[(-1,0),(-1,0),(0,2),(-1,0)]`, while the existing next-character profile encodes the final `c` in the third token.

Reserved `lz77_lpf_suffix_array` for a bounded byte-output profile over
`[n, symbols...]`, with `0<=n<=32` and symbols in `0..255`. The primary builds
a suffix array, derives PSV/NSV by monotone stacks, and computes LCPs for the
two candidates; the independent oracle scans all earlier text positions and
compares suffix ranks to reconstruct PSV/NSV without an SA or monotone stack.
The primary source's `(p,l)` phrase pair is retained as two little-endian i64
values per phrase; source `-1` denotes a literal, at most 512 output bytes.
The bounded suffix sort and direct LCPs make no claim to the paper's linear-time
bound. Ten clean-room language ports, workload, README/RIGHTS, two references,
and a static inventory are present. The byte-output runner/verifier, CATALOG,
root README, and Encyclopedia crosswalk register the profile. Static source
review found aligned tie, sentinel, validation, and capacity behavior across
the ports. The book and paper are copyrighted; only algorithm descriptions are

## Encyclopedia of Algorithms 212: outer capacitated T-Hunt local search (`capacitated_facility_location_t_hunt_local_search`) — package complete

Arya et al.'s [“Local Search Heuristics for k-Median and Facility Location
Problems”](https://www.cse.iitd.ac.in/~pandit/lsearchSICOMP.pdf), §2 Figure 1,
defines a generic strict-improvement loop from an arbitrary feasible start.
Section 5 states that the service cost for a fixed multiset of facility copies
is its minimum-cost feasible assignment; §5.1 equation (9) defines the
capacitated neighborhood with single-copy additions and multi-copy add/drop
moves. Figure 13 on p. 559 specifies T-Hunt: for `l=1..m`, solve the profit
knapsack with capacity `l*u[s']`, returning the first subset whose modeled
cost strictly improves. The paper leaves initial states, improving-neighbor
selection, and ties arbitrary, and notes T-Hunt may miss some improving
neighbors. Therefore the package exposes an explicit deterministic profile:
type-ID scan order, single-copy addition before T-Hunt, exact minimum-cost
assignment after each accepted move, and a scan-specific stop condition.
It does not claim that termination certifies local optimality over every
neighbor in the full mathematical neighborhood.

The package `capacitated_facility_location_t_hunt_local_search` is distinct
from [`capacitated_facility_location_t_hunt`](c/capacitated_facility_location_t_hunt/README.md),
which evaluates a single supplied state and target, and from the uncapacitated
one-copy add/delete/swap search in
[`facility_location_add_delete_swap`](f/facility_location_add_delete_swap/README.md).
Its byte-output ABI accepts
`[n,F,Q,D[(n+F)^2],opening_fee[F],capacity[F],copy_type[Q]]`, with
`1<=n<=4`, `1<=F<=3`, `1<=Q<=4`, metric entries and fees in `0..20`, and
capacities in `1..n`. The initial multiset must have enough aggregate
capacity. Maximum input/parseable lengths are 62/63 words. It emits
`[final_cost,accepted_steps,copy_count,copy_type[copy_count],assignment[n]]`
as little-endian i64 values, with a proved maximum of 5,208 bytes. Integer
objective bound 160 implies at most 160 strict improvements and at most 644
final copies. All ten language ports, primary exact-weight DP oracle,
independent weight-class knapsack reference, workload, README/RIGHTS, static
inventory checker, byte-output runner/verifier registration, CATALOG/root
README entries, and Encyclopedia crosswalk are complete. The book entry's
Capacitated Variants subsection cites Arya et al. and summarizes the
locality-gap result but does not give this outer-loop schedule; the profile
follows the paper's generic procedure and T-Hunt description. Only algorithm
descriptions are used, with no copied code or prose. No programs, tests,
scripts, checkers, builds, compilers, profilers, or benchmarks have been run.

## Encyclopedia of Algorithms 171: Nagamochi–Ibaraki sparse k-connectivity certificate — package and suite complete

Nagamochi and Ibaraki's [“A Linear-Time Algorithm for Finding a Sparse
k-Connected Spanning Subgraph of a k-Connected Graph,” §2](https://gi.cebitec.uni-bielefeld.de/_media/teaching/2013summer/936nagamochi-ibaraki-1992-sparse-k-connected-subgraph.pdf)
defines FOREST, which assigns each edge to a forest layer by repeatedly
scanning an unscanned maximum-rank vertex. The first `k` layers preserve every
pairwise edge-connectivity value up to `k`. The local profile uses a simple
graph with `3<=n<=8`, `0<=m<=28`, `1<=k<=3`, lowest-ID maximum-rank ties, and
input-record adjacency order. Ten language ports emit input-aligned layer
labels, with zero for layers beyond the retained prefix. The primary follows
the rank scan; an independent full-edge scan is checked against all pairwise
cuts. Package docs, RIGHTS, bounded workload, callable static review, byte-
output runner/verifier, CATALOG, root README, and the DOI 171 crosswalk are
complete. No programs, tests, scripts, checkers, builds, compilers, profilers,
or benchmarks were run.

## Encyclopedia of Algorithms 171: Cheriyan–Thurimella matching-based 2-VCSS — package and suite complete

Cheriyan and Thurimella's [matching-based heuristic, §3.1](https://www.cs.du.edu/~ramki/papers/spanSubgraphs.pdf) first finds a minimum-size spanning edge set with degree at least `k-1`, then scans the remaining edges and keeps only those whose removal would break `k`-vertex-connectivity. The local profile fixes `k=2`: subset DP computes a maximum matching, which is completed to a minimum edge cover; a sequential input-order scan removes each non-cover edge if the graph remains connected after every single-vertex deletion. This is distinct from the two Khuller–Vishkin DFS constructions and from connectivity decision algorithms.

The package has ten language ports, a bottom-up DP reference, an independent matching-enumeration/articulation reference, bounded fixtures, a rights note, and byte-output runner/verifier registration. Input is a simple 2-vertex-connected graph with `3<=n<=8` and `3<=m<=28`; output contains selected normalized edge records in original input order. Static suite and metadata edits are complete. Compilation and execution remain outstanding.

## Encyclopedia of Algorithms 171: Khuller–Raghavachari phased 3-ECSS — package and suite complete

Khuller and Raghavachari's [unweighted phased algorithm, §3.1](https://www.cs.du.edu/~snarayan/sada/research/docs/p1-khuller.pdf) raises edge connectivity by two in each DFS phase. The local profile specializes the odd case `k=3`: root an input-order DFS at vertex 0, scan tree edges in postorder, and add the highest-going unused back edge whenever a one-edge cut still separates that tree edge's endpoints. Then scan the residual graph in input order to add a maximal spanning forest. This procedure is distinct from the Khuller–Vishkin 2-edge DFS construction, the fixed 2-edge deletion heuristic, and the Nagamochi–Ibaraki rank-layer certificate.

The package has ten language ports, a recursive/iterative DFS pair of references using independent edge-deletion and cut tests, 3-edge-connectivity fixtures, a rights note, and byte-output runner/verifier registration. Input is a simple 3-edge-connected graph with `4<=n<=8` and `6<=m<=28`; output lists selected input records. Static suite and metadata edits are complete. Compilation and execution remain outstanding.

Static source review confirms the cited paper title is “Improved Approximation Algorithms for Uniform Connectivity Problems.” The complete-graph K5 fixture follows the fixed DFS order: its first phase adds edge `(0,4)`, and the residual maximal forest skips `(2,4)`, yielding the documented nine-edge, 152-byte output. This was checked by tracing the bounded profile; no oracle, program, or test was run.

## Encyclopedia of Algorithms 634: Kosaraju–Manzini LZ78RL run transform — package and suite complete

The cited primary paper, Kosaraju and Manzini, [“Compression of Low Entropy
Strings with Lempel–Ziv Algorithms,” §3.1](https://doi.org/10.1137/S0097539797331105),
defines LZ78RL by replacing each maximal run `alpha^m` with the binary digits
of `m`, using `alpha` for one bits and a reserved zero symbol for zero bits,
then applying greedy LZ78 to the transformed stream. This composition is
distinct from ordinary/flexible LZ78 and standalone run-length encoding.
Implemented `lz78_run_length_transform` as a bounded clean-room profile with
source alphabet codes 1..3, a reserved zero transform symbol, explicit
terminal-phrase framing, and 776-byte maximum output. All ten language ports,
primary trie and independent phrase-set references, workload, README/RIGHTS,
and static package inventory are present. The i64-token ABI is registered in
the shared byte-output suite but does not measure the paper's theorem about
encoded bit length. The paper's code and prose are not reused; sources are
cited for algorithm attribution only. No project programs, tests, scripts,
checkers, builds, compilers, profilers, or benchmarks were run.

## OI Wiki divide-and-conquer DP partition optimization — implemented

Added `divide_conquer_dp_partition`, a bounded layered DP that partitions a
nonnegative sequence into exactly `k` contiguous groups and minimizes the sum
of squared group totals. The cost matrix satisfies the quadrangle inequality;
the leftmost optimal split positions are monotone, so each DP row is computed
with divide-and-conquer optimization. This is distinct from
[`knuth_optimized_optimal_binary_search_tree`](k/knuth_optimized_optimal_binary_search_tree/README.md),
which narrows roots in an interval-BST recurrence, and from convex-hull-trick,
WQS, and CDQ DP profiles. A full quadratic split scan is the independent
reference. Ten language ports, workload fixtures, README/RIGHTS, a
package-local static inventory checker, and `i64_array_scalar` runner/verifier
registration are present. The OI Wiki
[quadrangle-inequality chapter](https://en.oi-wiki.org/dp/opt/quadrangle/)
supplies the high-level algorithm description under CC BY-SA 4.0/SATA terms;
only that description was used.

The OI Wiki [Dynamic DP chapter](https://en.oi-wiki.org/dp/dynamic/)
describes maximum-weight independent set under vertex-weight replacements.
This is distinct from the one-shot [`tree_weighted_vertex_cover`](t/tree_weighted_vertex_cover/README.md)
profile: although complementing a vertex cover gives the static independent-set
value, the dynamic method maintains the answer through HLD, max-plus 2x2
matrices, and per-heavy-chain segment trees. Implemented as
[`dynamic_tree_maximum_weight_independent_set`](d/dynamic_tree_maximum_weight_independent_set/README.md)
with ten language ports, a full-DP replay oracle, bounded workload, static
inventory checker, and `i64_array_bytes_output` runner/verifier registration.
Existing dynamic tree packages maintain other aggregates and do not implement
this DP. Static-only; no programs, tests, scripts, static checkers, builds,
compilers, benchmarks, or profilers were run.

## CP-Algorithms Fermat factorization — implemented (2026-11-16)

Implemented `fermat_factorization` as a bounded odd-integer difference-of-squares
search. It starts at `ceil(sqrt(N))` and checks a fixed number of successive
`a` values for an exact square `a*a-N`, returning the first proper factor
`a-b`; a bounded miss returns zero. This differs from local trial division and
sieve profiles, Pollard rho's pseudorandom walk, Pollard p−1's smooth-order
modular exponentiation, and the Fermat-congruence benchmarks. The profile uses
`[N,max_steps]`, odd `3<=N<=10^12`, and `0<=max_steps<=4096`, keeping all squares
within signed 64-bit range. Ten language ports, primary and independent
oracles, workload fixtures, README/RIGHTS, and static inventory are present;
the scalar runner and verifier now register the workload. Source:
CP-Algorithms [Fermat's factorization method](https://cp-algorithms.com/algebra/factorization.html#fermats-factorization-method),
CC BY-SA 4.0; algorithm description only. No programs, tests, scripts, static
checkers, builds, compilers, benchmarks, or profilers were run.

## CP-Algorithms generalized Chinese remainder theorem — implemented (2026-11-16)

Implemented `generalized_chinese_remainder_theorem` for systems whose moduli
may share prime factors. The primary consolidates residues at each prime's
highest supplied power, rejects conflicts against the lower powers, then
combines the resulting pairwise-coprime constraints. The independent oracle
merges original congruences in order using extended gcd, without factoring.
The input is `[Q,r0,m0,...]`, with `1<=Q<=4`, `2<=m_i<=64`, canonical
residues, and product of supplied moduli at most 16,777,216. Inconsistent
systems return -2; malformed inputs return -1. Ten ports, dual oracles,
fixtures, README/RIGHTS, static inventory, and scalar runner/verifier
registration are present. This differs from the local pairwise-coprime
[`chinese_remainder_theorem`](c/chinese_remainder_theorem/README.md) profile.
Source: CP-Algorithms [solution for not coprime moduli](https://cp-algorithms.com/algebra/chinese-remainder-theorem.html#solution-for-not-coprime-moduli),
CC BY-SA 4.0; algorithm description only. No programs, tests, scripts, static
checkers, builds, compilers, benchmarks, or profilers were run.

fixtures by hand-derived objective values. The Library Checker
[task](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/yosupo06/library-checker-problems/master/graph/general_weighted_matching/task.md)
is the operation source. Korte and Vygen, *Combinatorial Optimization*,
Chapter 11, provide the explicit O(N^3) weighted-matching method reference.
Ten ports, dual small-domain references, fixtures, README/RIGHTS, a static
inventory, and scalar runner/verifier registration are present. The suite was
integrated statically; no programs, tests, checkers, builds, or benchmarks were
run.

## CP-Algorithms multiplicative order — implemented (2026-11-16)

Added the bounded `multiplicative_order` profile for a supplied residue and
modulus. It returns the least positive exponent taking a unit to one; valid
nonunits return zero. The primary factors `φ(m)` and reduces its prime factors
with modular-power tests, while the independent oracle enumerates successive
powers. This is distinct from `primitive_root`, whose local contract searches
candidate residues by enumerating distinct powers and returns a generator;
the algorithm article's order-reduction criterion is applied here to one
supplied unit. It is also distinct from `perfect_shuffle_order`, which finds a
permutation cycle length by simulating deck shuffles. Ten ports, references,
workload, README/RIGHTS, and static inventory are present for `2<=m<=1000`.
The scalar verifier uses the independent repeated-power oracle, exhaustively
generates all bases for moduli through 64, and checks null-input frames through
the declared parseable bound. Source: CP-Algorithms [Primitive Root](https://cp-algorithms.com/algebra/primitive-root.html),
CC BY-SA 4.0; mathematical criterion only. Suite integration was static; no
programs, tests, scripts, checkers, builds, compilers, benchmarks, or profilers
were run.

## CP-Algorithms continued-fraction convergents — implemented (2026-11-16)

Added `continued_fraction_convergents`, which emits the reduced numerator and
positive denominator for every finite prefix. The primary advances the standard
two-term numerator and denominator recurrences; the independent reference
evaluates each prefix as a nested rational expression. The bounded contract
supports 1 to 16 coefficients and writes little-endian signed 64-bit pairs via
the byte-output ABI. Ten ports, references, fixtures, README/RIGHTS, and a
static inventory are present. The byte-output recorder and verifier include
the workload checker, independent oracle, and bounded output capacity.
Source: CP-Algorithms [continued fractions](https://cp-algorithms.com/algebra/continued-fractions.html#convergents),
CC BY-SA 4.0; recurrence description only. No programs, tests, scripts,
checkers, builds, compilers, benchmarks, or profilers were run.

## TheAlgorithms Java observed-remove set (`observed_remove_set`) — implemented (2026-11-16)

Added [`observed_remove_set`](o/observed_remove_set/README.md) for the
add-wins observed-remove CRDT described by TheAlgorithms/Java's `ORSet.java`.
Existing `grow_only_set`, `lww_element_set`, and `two_pset` have different
update and conflict semantics. The bounded profile uses two replicas, 16
element IDs, at most 32 operations, and deterministic value tags
`(element, creator_replica, creator_sequence)`. A removal tombstones only tags
observed by that replica; merging a concurrent fresh tag preserves add-wins
behavior. The pinned Java `Pair` uses object identity equality, so the benchmark
is clean-room from the intended OR-Set state machine and does not copy that
implementation. Ten language ports, primary and independent references,
workload fixtures, README/RIGHTS, and a static inventory checker are present.
The scalar runner and verifier now check both references, include generated
traces and null-input boundaries, and register all ten ports. Source:
[TheAlgorithms/Java ORSet.java](https://github.com/TheAlgorithms/Java/blob/master/src/main/java/com/thealgorithms/datastructures/crdt/ORSet.java).

## TheAlgorithms Java virtual-time token bucket — implemented (2026-11-16)

Added [`token_bucket_rate_limiter_virtual_time`](t/token_bucket_rate_limiter_virtual_time/README.md)
as a deterministic profile for the pinned real-time token-bucket state machine.
Each request supplies whole elapsed ticks; the bucket refills before the

## CP-Algorithms current-index audit (2026-11-16)

## NIST DADS type-index crosswalk (2026-11-20)

Compared the six category headings on NIST's [type index](https://xlinux.nist.gov/dads/termsType.html)
with local package README contracts and active reservations. The page itself
reports a generated-index run date of 7 February 2025 and a footer update of
18 September 2017; this is a crosswalk of the currently served index, not a
claim that every definition page has been re-reviewed.

| Type-index heading | Disposition | Crosswalk result |
|---|---|---|
| Algorithmic Techniques | Excluded as umbrella entries; implemented through concrete methods | Broad labels such as divide and conquer, dynamic programming, greedy, backtracking, exhaustive search, and randomization do not by themselves pin one input/output kernel. Concrete methods under those labels map to local packages (for example, shortest paths, matching, selection, graph search, and dynamic programming). No standalone technique contract is added. |
| Data Structures | Implemented, duplicate/alias, or excluded when the title has no operation contract | Existing contracts cover representative structures including pairing heaps, interval trees, buddy allocation, cactus stacks, ROBDDs, extendible and linear hashing, and multiple probing/filter profiles. Index aliases map to canonical entries (including HMM, DAWG, ROBDD, SSTable, and 2-left hashing names). Generic representations and stub entries without specified operations do not establish additional benchmarks. |
| Definitions | Excluded as glossary vocabulary | This heading defines terms, complexity notation, graph properties, and computational models; it is not a list of procedures. Synonyms and cross-references are duplicates of their canonical terms. |
| Classic Problems | Implemented/variant where a local bounded problem contract exists; otherwise excluded as a problem statement without one method | Local examples include Chinese postman, DAG minimum path cover, selection, knapsack, path search, matching/flow, string matching, and finite-state-machine minimization. The index often names an objective rather than a unique algorithm, so no second package is inferred from aliases (for example, TSP/traveling salesman or LCS/longest common subsequence). Undecidable or unbounded formulations are excluded from this finite array-call suite. |
| Algorithms | Implemented, variant, duplicate, or excluded by method-level comparison | The targeted mappings recorded in the DADS register row and earlier DADS follow-ups cover the distinct sorting, search, hashing, coding, geometry, graph, and numerical methods reviewed to date. Alias pairs such as Ford–Bellman/Bellman–Ford, GCD/greatest common divisor, BWT/Burrows–Wheeler transform, and JSort/J sort do not create separate kernels. DADS Randomized-Select is a duplicate of the seeded randomized pivot-and-one-side-selection method in [`minimum_element_of_array`](m/minimum_element_of_array/README.md), with [`kth_order_statistic`](k/kth_order_statistic/README.md) covering the same quickselect family under a different local pivot contract. Quantum algorithms (Deutsch–Jozsa, Grover, Simon, and Shor) are excluded because the suite's classical ports cannot measure their oracle/gate algorithms; the local `shors_algorithm` is explicitly a classical order-finding sketch, not Shor's quantum circuit. |
| Entries with No Type | Individually classified below | The index's twelve entries include existing interval-tree, pairing-heap, OBDD, and path-cover coverage, plus stubs or underspecified terms that do not justify new contracts. |

The twelve no-type entries have these dispositions:

| Entry | Disposition and local comparison |
|---|---|
| [double left rotation](https://xlinux.nist.gov/dads/HTML/doubleLeftRotat.html); [double right rotation](https://xlinux.nist.gov/dads/HTML/doubleRightRotation.html) | Excluded: both DADS pages say no definition is present; no tree shape, precondition, or operation result is pinned. |
| [expandable hashing](https://xlinux.nist.gov/dads/HTML/expandableHashing.html) | Excluded for this index pass: the DADS page says no definition is present and cites Knott's paper only. It cannot be equated with the local extendible-hashing contract from the title alone. |
| [interval tree](https://xlinux.nist.gov/dads/HTML/intervaltree.html) | Implemented: [`interval_tree_point_stabbing`](i/interval_tree_point_stabbing/README.md) has a bounded static interval-tree stabbing contract. |
| [k-clustering](https://xlinux.nist.gov/dads/HTML/kclustering.html) | Excluded: the DADS page has no definition, and the title does not choose an objective, metric, or clustering method; local clustering packages have their own pinned contracts. |
| [OBDD](https://xlinux.nist.gov/dads/HTML/obdd.html); ordered binary decision diagram | Duplicate/covered representation family: [`binary_decision_graph`](b/binary_decision_graph/README.md) constructs a fixed-variable-order ROBDD; these two index labels are aliases, not separate operations. |
| [pairing heap](https://xlinux.nist.gov/dads/HTML/pairingHeap.html) | Implemented: [`pairing_heap`](p/pairing_heap/README.md) pins an ascending two-pass pairing-heap extraction trace. |
| [path cover](https://xlinux.nist.gov/dads/HTML/pathcover.html) | Duplicate/variant, with no further reservation: [`dag_minimum_path_cover`](d/dag_minimum_path_cover/README.md) covers the DAG reduction and [`cocomparability_ldfs_minimum_path_cover`](c/cocomparability_ldfs_minimum_path_cover/README.md) covers the cocomparability LDFS+ application. The DADS stub says only “of a digraph,” which is not enough to choose another problem variant. |
| [Post machine](https://xlinux.nist.gov/dads/HTML/postMachine.html) | Excluded: the DADS page describes a queue model but cites Post's 1936 paper, whose formulation uses an unbounded tape. The conflict leaves no unambiguous machine semantics, and a general computation-model simulator is outside the suite's bounded kernels. |
| [Randomized-Select](https://xlinux.nist.gov/dads/HTML/randomzdSlct.html) | Duplicate/covered: [`minimum_element_of_array`](m/minimum_element_of_array/README.md) implements seeded random-pivot quickselect with one-sided partition selection. [`kth_order_statistic`](k/kth_order_statistic/README.md) is another contract for the same quickselect family; the differences in PRNG, rank indexing, and deterministic pivot standardization do not justify another package. The method distinction is consistent with CLRS, *Introduction to Algorithms*, §9.2, and the [MIT 6.046J lecture note](https://live.ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-046j-design-and-analysis-of-algorithms-spring-2015/08020963ae819d4c6dcf177983bb7c6b_MIT6_046JS15_Recitation4.pdf). |
| [virtual hashing](https://xlinux.nist.gov/dads/HTML/virtualHashing.html) | Excluded pending an article-level method review: the DADS page has no definition and only cites Litwin's paper. Its title is not treated as a synonym for the local linear-hashing split-pointer method. |

Compared the current official [navigation index](https://github.com/cp-algorithms/cp-algorithms/blob/main/src/navigation.md)
and its algorithm categories against local package README contracts and active
reservations. No high-confidence, sufficiently specified omission emerged in
this index-level pass. Strong candidate checks found existing coverage for
broken-profile domino tilings, k-th order statistics, dynamic MEX, connected
labeled graph counting, Stern–Brocot navigation, 15-puzzle solvability,
minimum queues, the two-machine flow-shop rule, and the deadline/max-jobs
schedule. The source's generic “delete from a data structure in
O(T(n) log n)” article does not define a single operation/result workload, so
it is not a benchmark candidate by itself. Recent indexed additions such as
Stoer–Wagner minimum cut, centroid decomposition, minimum enclosing circle,
Manhattan distance, and factoring exponentiation are already represented by
local packages or crosswalk entries. Existing active push–relabel work remains
reserved and was not duplicated. This records an index audit rather than a
claim that every article body has been exhaustively re-reviewed. That
index-level pass changed no package or suite files; no programs, tests,
checkers, scripts, builds, compilers, or benchmarks were run.

**Article-level follow-up — implemented `factorial_divisor_composite_k`:** the
official [composite-k section](https://cp-algorithms.com/algebra/factorial-divisors.html#composite-k)
specifies the valuation minimum needed for the maximum exponent of a
composite divisor in `n!`. Prime-only queries overlap existing packages and
are excluded. Ten language ports, independent quotient-sum and digit-sum
references, workload, static inventory, and `binary_scalar` suite wiring are
integrated in source. No executable checks were run.

**Implemented, unverified — `prim_sparse_heap` (CP-Algorithms follow-up):**
the sparse-graph Prim profile maintains one candidate key per unselected
vertex in an indexed binary min-heap, with extract-min and decrease-key
operations. This is method-distinct from local [`prim`](p/prim/README.md),
which scans all remaining vertices in O(V) per selected vertex and is the
dense-graph variant. The package has ten ports, an independent Kruskal
reference, bounded workload, provenance/rights, and static inventory. Source:
[CP-Algorithms — Prim's minimum spanning tree, sparse graphs](https://cp-algorithms.com/graph/mst_prim.html),
CC BY-SA 4.0; algorithm description only. **The ten-port package is now
registered in the scalar runner/verifier**, with a 12,290-word parseable input
cap and a 200,704-byte workspace contract. No programs, tests, scripts,
checkers, builds, compilers, profilers, or benchmarks were run.

**Implemented, unverified — `jsort` (`tree_center_ports`):** this in-place
signed-i64 sort follows the NIST DADS sequence: build a bottom-up min-heap,
reverse the array and build a bottom-up max-heap, reverse it back, then run
ascending insertion sort. This distinct pair of heap partial-ordering passes
is not ordinary heapsort or weak-heapsort. The bounded `sort_call` profile
supports lengths through 1,024. Ten language ports, a bottom-up mergesort
oracle, an independent built-in-sort reference, semantic workload fixtures,
rights and inventory notes, a static package checker, and a sort-suite
verifier are present. Sources: [NIST DADS JSort entry](https://xlinux.nist.gov/dads/HTML/JSort.html)
and [Morin's sorting-source index](https://cglab.ca/~morin/misc/sortalg/);
algorithm descriptions only. No programs, tests, scripts, checkers, builds,
compilers, profilers, or benchmarks were run.

**Implemented, unverified — `linear_probing_sort` (`tree_center_ports`):** this
distribution sort interpolates byte-valued keys to an expanded slot table,
resolves collisions by linear probing, then compacts occupied slots. Its
bounded profile uses at most 1,024 keys in `0..255`, with `m = 256*(n+1)+1`
main slots and `n` overflow slots; the dedicated sort verifier includes a
maximum-key probe run in the overflow region. It is distinct from local bucket
sort's per-bucket insertion pass, Flash Sort's class/cycle-permutation phase,
and linear-probing hash maps. Ten language ports, a primary table reference, an
independent built-in-sort reference, workload, rights/inventory, and a custom
`sort_call` verifier are present. Source: [NIST DADS Linear Probing
Sort](https://xlinux.nist.gov/dads/HTML/linearProbingSort.html); algorithm
description only. No programs, tests, scripts, checkers, builds, compilers,
profilers, or benchmarks were run.

**DADS sorting additions and queued audit:**
[FGK](https://xlinux.nist.gov/dads/HTML/algorithmFGK.html) and
[Vitter's algorithm](https://xlinux.nist.gov/dads/HTML/vittersAlgorithm.html)
are distinct adaptive Huffman methods. [Polyphase merge sort](https://xlinux.nist.gov/dads/HTML/polyphmrgsrt.html)
and [oscillating merge sort](https://xlinux.nist.gov/dads/HTML/oscillatingMergeSort.html)
use distinct external merge schedules. FGK and Vitter now have ten language
exports each and separate byte-output suite profiles.
Polyphase Merge Sort has ten ports, a bounded Fibonacci-tape workload, two
references, and a dedicated sort verifier. Oscillating Merge Sort has ten
in-place `sort_call` ports, a recursive alternating-run reference, an
independent built-in-sort reference, and a dedicated sort verifier. The separate DADS
[UnShuffle sort](https://xlinux.nist.gov/dads/HTML/unshufflsort.html) uses
ordered endpoint piles followed by a priority-queue ideal merge; it differs
from local strand sort's repeated increasing-subsequence extraction and now
has a package contract, workload, references, dedicated verifier, and ten
language ports present but unbuilt.
The DADS [Histogram Sort](https://xlinux.nist.gov/dads/HTML/histogramSort.html),
also called Interpolation Sort, is covered by
[`rodinia_hybridsort`](r/rodinia_hybridsort/README.md): both count bucket
frequencies, prefix-sum bucket starts, stably scatter into bucket ranges, and
sort each bucket. DADS describes an approximate monotone rank over `n` bins;
the local Rodinia profile uses uniform interval mapping into 1,024 Float32
bins. That bin-mapping and cleanup-profile difference does not add a distinct
sorting method, so no second package is reserved.
The DADS [external quicksort](https://xlinux.nist.gov/dads/HTML/externalQuicksort.html)
uses an endpoint buffer as a pivot and balances reads and writes across both
ends. It is distinct from the local in-memory pivot quicksorts and external
merge schedules. A bounded `sort_call` package now has ten language ports,
primary and independent references, workload fixtures, rights/inventory, a
static package checker, and a dedicated verifier; it remains uncompiled and
unexecuted.
Generic shuffle, k-way merge, and existing
interpolation search entries were excluded as aliases or overlaps. No DADS
source code or prose was copied.

**Implemented, unverified — `adaptive_heap_sort` (`tree_center_ports`):** this
bounded signed-i64 sort mutates the input array and uses five fixed arrays. It
constructs a min Cartesian tree and keeps a binary min-heap over the roots of
unreported subtrees. Each extraction emits the next value and adds its
children to the frontier. This differs from
ordinary heapsort, weak-heapsort, and adaptive merge sort. The NIST DADS entry
uses randomized binary search tree wording; the detailed Levcopoulos–Petersson
method restatement specifies a deterministic Cartesian tree plus a frontier
heap. The package documents this source-description mismatch and follows that
explicitly attributed LP93 method. Ten language ports, bottom-up mergesort and
built-in references, bounded workload, rights/inventory, a static package
checker, and a custom `sort_call` verifier are present. Sources: [NIST
DADS](https://xlinux.nist.gov/dads/HTML/adaptiveHeapSort.html),
Levcopoulos–Petersson [*Adaptive Heapsort*](https://doi.org/10.1006/jagm.1993.1021),
and Haeupler et al.'s [detailed restatement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.04552);
algorithm descriptions only. No programs, tests, scripts, checkers, builds,
compilers, profilers, or benchmarks were run.

**Implemented, unverified — `suffix_array_blind_trie` (NIST DADS type-index audit):** the
[blind-sort entry](https://xlinux.nist.gov/dads/HTML/blindSort.html) describes
building a blind trie over suffixes and traversing it left to right to emit a
suffix array. Local suffix-array contracts cover rank doubling, DC3, SA-IS,
read-only in-place induced sorting, and reverse-insertion scapegoat trees; none
uses a blind trie. Bounded profile: byte input `[n, bytes...]`,
`0 <= n <= 32`, with the suffix starts returned as little-endian i64 values
through `i64_array_bytes_output`; primary blind-trie construction and
lexicographic traversal, independent direct suffix-order reference. Ten
language ports, workload, provenance, and static inventory are present, with
byte-output runner/verifier registration. The maximum result is 256 bytes and
the required workspace is 2,304 bytes. This bounded all-suffix profile follows
Manzini–Ferragina §3.1's blind-trie insertion and ordered traversal, not their
full deep-shallow sorter. No programs, tests, scripts, checkers, builds,
compilers, profilers, or benchmarks were run.

**Implemented, unverified — `alphabetic_anagrams`:** this bounded profile ranks
one word among the distinct permutations of its multiset using multinomial
block sizes. It differs from local `kth_lexicographic_permutation`, which
selects from distinct symbols at a zero-based rank, and `unique_permutation`,
which enumerates arrangements. Ten language ports, a next-permutation
independent reference, workload, rights/inventory, and `i64_array_scalar`
runner/verifier wiring are present. Generic sources: Knuth, [TAOCP Volume
4A](https://cs.stanford.edu/~knuth/taocp.html), §7.2.1.2, and NIST
[DLMF §26.16](https://dlmf.nist.gov/26.16). The public Codewars title was used
only for discovery. No problem text, examples, tests, submissions, programs,
checkers, scripts, builds, compilers, or benchmarks were used or run.

**Implemented, unverified — `infinite_knight_distance`:** the profile computes
the shortest distance for bounded signed displacements on an unbounded integer
grid with the Das–Chatterji closed formula, parity correction, and two local
exceptions. It is distinct from the local finite-board knight-tour packages.
Ten ports, small-offset BFS reference, large formula-derived fixtures, rights
and inventory, and scalar-suite wiring are present. Source: Das and Chatterji,
[“Knight's distance in digital geometry”](https://doi.org/10.1016/0167-8655(88)90105-5).
Only the public Codewars title was used for discovery; no task text, examples,
tests, submissions, programs, checkers, scripts, builds, compilers, or
benchmarks were used or run.

**Implemented, unverified — `egg_drop_max_floors_by_moves`:** this bounded
profile returns the maximum floor count distinguishable with up to 32 eggs and
32 moves. Its primary updates move-major coverage using
`T(m,e)=T(m-1,e)+T(m-1,e-1)+1`; the independent reference uses partial
binomial sums. It is distinct from local egg-drop primaries that minimize
trials for a supplied floor count. Ten language ports, workload, rights and
inventory, and `i64_array_scalar` runner/verifier wiring are present. Method
source: Boardman, [The Egg-Drop Numbers](https://doi.org/10.1080/0025570X.2004.11953281).
The Codewars title was used only for discovery. No task text, examples, tests,
solutions, programs, checkers, scripts, builds, compilers, or benchmarks were
used or run.

**Implemented, unverified — `rectangle_union_area_sweep`:** the primary sorts
x-events and maintains covered y-length with a compressed segment tree in
`O(n log n)` time for up to 64 rectangles. Its small-coordinate independent
reference counts covered unit cells; the package primary reference uses
slabs and merged intervals. It differs from the fixed two-rectangle overlap
formula. Ten language ports, fixtures, rights/inventory, and
`i64_array_scalar` runner/verifier wiring are present. Source: Bentley,
[The Measure Problem for Rectangular Ranges in d-Space](https://doi.org/10.1016/0196-6774(81)90027-4);
algorithm description only. No programs, tests, scripts, checkers, builds,
compilers, profilers, or benchmarks were run.

**Implemented, unverified — `hsadelta_differential_compression`:** this
bounded fixed-block profile hashes reference blocks, uses suffix-array prefix
intervals to find candidate matches, extends exact byte matches, and emits
INSERT/COPY commands. The independent reference scans every aligned reference
block without fingerprints or a suffix array. It is distinct from static
Huffman coding; the paper's block-size-proportional variant is excluded.
Ten language ports, workload, rights/inventory, and
`i64_array_bytes_output` runner/verifier wiring are present; fixed arrays fit
the declared 2,048-byte workspace. Sources: [NIST DADS](https://xlinux.nist.gov/dads/HTML/hsadelta.html)
and Agarwal et al.'s [IBM Journal paper](https://doi.org/10.1147/rd.501.0149);
algorithm descriptions only. No programs, tests, scripts, checkers, builds,
compilers, profilers, or benchmarks were run.

## CP-Algorithms lexicographic balanced-parenthesis successor (2026-11-17)

The official [balanced bracket sequences article](https://cp-algorithms.com/combinatorics/bracket_sequences.html#finding-the-lexicographical-next-balanced-sequence)
describes finding the rightmost opening parenthesis that can become a closing
parenthesis, then rebuilding the suffix in its lexicographically smallest
valid form. The local [`parentheses_generator`](p/parentheses_generator/README.md)
recursively enumerates the complete Catalan family and does not implement this
single-successor update. Implemented as `balanced_parenthesis_successor` with a
bounded `i64_array_bytes_output` contract: `[pair_count,symbols...]`, where
`1<=pair_count<=10`, symbols are 0 for `(` and 1 for `)`, and the exact input
length is `1+2*pair_count`. A valid nonmaximal sequence returns the next
lexicographic ASCII sequence; with adequate non-null output storage, the
maximum sequence returns `-3`. Malformed input returns `-1`, and null/short
output returns `-2` without writes, including for a maximum word. The primary
uses the right-to-left successor scan; an independent oracle enumerates all
bounded Dyck words and selects the following sequence. Ten clean-room ports,
workload, rights/provenance, and static inventory are present, and the profile
is registered in the `i64_array_bytes_output` suite. Algorithm description
only; no code or prose is copied. No programs, tests, checkers, scripts, builds,
compilers, profilers, or benchmarks were run.

## CP-Algorithms balanced-parenthesis rank and unrank (2026-11-17)

The official [balanced bracket sequences article](https://cp-algorithms.com/combinatorics/bracket_sequences.html#sequence-index)
provides dynamic-programming completion counts for mapping a Dyck word to its
zero-based lexicographic index and for reconstructing the word at a supplied
index. The local [`catalan_number`](c/catalan_number/README.md) returns only the
number of words, while [`parentheses_generator`](p/parentheses_generator/README.md)
enumerates all words recursively; neither ranks nor selects one word.
Implemented as [`balanced_parenthesis_rank_unrank`](b/balanced_parenthesis_rank_unrank/README.md),
a bounded `i64_array_scalar` two-mode
profile for `1<=n<=10`: mode 0 takes `[0,n,symbols...]` and returns the
zero-based rank, where 0 encodes `(` and 1 encodes `)`; mode 1 takes
`[1,n,rank]` and returns the sequence as a fixed-width `2n`-bit integer formed
by shifting left and appending each symbol. Out-of-range ranks, invalid modes,
malformed frames, invalid symbols, or non-Dyck words return `-1`. The primary
uses suffix-completion DP; the independent reference enumerates fixed-size
opening-position sets in lexicographic order. Ten clean-room ports, workload,
rights/provenance, and package inventory are present, and the profile is
registered in the `i64_array_scalar` suite. Algorithm description only; no
code or prose is copied. No programs, tests, checkers, scripts, builds,
compilers, profilers, or benchmarks were run.

The title is used only as the discovery lead. |

A Rosetta Code title was used only as a discovery lead; ten ports, an independent row-tuple reference, workload, and `i64_array_bytes_output` runner/verifier dispatch are integrated in source. No executable checks were run. |

| Coloured Triangles | Implemented as [`coloured_triangle_reduction`](c/coloured_triangle_reduction/README.md). Its mod-3 adjacent-pair reduction uses `(-1)^(n-1) * sum_i C(n-1,i)*x_i (mod 3)`, with base-three Lucas digits, in a bounded 256-color profile. Ten ports, direct repeated-reduction reference, fixtures, and `i64_array_scalar` runner/verifier dispatch are present; no executable checks were run. Discovery lead: [Codewars task](https://www.codewars.com/kata/5a25ac6ac5e284cfbe000111); mathematical method: [Lucas' theorem](https://math.hmc.edu/funfacts/lucas-theorem/). |

It counts positive values across lengths 1 through the bound; both Codewars titles map to this one algorithm. Ten ports, an incremental prefix-tree reference, an independent exhaustive-number reference, workload fixtures, and `i64_array_scalar` runner/verifier dispatch are present; no executable checks were run. Mathematical sources: [OEIS A397953](https://oeis.org/A397953) and the [Stanford CS106AX problem](https://web.stanford.edu/class/archive/cs/cs106ax/cs106ax.1252/res/handouts/16-CS106AX-Midterm). It is distinct from the local [`fibonacci_integer_code`](f/fibonacci_integer_code/README.md), which encodes nonnegative inputs as Zeckendorf bits for `x+1`. Ten ports, interval-recurrence and exhaustive legal-mask references, fixtures, and `i64_array_bytes_output` runner/verifier dispatch are integrated in source. Mathematical sources: [OEIS A215022](https://oeis.org/A215022) and [Bunder, “Zeckendorf representations using negative Fibonacci numbers”](https://www.fq.math.ca/Scanned/30-2/bunder.pdf); the Codewars title is a discovery lead only. No executable checks were run. |

Its aggregation output is a task composition, not a new prime-factorization method. Discovery lead: [Codewars kata](https://www.codewars.com/kata/54d496788776e49e6b00052f). |

| Quantum Entanglement: The Graph-State Cut | Duplicate computational kernel: the graph-state entropy across a bipartition is the rank over GF(2) of the cross-cut adjacency block, so the measured work is binary Gaussian elimination. The existing [`matrix_det_mod_2`](m/matrix_det_mod_2/README.md) profile already implements packed GF(2) elimination; a rectangular cut-rank input would be a different contract but not a distinct elimination algorithm, so no second benchmark is reserved. Independent method source: Zhou et al., [“Detecting multipartite entanglement structure with minimal resources”](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41534-019-0200-9). |
| Clock Patience | Duplicate title for the existing [`clock_patience_simulation`](c/clock_patience_simulation/README.md) profile; its rules and operation are already specified independently. |
| First non-repeating character, Number of trailing zeros of N!, Josephus Survivor, Manhattan Distance, Largest 5 digit number in a series, and Coloured Triangles | Already mapped to the existing first-unique-character, factorial-trailing-zero, Josephus, L1-distance, sliding-window-maximum, and coloured-triangle-reduction packages respectively. |
| Many Repunit Sum, Remove the parentheses, Simple Encryption #2 - Index-Difference, Valley Domains, Identify the array's ordering, Hanging the curtains, TV Remote, Real Password Cracker, Fleet Workload Balancer, and Duel Arbiter | Excluded from this title-only pass: the titles do not specify enough input semantics or a distinct algorithm to justify a new benchmark contract. |
| Binary multiple of 3 | Implemented as [`binary_divisibility_by_three_dfa`](b/binary_divisibility_by_three_dfa/README.md), a 4096-bit MSB-first stream scan using the three remainder states modulo 3. This is distinct from signed-i64 binary conversion and numeric scalar divisibility. The Codewars title/tag listing was used only for discovery; the method comes from Cornell's [CS 4810 DFA notes](https://www.cs.cornell.edu/kozen/Papers/481.pdf). Ten language ports, an alternating-sign independent reference, bounded fixtures, rights notes, and byte-output suite registration are included. |

## KmpSkip exact string matching (`kmp_skip_search`) (2026-11-16)

Charras–Lecroq's [algorithm description](https://igm.univ-mlv.fr/~lecroq/string/node32.html), the [1998 paper](https://doi.org/10.1007/BFb0030780), and [NIST DADS](https://xlinux.nist.gov/dads/HTML/kmpskipsrch.html) identify KmpSkip's small-alphabet bucket samples combined with Morris–Pratt/KMP shift reconciliation. It differs from ordinary KMP's sequential walk and Alpha Skip's fixed-factor sampling. Added a bounded all-occurrences profile with primary and direct-window references, fixtures, rights note, static inventory, ten language ports, and `i64_array_scalar` runner/verifier registration. No programs, tests, scripts, checkers, builds, compilers, profilers, or benchmarks were run.

## Forward DAWG Matching (`forward_dawg_matching`) (2026-11-16)

Chapter 13 of Charras and Lecroq's [Forward DAWG Matching reference](https://igm.univ-mlv.fr/~lecroq/string/fdm.html) describes a left-to-right scan of the pattern suffix automaton, following suffix links on absent transitions and reporting when the longest recognized pattern factor reaches the full pattern length. Added a bounded four-symbol all-occurrences profile with primary automaton and independent direct-window references. Ten language ports, workload, rights note, static inventory, and `i64_array_scalar` suite wiring are integrated. No programs, tests, scripts, checkers, builds, compilers, profilers, or benchmarks were run.

## Reverse Colussi exact string matching (`reverse_colussi_search`) (2026-11-16)

Charras–Lecroq's [Reverse Colussi description](https://igm.univ-mlv.fr/~lecroq/string/node17.html) specifies a pattern-derived `h` comparison order and separate good-suffix and alphabet-indexed bad-character shifts. Added a bounded all-occurrences profile over a four-symbol alphabet with direct table derivation and an independent direct-window reference. Ten language ports, workload, rights note, static inventory, and `i64_array_scalar` runner/verifier registration are integrated. No programs, tests, scripts, checkers, builds, compilers, profilers, or benchmarks were run.

## Reverse Factor string search (`reverse_factor_search`) (2026-11-17)

Charras–Lecroq's [Reverse Factor description](https://igm.univ-mlv.fr/~lecroq/string/node23.html) builds the reversed pattern's suffix automaton and uses terminal suffix states to determine backward-scan shifts. Added a bounded four-symbol all-occurrences profile with primary automaton and independent direct-window references, fixtures, rights note, static inventory, ten language ports, and `i64_array_scalar` runner/verifier registration. Its algorithm has `O(m*n)` worst-case search; the package separately documents the published average inspection bound for `m>=2` and its `m=1` path. No programs, tests, scripts, checkers, builds, compilers, profilers, or benchmarks were run.

## Turbo Reverse Factor string search (`turbo_reverse_factor_search`) (2026-11-17)

ESMAJ's [Turbo Reverse Factor description](https://www-igm.univ-mlv.fr/~lecroq/string/node24.html), its [reference PDF](https://ligm.univ-eiffel.fr/~lecroq/string/string.pdf), and Crochemore et al.'s [1994 analysis](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01185427) describe a weighted reversed-pattern suffix automaton combined with preceding-shift memory and bounded reinspection of periodic or nonperiodic prefixes. Added a bounded four-symbol all-occurrences profile with a primary weighted-automaton oracle, independent direct-alignment reference, fixtures, rights note, static inventory, ten language ports, and `i64_array_scalar` runner/verifier integration. It is distinct from base Reverse Factor's rescanning behavior and Turbo Boyer–Moore's suffix memory and shift rules. No programs, tests, scripts, checkers, builds, compilers, profilers, or benchmarks were run.

## Smith exact string search (`smith_string_search`) (2026-11-17)

Smith's [1989 paper](https://doi.org/10.1002/spe.4380211006) and Charras–Lecroq's [algorithm description](https://igm.univ-mlv.fr/~lecroq/string/node21.html) specify a combined shift equal to the maximum of Horspool's window-end shift and Quick Search's lookahead shift. Added a bounded all-occurrences byte-output profile with a virtual end-of-input symbol, primary table-driven and independent direct-window references, shift-branch fixtures, malformed-frame and output-buffer cases. Ten language ports, rights note, workload, static inventory, and `i64_array_bytes_output` runner/verifier registration are integrated in source. ## Smallest number with exactly `d` divisors (`smallest_number_with_n_divisors`) (2026-11-17)

The [OEIS A005179 definition](https://oeis.org/A005179) and [Rosetta Code task](https://rosettacode.org/wiki/Sequence:_smallest_number_with_exactly_n_divisors) describe the inverse of the divisor-count function. Added a bounded profile that enumerates nonincreasing factorizations of `d` and maps their factors to exponents of the smallest primes, returning the least qualifying value within an inclusive cap. The NIST [Baum–Welch entry](https://xlinux.nist.gov/dads/HTML/baumWelch.html) and Rabiner's [HMM tutorial](https://doi.org/10.1109/5.18626) specify forward–backward posterior updates to HMM initial, transition, and emission probabilities. ## Sieve of Sundaram (sieve_of_sundaram) (2026-11-17)

The prime-generation source-index audit found no local Sundaram package,
language source, or active reservation. The existing Eratosthenes, Atkin,
linear, segmented, and stream sieves use different marking or generation
rules. Sundaram marks the indices i+j+2ij for 1<=i<=j, then maps survivors
to odd candidates; the identity 2(i+j+2ij)+1=(2i+1)(2j+1) distinguishes its
composite-index construction from the local sieves. The algorithm is described
in Ghidarcea and Popescu's publisher-hosted
[2024 paper](https://www.scientificbulletin.upb.ro/rev_docs_arhiva/fullb1a_720372.pdf),
Algorithm 2.1, and the [prime-sieving review](https://www.mdpi.com/1999-4893/17/4/157);
the method is attributed to V.
Ramaswami Aiyar's 1934 note. Added a bounded count-through-limit package, a
Sundaram reference and independent trial-division oracle, workload, rights
note, static inventory, and ten language ports. Registered with `run_scalar.py`
and `verify_scalar.py`. No programs, tests, scripts, checkers, builds,
compilers, profilers, or benchmarks were run.

The subject/window input distinction does not introduce another clipping algorithm. RosettaGit was used as title-only discovery; no task content or code was consulted. |
| Thiele's interpolation formula | No local package or active reservation used Thiele's rational continued fraction; `newton_divided_difference_interpolation` and `polynomial_interpolation` reconstruct polynomials. Implemented as `thiele_rational_interpolation`, ABI `float64_slice_io`, ten ports and package references/workload/static inventory, plus runner/verifier registration and root catalog entries. Frame `[N,(x_i,y_i)*N,query]`, `1<=N<=6`, length 4..14, parseable through 15; all numeric fields are finite binary64 multiples of `2^-54` in `[-8,8]`, N is integer-valued, and nodes have minimum pairwise separation `1/16`. The rational type has `deg(P)<=floor(N/2)`, `deg(Q)<=floor((N-1)/2)` and projective coefficient normalization. Ports define validity by the ordered inverse-difference table and guarded continued-fraction evaluation: denominator, diagonal coefficient, and tail magnitudes must be strictly between `1/32+2^-32` and `64-2^-32`, with all other intermediates/results finite and below the upper cap. Near-poles in the lower guard band return -1; valid null/short output returns -2. The exact linear-system rank and pole checks provide independent consistency checks for pinned workload cases, not extra global port preconditions; if exact algebra cannot provide a unique finite value, the independent oracle falls back to guarded binary64 output under the same status rules. Workload cases cover fractional inputs, node lookup, constant two-point method degeneracy, rank-deficient linear data, exact and near poles, and guard boundaries. Primary source: Stoer and Bulirsch, *Introduction to Numerical Analysis*, §2.2.2, [textbook copy](https://www.math.kent.edu/~reichel/courses/numerical.analysis.2/Numerical-book.pdf); independent algorithm source: Levrie and Bultheel, [“A Note on Thiele n-Fractions”](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02144105). The Rosetta title index is discovery only. |
| Strong and weak primes | No local package/reservation classifies a prime using the arithmetic mean of its immediately preceding and following primes; local Miller–Rabin “strong probable prime” and cryptographic strong-prime checks are different concepts. Implemented as [`strong_weak_balanced_prime_distribution`](s/strong_weak_balanced_prime_distribution/README.md): input `[inclusive_limit]`, `3<=limit<=100000`, classify each prime `p` from 3 through the inclusive limit by exact comparison `2p` versus `p_prev+p_next`, and pack `(strong,weak,balanced)` counts in base 100000. All ten language ports use an Eratosthenes sieve through `2*limit` and a rolling three-prime window; Bertrand's postulate ensures the successor for every counted `p` is below `2p`. The independently structured oracle generates the prime list by trial division before classifying adjacent triples. Workload, rights/provenance, static inventory, and `i64_array_scalar` runner/verifier wiring are present. RosettaGit is title-index discovery only. Algorithm sources: OEIS [A051634](https://oeis.org/A051634), [A051635](https://oeis.org/A051635), and [A006562](https://oeis.org/A006562); fixture totals cross-check [A159687](https://oeis.org/A159687), [A006880](https://oeis.org/A006880), and [A055206](https://oeis.org/A055206). The sieve description is from [CP-Algorithms](https://cp-algorithms.com/algebra/sieve-of-eratosthenes.html), and the finite successor bound uses [Bertrand's postulate](https://mathworld.wolfram.com/BertrandsPostulate.html). No programs, tests, scripts, checkers, builds, compilers, profilers, or benchmarks were run. |
| General percolation variants, Voronoi diagrams, transportation problem, universal Turing machine | Excluded from title-only reservation: the title/category alone does not settle a deterministic input family, stochastic tape/statistic, precise output, or one fixed bounded construction. |
| Topswops | Duplicate of [`fannkuch`](f/fannkuch/README.md): both enumerate permutations and apply the deterministic prefix reversal whose length is the current top value until the distinguished minimum reaches the top, then return the maximum flip count. The [RosettaGit task](https://rosettagit.org/tasks/topswops/) explicitly identifies Topswops as Fannkuch; no second benchmark is needed. |

The audit records title-level crosswalks only and does not claim a full review of

## RosettaGit S–Z follow-up: Topswops duplicate confirmed (2026-11-18)

The [Topswops task definition](https://rosettagit.org/tasks/topswops/) says to
enumerate starting permutations, repeatedly reverse the prefix whose length is
the top card, stop when card 1 reaches the top, and report the maximum number
of reversals. It also identifies the task as Fannkuch. This matches the
permutation maximum already returned by [`fannkuch`](f/fannkuch/README.md),
which preserves the counter-driven traversal and prefix-reversal procedure.
The upstream scalar profile additionally computes a checksum internally, but
that does not create a distinct algorithm or output contract here. The
duplicate is recorded; no additional benchmark was added. No task code or
examples were reused, and no programs, tests, scripts, checkers, builds,
compilers, profilers, or benchmarks were run.

## RosettaGit A–C title-index follow-up (2026-11-17)

This focused title-only pass compared selected A–C entries in the [RosettaGit
task-title index](https://rosettagit.org/tasks/) against catalog descriptions,
package paths, and current reservations. The A* search, Banker's algorithm,
Cholesky decomposition, Canny edge detector, Damm check digit, Euler methods,
and exact-cover titles are represented by existing packages. The title
`Averages/Mean angle` had no local circular-mean or mean-direction package and
is distinct from arithmetic means. Implemented as `circular_mean_direction` for
the conventional resultant-vector direction (not the L1 “true circular mean”) in
a bounded `float64_slice_io` profile: input `[N,theta_0,...,theta_(N-1)]`,
`1<=N<=64`, finite radians in `[-8π,8π]`; normalize each observation to
`[-π,π)`, sum unit vectors, and return the resultant direction normalized to
`[-π,π)`. The angle `+π` maps to `-π`; a resultant magnitude at or below
`N*2^-28` is undefined and returns `-1`. Input and output normalization use
the shared binary64 `π` and `2π` constants, including mapping the binary64
`+π` constant to `-π`. The explicit formula is
`atan2(sum(sin(theta_i)), sum(cos(theta_i)))`. Ten language ports, primary and
independent references, workload, rights note, static inventory, and float64
runner/verifier wiring are present; valid null or short output returns `-2`. Primary
algorithm description: Utrecht University, [Tutorial 2: Circular descriptives](https://cdm.sites.uu.nl/wp-content/uploads/sites/31/2018/06/Tutorial2-descriptives.pdf),
which defines mean direction from the summed sine and cosine coordinates.
Independent reference: Brigham Young University Center for Remote Sensing,
[True Circular Mean](https://www.scp.byu.edu/mers/circularmean.html), which
distinguishes the conventional resultant direction from an L1 angular mean. RosettaGit
is a title-index discovery source only; no task text, examples, submissions,
tests, or code were consulted.
