## Encyclopedia of Algorithms audit, Chapters 591–600 (2026-11-17)

The local EPUB chapter map and crosswalk were compared with benchmark package
methods. Chapter 591, *Parity Games*, gives a concrete recursive Zielonka
procedure in Algorithm 1: select the least active priority, compute that
priority's player's attractor, solve the remaining game, and when needed
compute the opponent attractor and recurse again. That profile is implemented
as [`zielonka_parity_game_solver`](z/zielonka_parity_game_solver/README.md).
The chapter also lists Jurdziński's small progress measures; the cited STACS
paper fully specifies the odd-priority rank domain, `Prog`, owner-dependent
`Lift`, and least-fixed-point iteration. Its separate bounded profile is
[`small_progress_measure_parity_game_solver`](s/small_progress_measure_parity_game_solver/README.md),
which returns the Even-winning region from finite measures after deterministic
ascending-ID lifting. Both use minimum-priority-even semantics on total arenas
but compute the partition by materially different methods. Ten ports, an
independent positional-strategy oracle, bounded fixtures, rights/provenance,
static inventory, and scalar-suite registration are included for each.
`games_on_arbitrary_graphs` classifies normal-play positions with draws, while
the `parity` family counts/tests integer parity; neither is a duplicate parity
game solver.

The rest of the range was already crosswalked: Chapter 592's list-ranking
families have distinct deterministic independent-set contraction and
Random_Mate packages; Chapter 593's jamming-resistant MAC protocols depend on
a distributed wireless/adversary model; Chapter 594's exact ring covering
protocol is already implemented; Chapter 595 is a distributed mobile-robot
model; Chapter 596 surveys generalized Moran-process fixation approximations
without one chapter-wide bounded kernel; Chapter 597's graph-coloring results
are probabilistic/asymptotic in a random-intersection model; Chapter 598's
network strength-of-connection measure now has a bounded profile in
[network_erosion_strength_of_connection](n/network_erosion_strength_of_connection/README.md).
It uses positive unit-length directed arcs and distinct endpoints, follows
Campbell, Thakar, and Albert's primary-paper normalization for that branch,
and returns the measure as an exact fraction. Chapter 599 surveys phylogenetic
networks without a single bounded reconstruction algorithm; and Chapter
600's Musite pipeline is application/model-specific. No other distinct
bounded candidate was reserved in this range. Primary sources:
[Chapter 591](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4939-2864-4_591),
[Chapter 598](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4939-2864-4_598),
Campbell, Thakar, and Albert's [network-analysis paper](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevE.84.031929),
and Chapter 591's cited McNaughton paper, [“Infinite Games Played on Finite Graphs”](https://doi.org/10.1016/0168-0072(93)90036-D).

## CP-Algorithms intersecting-segments sweep (2026-11-17)

The official [intersecting-segments article](https://cp-algorithms.com/geometry/intersecting_segments.html)
gives an endpoint sweep with an ordered active set that checks only newly
adjacent segment pairs. The local line-segment package checks one supplied
pair in O(1), and line_sweep profiles inclusive one-dimensional interval
overlap; neither searches a set of 2D segments. Reserved as
`intersecting_segments_sweep`, a bounded `i64_array_scalar` profile for up to
24 nonvertical segments with unique endpoint x-coordinates and integer
coordinates in [-100,100]. It reports whether any pair intersects, including
endpoint contact and collinear overlap. Ten ports use an exact rational
array-backed active order. Its worst-case bound is O(n^2) due to insertion
sort and active-array shifts; the independent reference checks all pairs.
Runner/verifier wiring includes source oracle comparison, package workload
inventory, maximum parseable frame, and null-input framing. This uses the
article's sweep idea without copying code or prose. No programs, tests,
checkers, scripts, builds, compilers, profilers, or benchmarks were run.

## CP-Algorithms SCC condensation DAG (2026-11-17)

The official [Strongly Connected Components and Condensation Graph article](https://cp-algorithms.com/graph/strongly-connected-components.html)
includes an optional construction that maps each inter-component input edge
to an edge in the SCC quotient DAG. Local `kosaraju`, `tarjan_scc`, and
`gabow_scc` return the SCC partition but do not return the condensation edges.
Recorded as `scc_condensation_dag` with a bounded `i64_array_bytes_output`
profile for directed graphs with `0<=n<=8` and up to 28 input edges. The output
is `[component_count, component_id[0..n), row_mask[0..component_count)]`;
components are numbered by ascending minimum vertex, and each row mask has
bit `j` set exactly when at least one input edge leaves component `i` for
component `j`. Duplicate input edges collapse to one DAG edge, and
intra-component edges are discarded. The primary uses Kosaraju followed by
quotient construction; an independent mutual-reachability reference derives
the component partition and DAG. The maximum output is 17 bytes. The package,
workload, references, static inventory, and ten language ports are registered
in the independent byte-output runner/verifier, including workload validation
and frame bounds. Algorithm description only; no code or prose is copied. No
programs, tests, checkers, scripts, builds, compilers, profilers, or benchmarks
were run.

## CP-Algorithms maximum-average threshold search (`binary_search_maximum_average_segment`) — implemented (2026-11-17)

The [maximum/minimum subarray article's maximum-average section](https://cp-algorithms.com/others/maximum_average_segment.html#search-for-a-subarray-with-a-maximum-minimum-average)
selects the average by binary search and tests a candidate `x` by subtracting
`x` from every element, reducing feasibility to a nonnegative-sum subarray
test. Local [`max_average_length_bounded_segment`](m/max_average_length_bounded_segment/README.md)
exhaustively scans every interval in a caller-supplied `[L,U]` length range and
returns an exact ratio and witness; it does not use transformed-prefix
feasibility, and it has a different length profile. The CP profile is
implemented as `binary_search_maximum_average_segment` with input `[n,L,values...]`,
`1<=n<=32`, `1<=L<=n`, and values in `[-1000,1000]`; it returns
`floor(1000 * maximum_average)` using integer-threshold binary search and exact
prefix-sum feasibility, with `-1000001` reserved for malformed input. The
primary performs `O(n log 2,000,001)` transformed-prefix scans; the independent
oracle enumerates all admissible intervals and cross-multiplies exact sums and
lengths. The package has ten language ports, workload, rights/provenance,
static inventory and package preflights, and `i64_array_scalar` runner/verifier
registration. The Elisa implementation uses a bounded input view and fixed
prefix array. Source description only; no CP-Algorithms code or prose is
copied. No programs, tests, scripts, checkers, builds, compilers, profilers, or
benchmarks were run.

## Encyclopedia of Algorithms Chapter 651: orthogonal-drawing bend minimization implemented (2026-11-17)

The supplied EPUB's Chapter 651, “Bend Minimization for Orthogonal Drawings
of Plane Graphs,” gives Tamassia's concrete minimum-cost integral-flow
reduction. A vertex supplies 4 units; an internal face demands
`2*deg(f)-4`, and the external face demands `2*deg(f)+4`; each primal edge
creates two directed dual arcs of unit cost and lower bound zero; each
vertex-face corner creates a zero-cost arc with lower bound one. The chapter
states that an integral flow of value `4*n` and cost `b` corresponds to an
orthogonal drawing with `b` bends. Local `min_cost_max_flow` accepts a generic
single-source/sink graph and does not construct this embedding-derived
dual/corner network or compute the bend optimum. Implemented as
[`orthogonal_drawing_minimum_bends`](o/orthogonal_drawing_minimum_bends/README.md), a bounded simple 2-connected plane-graph
profile with explicit faces and connected degree-two vertex links. It returns
the minimum bend count and omits drawing coordinates. The package includes ten language ports, primary
and independent flow references, workload fixtures, rights/provenance, a static
inventory, and `i64_array_bytes_output` suite integration. Source: Chapter 651,
[DOI 10.1007/978-1-4939-2864-4_651](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4939-2864-4_651),
algorithm description only. No book or reference code is copied. No programs,
tests, scripts, checkers, builds, compilers, profilers, or benchmarks were run.

## NetworkX algorithms index follow-up: Havel–Hakimi realization implemented (2026-11-17)

The NetworkX [`havel_hakimi_graph` constructor](https://networkx.org/documentation/stable/reference/generated/networkx.generators.degree_seq.havel_hakimi_graph.html) realizes a graphical degree sequence as a simple edge list. Local [`erdos_gallai_graphical_sequence`](e/erdos_gallai_graphical_sequence/README.md) decides graphicality but does not construct a graph, so its independent Erdős–Gallai logic is not the same measured operation. Implemented as [`havel_hakimi_graph_realization`](h/havel_hakimi_graph_realization/README.md), this bounded `i64_array_bytes_output` profile accepts `N<=8`, rejects out-of-range degree values as malformed, returns `[0]` for an in-range non-graphical sequence, and otherwise emits `[1,m,u0,v0,...]`. It pins ties by smallest vertex ID for the hub and by residual degree descending then ID ascending for neighbors. The primary repeatedly sorts; the independent reference checks Erdős–Gallai and uses a heap with the same tie key, plus a separate edge-certificate check. Ten ports, workload, rights/provenance, inventory, and byte-output suite registration are integrated. Sources: NetworkX's constructor documentation, Hakimi, [“On Realizability of a Set of Integers as Degrees of the Vertices of a Linear Graph. I”](https://doi.org/10.1137/0110037), and NetworkX's [Erdős–Gallai documentation](https://networkx.org/documentation/stable/reference/algorithms/generated/networkx.algorithms.graphical.is_valid_degree_sequence_erdos_gallai.html). No code, examples, or prose were copied; no programs, tests, scripts, checkers, builds, compilers, profilers, or benchmarks were run.

## NetworkX algorithms index follow-up: 1-WL color refinement implemented (2026-11-17)

The official [NetworkX repository](https://github.com/networkx/networkx),
its [algorithms index](https://networkx.org/documentation/stable/reference/algorithms/index.html),
and the `weisfeiler_lehman_graph_hash` method description were compared with
local package paths, README contracts, and active reservations. HITS,
Louvain, label propagation, and Kernighan–Lin bisection map to local
`hits_fixed_point`, `louvain_multilevel_community_detection`,
`gbbs_label_propagation_clustering`, and `ptrdist_ks`. Before this addition,
no local package or reservation implemented 1-dimensional Weisfeiler–Lehman color refinement;
`is_isomorphic` is a character-substitution predicate, and
`hypergraph_incidence_graph_encoding` constructs a graph representation but
does not refine graph colors.

Implemented as `weisfeiler_lehman_color_refinement`, a bounded hash-free core
profile over simple undirected graphs with `0<=n<=8`, encoded as
`[n,adjacency_mask_0,...,adjacency_mask_(n-1)]`. Initialize each vertex with
its degree, as NetworkX does for an unlabeled graph.
Each round forms `(own_color, sorted multiset of neighbor colors)`, sorts the
distinct signatures lexicographically, and assigns their zero-based ranks.
Stop when the number of classes no longer increases and pack the stable
per-vertex colors in base 9, least-significant digit for vertex 0. The primary
uses sorted signatures; the independent reference refines explicit partition
blocks by neighbor-color multisets. This measures hash-free 1-WL color
refinement; it does not compute NetworkX's digest or claim complete graph-
isomorphism testing. Ten language ports, workload, rights/provenance, inventory,
and `i64_array_scalar` suite integration are present. Elisa copies the bounded
ABI frame into local arrays before the refinement. Primary method source: the NetworkX
[`weisfeiler_lehman_graph_hash` description](https://networkx.org/documentation/stable/reference/algorithms/generated/networkx.algorithms.graph_hashing.weisfeiler_lehman_graph_hash.html);
independent algorithm source: Shervashidze et al., [“Weisfeiler-Lehman Graph
Kernels”](https://jmlr.org/papers/v12/shervashidze11a.html). Source code and
documentation prose are not copied. No programs, tests, scripts, checkers, builds, compilers, profilers, or
benchmarks were run.

## RosettaGit title-index gap: Hickerson almost-integer sequence — implemented (2026-11-17)

The public [RosettaGit title index](https://rosettagit.org/tasks/) surfaced
“Hickerson series of almost integers.” Local path, README, catalog, and
reservation searches found no Hickerson or near-integer sequence package.
[`bailey_borwein_plouffe`](b/bailey_borwein_plouffe/README.md) extracts a
hexadecimal digit of π and does not evaluate this expression. Reserved as
`hickerson_almost_integer` on the `i64_array_float64` lane: input `[n]`,
`1<=n<=17`, output the binary64 approximation
`h_n=n!/(2*(ln(2)^(n+1)))`; malformed input returns `-1e300`. Ports will use
the equivalent recurrence `h_1=1/(2 ln(2)^2)` and
`h_n=(n/ln 2)*h_(n-1)`; the independent Decimal reference evaluates the
factorial/power expression directly. The first decimal digit is 0 or 9 for
`n=1..15`, but not for 16 or 17. The result remains the floating-point
approximation, distinct from the exact ordered Bell integer sequence. Sources:
Wolfram MathWorld, [Almost Integer](https://mathworld.wolfram.com/AlmostInteger.html);
OEIS [A034172](https://oeis.org/A034172), citing H. S. Wilf,
[*Generatingfunctionology*](https://www2.math.upenn.edu/~wilf/gfology2.pdf).
RosettaGit is discovery only; no task content or code is used. The package in
`benchmarks/h/hickerson_almost_integer` has ten ports, workload, two references,
rights/provenance, and static inventory. The binary64 array runner and
independent verifier are registered. No programs, tests, scripts, checkers,
builds, compilers, profilers, or benchmarks were run.

`jacobson_matthews_latin_square_chain`, `hilbert_curve`, and the local Jaro/
Jaro–Winkler packages. “Egyptian division” is a method duplicate of
[`divide_two_integers`](d/divide_two_integers/README.md), which also forms
power-of-two divisor multiples and subtracts them to obtain quotient and
remainder. “Fusc sequence” was not reserved separately because
[`calkin_wilf_index`](c/calkin_wilf_index/README.md) already returns consecutive
Stern-diatomic values as the indexed rational's numerator and denominator.
Titles centered on language/runtime features, file or network services, GUI,
audio/video, animation, and underspecified game demonstrations were excluded
as non-algorithmic or lacking a single bounded operation from their title
alone.

Implemented package [`hofstadter_conway_10000_sequence`](h/hofstadter_conway_10000_sequence/README.md)
as a distinct nested recurrence. Its scalar contract is input `[N]`,
`2<=N<=8192`, returning `a(N)` for `a(1)=a(2)=1` and
`a(n)=a(a(n-1))+a(n-a(n-1))` for `n>=3`. The primary fills a bottom-up
table in each of ten language ports; an independent explicit dependency-stack/memo
reference evaluates the same defining recurrence in demand order. The package
includes bounded fixtures, provenance/rights, and static inventory metadata, and
is registered in the scalar runner/verifier and catalog.
Induction gives `1<=a(n)<=n`,
so signed-i64 values and indices are safe; the bounded table uses at most
65,544 bytes. This differs from [`hofstadter_q_sequence`](h/hofstadter_q_sequence/README.md),
whose two lagged offsets are `n-Q(n-1)` and `n-Q(n-2)`, and from
[`hofstadter_figure_figure_sequences`](h/hofstadter_figure_figure_sequences/README.md),
which constructs complementary greedy sequences. Method sources: Kubo and
Vakil, [“On Conway's recursive sequence”](https://doi.org/10.1016/0012-365X(94)00303-Z),
MathWorld's [Hofstadter–Conway sequence definition](https://mathworld.wolfram.com/Hofstadter-Conway10000-DollarSequence.html),
and [OEIS A004001](https://oeis.org/A004001). RosettaGit is title discovery
only. No programs, tests, scripts, checkers, builds, compilers, profilers, or
benchmarks were run.

## CP-Algorithms power-of-two Sqrt Tree (`sqrt_tree_constant_time`) — implemented (2026-11-17)

The [Sqrt Tree article's query-optimization section](https://cp-algorithms.com/data_structures/sqrt-tree.html#optimizing-the-query-complexity) replaces recursive ceil-sqrt descent with padded power-of-two layers of equal-size segments. Each layer stores block prefix/suffix minima and a compact whole-block interval table; the highest differing bit of `left XOR right` selects the unique layer, giving O(1) query time with O(N log log N) construction and active summaries. This is a materially different layout and query path from local [`sqrt_tree`](s/sqrt_tree/README.md), which descends recursively for O(log log n) queries, and from [`sparse_table`](s/sparse_table/README.md), which stores overlapping intervals in O(n log n) space. Implemented as [`sqrt_tree_constant_time`](s/sqrt_tree_constant_time/README.md), bounded by `n,q<=64`, with ten language ports, direct-scan independent oracle, workload fixtures, rights/provenance, static inventory, and `i64_array_bytes_output` runner/verifier registration. The CP-Algorithms page is CC BY-SA 4.0; only the method description was used. Clean-room implementations; no code or prose copied. No programs, tests, scripts, checkers, builds, compilers, profilers, or benchmarks were run.

## Encyclopedia of Algorithms Chapter 652: Thomassen convex-drawing extendibility — implemented (2026-11-17)


The book's [“Convex Graph Drawing” entry](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4939-2864-4_652), Theorem 1, gives three necessary and sufficient conditions for extending a supplied convex outer polygon to a convex drawing of a biconnected plane graph. Implemented as [`thomassen_convex_drawing_extendibility`](t/thomassen_convex_drawing_extendibility/README.md), the bounded profile validates a complete combinatorial sphere embedding and the side-path partition, then returns `1` for extendible, `0` when a condition fails, and `-1` for malformed input. It does not construct coordinates. The package has ten ports, max-flow and path-enumeration references, a 92-word maximum valid frame, a 93-word parse limit, 16,384-byte workspace, bounded fixtures including a maximum triangulation and one isolating failure per theorem condition, rights/provenance, static inventory, and `i64_array_scalar` runner/verifier registration. All implementations and fixtures are clean-room; only the theorem description was used. No programs, tests, scripts, checkers, builds, compilers, profilers, or benchmarks were run.

## Algovault algorithm-index follow-up (2026-11-17)

The public [Algovault index](https://github.com/sgtlaugh/algovault) was compared against local package names and README methods. Its data-structure entries for distinct subarray aggregates, Euler-tour trees, persistent leftist heaps, wavelet structures, ordered sets, Mo's algorithm, and Garsia–Wachs are represented locally by [`distinct_subarray_aggregates`](d/distinct_subarray_aggregates/README.md), [`euler_tour_tree`](e/euler_tour_tree/README.md), [`persistent_leftist_heap`](p/persistent_leftist_heap/README.md), [`wavelet_tree`](w/wavelet_tree/README.md) / [`wavelet_matrix`](w/wavelet_matrix/README.md), [`ordered_set_avl_order_statistics`](o/ordered_set_avl_order_statistics/README.md), [`mos_algorithm`](m/mos_algorithm/README.md), and [`garsia_wachs_alphabetic_tree`](g/garsia_wachs_alphabetic_tree/README.md). Its slope-trick, cactus/chordal graph, matroid-intersection, Steiner-tree, stable-matching, DAG path-cover, fast-prime-sum, Pell, Freivalds, Hunt–Szymanski LCS, subsequence-automaton, and dancing-links entries also map to local packages with those method profiles. These are source-title matches confirmed against package descriptions, not claims that similarly named variants have identical contracts.

The index's “Pisano Period” entry surfaced a distinct gap: [`fibonacci_matrix_exponentiation`](f/fibonacci_matrix_exponentiation/README.md) computes one `F(n) mod m`, whereas the Pisano period is the least positive index at which the consecutive residue pair returns to `(0,1 mod m)`. No local package or reservation for that period operation was found. Implemented as [`pisano_period`](p/pisano_period/README.md), bounded to `1<=m<=64`, with a direct modular-pair scan and an independent fast-doubling search through the inclusive `6m` ceiling. The package includes ten ports, workload, references, rights/provenance, static inventory, and `i64_array_scalar` runner/verifier registration. Sources: Algovault's MIT-licensed index and OEIS [A001175](https://oeis.org/A001175), with MathWorld's [Pisano-period entry](https://mathworld.wolfram.com/PisanoPeriod.html) for the least-period definition. The indexes and mathematical descriptions are used for discovery and method specification only; no repository code, examples, or tests are reused. No programs, tests, scripts, checkers, builds, compilers, profilers, or benchmarks were run.

The index also lists “Longest Common Increasing Subsequence.” This is not covered by [`longest_increasing_subsequence`](l/longest_increasing_subsequence/README.md) or [`longest_common_subsequence`](l/longest_common_subsequence/README.md) individually. The confirmed gap now has ten ports, an O(nm) one-row dynamic program, an independent matching-pair DAG reference, bounded fixtures, and scalar-suite registration. Its algorithm details use the cited LCIS papers; the Algovault index was discovery only.

## KACTL, NIST DADS, and TheAlgorithms/Rust index follow-up (2026-11-17)

KTH's KACTL [techniques index](https://github.com/kth-competitive-programming/kactl/blob/main/content/appendix/techniques.txt) also lists Lovasz Toggle. The local graph-coloring packages count proper colorings, search for a proper assignment, or use greedy proper coloring; they do not enforce a bounded number of same-color neighbors. Added [`lovasz_toggle_defective_coloring_trace`](l/lovasz_toggle_defective_coloring_trace/README.md), which picks the lowest-index bad vertex under the `r+b+1` degree condition and returns the terminal defective coloring with the toggle count. It includes ten language ports, a bit-mask primary and adjacency-set reference, bounded fixtures, rights/provenance, static inventory, and scalar-suite registration. The [University of Chicago notes](https://people.cs.uchicago.edu/~laci/reu03/notes13/node3.html) describe the toggle rule and degree condition. Only algorithm descriptions were used; no programs, tests, scripts, checkers, builds, compilers, profilers, or benchmarks were run.

The NIST type index also surfaced the move-to-root BST access heuristic, which repeatedly rotates a successful search result up one parent edge at a time. It is distinct from [`splay_tree`](s/splay_tree/README.md), whose zig-zig and zig-zag rules change the resulting shapes and access costs. Added [`move_to_root_bst_access_trace`](m/move_to_root_bst_access_trace/README.md) with ten language ports, an array-backed primary oracle, an independent node-object reference, fixtures covering the difference from splaying and miss stability, rights/provenance, static inventory, and `i64_array_scalar` suite registration. Allen and Munro's [“Self-Organizing Binary Search Trees”](https://doi.org/10.1145/322092.322094) is the algorithm reference; only method descriptions were used. No programs, tests, scripts, checkers, builds, compilers, profilers, or benchmarks were run.

The [NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures type index](https://xlinux.nist.gov/dads/termsType.html) and TheAlgorithms/Rust's public [directory index](https://github.com/TheAlgorithms/Rust/blob/master/DIRECTORY.md) were used to find title-level candidates. This was an index-level comparison, not a source-file-by-source-file audit.

The DADS [linear hashing entry](https://xlinux.nist.gov/dads/HTML/linearHashing.html) describes dynamic expansion by a level-dependent hash family and a pointer that advances through one-bucket splits. No local contract or reservation had that dynamic bucket-split behavior. The local [`linear_probing_hash_map`](l/linear_probing_hash_map/README.md) and [`hash_map_cuckoo_hashing`](h/hash_map_cuckoo_hashing/README.md) instead use open addressing with cluster repair and cuckoo displacement respectively; [`hash_map_separate_chaining`](h/hash_map_separate_chaining/README.md) does not implement incremental split-pointer growth. Added [`linear_hashing_trace`](l/linear_hashing_trace/README.md), a deterministic bounded insert/delete/membership trace with Euclidean bucket hashing, load-triggered one-bucket splits, ten language ports, a flat-list independent reference, fixtures, rights/provenance, static inventory, and `i64_array_scalar` suite registration. The workload pins the first expansion threshold and a trace that reaches 32 buckets. The main method reference is Litwin, [“Linear Hashing: A New Tool for File and Table Addressing”](https://www.vldb.org/dblp/db/conf/vldb/Litwin80.html). Candidate titles MODIFIND and Ferguson–Forcade remain excluded: DADS does not specify MODIFIND's partition mechanics sufficiently to distinguish a deterministic benchmark trace from the local selection profiles, and Ferguson–Forcade operates on real-valued tuples with no bounded exact input/output contract in the entry. The KACTL index exposed a Manhattan-MST method variant: [`manhattan_mst_candidate_edge_reduction`](m/manhattan_mst_candidate_edge_reduction/README.md) generates an `O(N)` candidate graph with four octant sweeps and applies Kruskal, while the existing [`manhattan_mst`](m/manhattan_mst/README.md) runs Prim over the complete point graph. CP-Algorithms describes why the nearest point in each octant yields a candidate graph containing an MST; KACTL's [header](https://github.com/kth-competitive-programming/kactl/blob/main/content/geometry/ManhattanMST.h) lists CC0. Added ten language ports, an independent complete-graph Prim reference, bounded fixtures, rights/provenance, static inventory, and `i64_array_scalar` runner/verifier registration. The benchmark restricts x and y coordinates to individually unique values so active predecessor keys remain unambiguous. Algorithm descriptions only; no code was copied and no programs or checks were run.

## Additional source-gap audits and candidate reservations (2026-11-17)

The NASA NPB inventory and HPCC suite index were compared against the existing benchmark crosswalk. NPB's IS/EP/CG/MG/FT/BT/SP/LU, UA/DC/DT/BT-IO, multi-zone and GridNPB entries map to existing numerical kernels or to orchestration/I/O profiles; no standalone NPB algorithm gap was confirmed. HPCC's DGEMM, STREAM vector operations, RandomAccess and 1-D FFT map to local profiles. PTRANS is `A <- A + B^T`, but its communication-heavy parallel exchange is outside this repository's single-call ABI, while the fused elementwise addition alone is a simple composition; it remains excluded. HPCG's bounded one-coarse-level profile is a bounded form of the same multigrid-PCG method, not a separate algorithm. Sources: [NASA NPB inventory](https://www.nas.nasa.gov/software/npb.html), [HPCC tests](https://www.hpcchallenge.org/), [HPCG overview](https://www.hpcg-benchmark.org/).

HPL does expose a distinct bounded kernel: right-looking blocked LU with row partial pivoting. Local [`blocked_lu_factorization`](b/blocked_lu_factorization/README.md) has blocked updates but no pivoting, and [`linpack_lu_solve`](l/linpack_lu_solve/README.md) uses scalar factorization/solve operations. A clean-room single-process panel plus trailing-update profile is implemented as `hpl_blocked_partial_pivot_lu`; HPL's MPI distribution and look-ahead schedule are excluded from the bounded profile. Source: [Netlib HPL algorithm](https://netlib.sandia.gov/benchmark/hpl/algorithm.html).

The current OI Wiki index spot-check found Tournament Sort already covered by [`tournament_sort`](t/tournament_sort/README.md). Its balanced-tree-in-segment method is an alternative composition for mutable range order statistics, overlapping existing Fenwick-of-value-tree and persistent segment-tree contracts; the persistent-block-array page remains an underspecified placeholder. No high-confidence missing algorithm was confirmed in the sampled OI Wiki categories. Source: [OI Wiki pages](https://oi-wiki.org/pages/).

LeetCode's public title/topic indexes surfaced three distinct algorithm candidates. `shortest_subarray_with_sum_at_least_k` admits negative values and uses a monotone deque over prefix sums; local [`minimum_size_subarray_sum`](m/minimum_size_subarray_sum/README.md) is positive-only, and [`subarray_sum_equals_k`](s/subarray_sum_equals_k/README.md) counts exact-sum intervals. `minimum_window_subsequence` preserves pattern order, unlike the multiplicity window in [`minimum_window_substring`](m/minimum_window_substring/README.md) and the yes/no queries in [`subsequence_automaton`](s/subsequence_automaton/README.md). `linear_partition_minimax` partitions a sequence into contiguous groups to minimize the largest group sum, unlike subset [`minimum_sum_partition`](m/minimum_sum_partition/README.md) or additive-cost [`divide_conquer_dp_partition`](d/divide_conquer_dp_partition/README.md). All three now have clean-room ten-language packages and suite registration. Method sources: Chen and Chao, [shortest sum-constrained segment](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ipl.2005.08.006); Das et al., [episode matching](https://cpm.cs.helsinki.fi/cpm97.html); Skiena, [linear partition problem](https://users.math.uoc.gr/~plex/mem291-Fall2023/ark/Skiena-The_Algorithm_Design_Manual.pdf). LeetCode is used as a title/topic discovery index only. No problem text or source code is reused.

## Encyclopedia Chapter 734 reservation — Simpath s–t path ZDD (2026-11-17)

Chapter 734, [“Counting by ZDD”](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4939-2864-4_734), describes Simpath construction of a zero-suppressed decision diagram for all simple paths between supplied terminals. Existing [`zdd_family_count`](z/zdd_family_count/README.md) only builds/counts a canonical ZDD from an explicitly materialized subset family; it does not scan graph edges with path-fragment mate states, frontier pruning, and per-level state merging. Ordinary path-enumeration packages return individual paths rather than the compressed family. Implemented as [`simpath_st_paths_zdd`](s/simpath_st_paths_zdd/README.md), with ten ports, frontier/mate and path-family references, a bounded workload, provenance, static inventory, and `i64_array_scalar` suite registration. The chapter points to Knuth's TAOCP Vol. 4A §7.1.4; Iwashita's [Hokkaido University technical report on top-down ZDD construction](https://www-alg.ist.hokudai.ac.jp/~thomas/TCSTR/tcstr_13_69/tcstr_13_69.pdf) gives the Simpath state and terminal checks, and Knuth's [official program index](https://cs.stanford.edu/~knuth/programs.html) identifies the public Simpath materials. No upstream code is reused; no executable checks were run.

## Encyclopedia of Algorithms Chapter 423: Hajiaghayi–Sorkin 3-SAT Algorithm A — implemented (2026-11-17)

Added [`random_3sat_hajiaghayi_sorkin_algorithm_a`](r/random_3sat_hajiaghayi_sorkin_algorithm_a/README.md) as a bounded deterministic tie specialization of Section 3, Algorithm A. It selects pure variables first; otherwise maximizes `(abs(i-j), i+j)` over current positive and negative degrees, then repeatedly propagates the first residual unit clause. It does not backtrack. ## NIST DADS type-index reservation: interval heap DEPQ (2026-11-17)

The interval-heap reservation is implemented as [`interval_heap_double_ended`](i/interval_heap_double_ended/README.md). The existing [`min_max_heap_double_ended`](m/min_max_heap_double_ended/README.md) stores one key per node on alternating min/max levels; an interval heap stores low/high key pairs in each complete-tree node and keeps each child interval inside its parent. The two methods share an abstract operation set, but their storage invariants and sift/repair steps differ. The profile accepts insert, find-min, find-max, extract-min, extract-max, and count operations, caps each call at 128 operations and 64 initial keys, and allows at most 192 live keys. Ten ports, paired-endpoint and sorted-multiset references, bounded workload, static inventory/checker, and `i64_array_bytes_output` registration are complete. Primary source: van Leeuwen and Wood, “Interval Heaps,” *The Computer Journal* 36(3), 209–216 (1993), [DOI 10.1093/comjnl/36.3.209](https://doi.org/10.1093/comjnl/36.3.209), Sections 1–2; discovery source: Paul Black’s [NIST DADS double-ended priority queue entry](https://xlinux.nist.gov/dads/HTML/doubleendpq.html). ## Encyclopedia of Algorithms Chapter 133: Schuler randomized general-CNF SAT implemented (2026-11-17)

Added [`schuler_randomized_general_cnf_sat`](s/schuler_randomized_general_cnf_sat/README.md), a bounded deterministic replay of Schuler's randomized SAT algorithm with supplied PPZ permutation/bit tapes and clause-selection indices. The existing [`procedure_s_general_cnf_sat`](p/procedure_s_general_cnf_sat/README.md) is a different Procedure S profile: it uses deterministic source-order branching over falsified clause prefixes and a bounded exhaustive k-CNF check. The Schuler profile truncates clauses to `1+ceil_strict(log2(m))` literals, runs PPZ, then recursively chooses a length-k prefix and falsifies its literals before simplifying the original formula. It also differs from the no-backtrack greedy DPLL trace and the 3-SAT degree-priority profile. The ten ports and both references walk every variable not fixed by an ancestor in permutation order, including absent variables; they index tape bits at that filtered position. Primary procedure: Schuler, “An Algorithm for the Satisfiability Problem of Formulas in Conjunctive Normal Form,” Section 2, [DOI 10.1016/j.jalgor.2004.04.012](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jalgor.2004.04.012), with the PPZ subroutine shown in Figure 1; chapter coverage: *Encyclopedia of Algorithms*, Chapter 133, [DOI 10.1007/978-1-4939-2864-4_133]. Ten language ports, independent references, bounded workload, static inventory, and `i64_array_bytes_output` runner/verifier integration are present. No source code, prose, or figures are reused. No executable checks were run.

## Encyclopedia of Algorithms Chapter 170: Wigderson 3-colorable graph Algorithm A implemented (2026-11-17)

[`wigderson_3_colorable_graph_coloring`](w/wigderson_3_colorable_graph_coloring/README.md) implements Wigderson's explicit Algorithm A in §2 for a promised 3-colorable simple graph: while current maximum degree reaches `floor(sqrt(original_n))`, choose the smallest-ID maximum-degree vertex, 2-color its induced current neighborhood with ascending-root/neighbor BFS, assign the center `i+2`, remove the closed neighborhood, and advance `i` by exactly two; finish with ascending-ID sequential first-fit from the current `i`. This preserves the source's overlapping center/next-neighborhood color label. The deterministic ties and promise check make a bounded byte profile. Its neighborhood bipartition and closed-neighborhood reduction distinguish it from local generic greedy, Welsh–Powell, DSatur, backtracking, and Pannotia priority-extrema coloring. The package has all ten language paths, active-graph and independent bitset references, bounded golden/capacity/invalid fixtures, rights and provenance, a static inventory reviewer, and `i64_array_bytes_output` runner/verifier registration. Primary source: Wigderson, JACM 30(4), 729–735 (1983), [DOI 10.1145/2157.2158](https://doi.org/10.1145/2157.2158), Algorithm A and Theorem 2.1; chapter context: *Encyclopedia of Algorithms*, Chapter 170, [DOI 10.1007/978-1-4939-2864-4_170](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4939-2864-4_170). ## Encyclopedia of Algorithms Chapter 601: heterotypic spatial-contact PMF integrated (2026-11-17)

The Chapter 601 package [`spatial_motif_different_type_contact_pmf`](s/spatial_motif_different_type_contact_pmf/README.md) profiles the exact internally random null distribution when `X != Y`. The `i64_array_bytes_output` contract accepts `[L,x1,y1,x2,y2]`, `1<=L<=10`, with nonnegative counts and `xj+yj<=L`; it fixes sequence 1's type counts and uniformly permutes sequence 2's multiset. For each total heterotypic contact count `m=0..L`, the primary reference sums the chapter's three-category multinomial mass over `h` X-X contacts, `i` X-Y contacts, `j=m-i` Y-X contacts, and `k` Y-Y contacts: `M(x1,h,i) M(y1,j,k) M(L-x1-y1,x2-h-j,y2-i-k)`, where `M(a,b,c)=a!/(b!c!(a-b-c)!)` and invalid counts contribute zero. The common denominator is `M(L,x2,y2)`. Output is `[L,denominator,N0,...,NL,E_num,E_den]` as little-endian i64, with reduced expectation derived from the PMF. The maximum number of distinct arrangements is 4,200; maximum output is 120 bytes and fixed workspace is capped at 1,024 bytes. The independent reference enumerates unique sequence-2 multiset arrangements and histograms contact totals. This is distinct from the implemented same-type `X-X` package: its single hypergeometric variable does not model the two dependent directional contact counts or their three-category marginalization. Ten language ports, two references, workload, provenance/rights, and static inventory are complete, with `i64_array_bytes_output` runner/verifier registration. Primary source: Jackups and Liang, “Combinatorial Analysis for Sequence and Spatial Motif Discovery in Short Sequence Fragments,” IEEE/ACM TCBB 7(3), 524–536 (2010), [DOI 10.1109/TCBB.2008.101](https://doi.org/10.1109/TCBB.2008.101), §II-B, Eqs. (2) and following marginal; chapter: *Encyclopedia of Algorithms*, Chapter 601, [DOI 10.1007/978-1-4939-2864-4_601](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4939-2864-4_601). No code has been executed.

## LeetCode title-index: minimum-cost bipartite edge cover integrated (2026-11-17)

The public LeetCode title “Minimum Cost to Connect Two Groups of Points” led to a bounded complete weighted bipartite edge-cover profile, implemented as `minimum_cost_bipartite_edge_cover_subset_dp` in all ten languages. A valid solution selects edges so every vertex on both sides is incident to at least one selected edge, minimizing total edge cost. The clean-room DP processes left vertices and tracks the covered-right bitmask; each transition chooses a nonempty right-side subset for the current left vertex. Use `1<=left,right<=8`, costs `0..1000`, exact input `[left_count,right_count,costs row-major]` (66 valid words, 67 parseable), result `0..8000`, and 8,192 bytes of workspace. This is distinct from one-to-one [`hungarian_algorithm`](h/hungarian_algorithm/README.md) and assignment-counting [`assignment_using_bitmask`](a/assignment_using_bitmask/README.md); [`cheriyan_thurimella_two_vertex_connected_spanning_subgraph`](c/cheriyan_thurimella_two_vertex_connected_spanning_subgraph/README.md) uses edge cover only as an internal subroutine and optimizes a different connected spanning subgraph. Discovery: [LeetCode title page](https://leetcode.com/problems/minimum-cost-to-connect-two-groups-of-points/). The edge-cover definition is consistent with Hessler and Wästlund, “Edge Cover and Polymatroid Flow Problems,” *Electronic Journal of Probability* 15 (2010), [article](https://www.maths.tcd.ie/EMIS/journals/EJP-ECP/article/view/846.html); the independent reference uses the minimum-weight-matching reduction described by Ferdous, Pothen, and Halappanavar, “Streaming Matching and Edge Cover in Practice,” SEA 2024, [DOI 10.4230/LIPIcs.SEA.2024.12](https://doi.org/10.4230/LIPIcs.SEA.2024.12). The scalar suite runner/verifier and catalog registration are complete. Community title material is discovery only. No LeetCode statement, examples, tests, submissions, or code are reused.

## OI Wiki Josephus batched small-step algorithm (2026-11-18)

Add `josephus_batched_small_k` from the [OI Wiki Josephus page](https://en.oi-wiki.org/misc/josephus/),
which specifies a logarithmic algorithm for small `k`: when `k<=n`, batch
`floor(n/k)` eliminations, recurse on `n-floor(n/k)`, then map the survivor
back with `r -= n mod k`, adding `n` if negative or otherwise adding
`floor(r/(k-1))`. When `k>n`, use the ordinary one-size recurrence. This
differs from local `josephus_problem`'s O(n) recurrence, the direct-recursion
profile, and list simulation; none batches complete sweeps. The scalar input
is `[N,K]`, `1<=N<=1,000,000`, `1<=K<=32`, returning the zero-based survivor.
The primary uses a fixed bounded frame stack to unwind the batched recurrence;
an independent O(N) one-step recurrence and tiny direct-elimination fixtures
check the result. Ten clean-room ports, workload, both references,
provenance/rights, package inventory, scalar runner/verifier, CATALOG, and
README registration are integrated under `benchmarks/j/josephus_batched_small_k/`.
No programs, tests, scripts, checkers, builds, compilers, profilers, or
benchmarks were run.

Planar Graphs Almost as Good as the Complete Graphs and Almost as Cheap as
Minimum Spanning Trees,” *Algorithmica* 8 (1992), 251–256, [DOI
10.1007/BF01758846](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01758846), §§2–3. This is
distinct from the Delaunay-triangulation benchmark (which returns the full
triangulation), the WSPD Euclidean t-spanner, and the weighted/general-graph
greedy spanners. Starting from the Euclidean MST of the supplied Delaunay
triangulation, the method doubles its directed edges into a contour, then
repeatedly absorbs the next Delaunay triangle along a stack-ordered boundary
edge. It keeps a shortcut when accumulated contour weight is strictly greater
than `(1 + 1/r)` times its Euclidean length; otherwise it carries that weight
onto the boundary shortcut. The bounded profile fixes `r=1`, uses integer
coordinates in strict general position (`3<=n<=8`, coordinates in `[-10,10]`),
and accepts a canonical precomputed Delaunay triangulation so that the timed
kernel measures the cited pruning procedure rather than a second triangulator.
Canonical geometric rotation, MST, and stack tie rules are specified in the
package contract. The primary reference follows the polygon/stack transitions;
the independent reference reconstructs facets from empty circumcircles and
uses a separate boundary scan. The workload includes a bounded five-face trace
whose carried path triggers an actually retained shortcut. Output is the
sorted retained undirected edge list in little-endian i64 bytes. Ten clean-room
language ports, two references, workload, provenance/rights, and static
inventory/checker are included under
`benchmarks/l/levcopoulos_lingas_planar_geometric_spanner/`. The
`i64_array_bytes_output` runner/verifier and repository catalog are wired. The
mathematical method is taken from the primary paper and Chapter 294; no source
code, prose, figures, or fixtures are reused. No programs, tests, scripts,
checkers, builds, compilers, profilers, or benchmarks were run.

## NIST DADS buddy system allocator (2026-11-18)

Add `buddy_system_allocator` from the [NIST DADS buddy system entry](https://xlinux.nist.gov/dads/HTML/buddysystem.html).
The bounded profile models a 256-unit arena, power-of-two request rounding,
lowest-address selection within the smallest available order, recursive
splitting of larger blocks, and recursive coalescing with a free equal-sized
buddy on release. This differs from `memory_management_algorithms`, whose
first/best/worst/next-fit policies only consume residual block sizes, and from
`bitmap_block_allocation`, which toggles caller-selected bitmap runs; neither
uses a buddy tree or recursively merges free blocks. Input is
`[operation_count,(opcode,id,arg)*operation_count]` with at most 64 operations,
193 valid words, and a 194-word parse bound for trailing-data rejection.
Allocation records provide a size and a live-unique ID; free records refer to
an active ID. Output provides a status/base/rounded-size record per operation,
then the canonical final free-block list. The primary follows size-class
free-list splitting; the independent reference models arena coverage as
maximal dyadic intervals. All ten language ports, workload, two references,
provenance/rights, package README, static inventory/checker, and workload
reference verifier are integrated under `benchmarks/b/buddy_system_allocator/`.
The `i64_array_bytes_output` runner/verifier and repository catalog are wired.
Algorithm behavior is based on the NIST
definition and Donahue et al., “Hardware Support for Fast and Bounded-Time
Storage Allocation,” §3.1; no code or fixtures are reused. No programs, tests,
scripts, checkers, builds, compilers, profilers, or benchmarks were run.

## NIST DADS: Brzozowski DFA minimization (2026-11-18)

Add `brzozowski_dfa_minimization` for the reverse–determinize method of
finite-automaton minimization. NIST DADS lists finite-state-machine
minimization as the candidate problem; the method follows Brzozowski's
reverse/subset-construction theorem, stated in the
[Prague Stringology proceedings](https://psc.fit.cvut.cz/cgi-bin/getfile.cgi?c=-&n=11&t=pdf&y=2002)
and attributed to his 1962 work. This is distinct from the reserved
[`hopcroft_dfa_minimization`](h/hopcroft_dfa_minimization/README.md), which
refines state partitions, and from finite-automaton construction for pattern
matching. The bounded contract accepts a complete binary DFA with `1<=N<=3`,
a start-state ID, an accepting-state bit mask, and two transitions per state;
it returns the number of states in the reachable minimal DFA. The first
reverse/subset stage has at most eight states, and the second has at most 256.
The primary performs both reverse/subset stages; an independent reference
marks original reachable states and uses iterative pair distinguishability.
The ten-port package, workload, provenance/rights, and static inventory/checker
are integrated under `benchmarks/b/brzozowski_dfa_minimization/`; the
`i64_array_scalar` runner/verifier and repository catalog are wired. No task
text, code, or examples are reused, and no programs, tests, scripts, checkers,
builds, compilers, profilers, or benchmarks were run.

## NIST DADS hashbelt aging hash table integrated (2026-11-18)

Added `hashbelt_aging_hash_table` for the short rotating array of hash tables
described by the [NIST DADS hashbelt entry](https://xlinux.nist.gov/dads/HTML/hashbelt.html)
and William Grosso's “The Hashbelt Data Structure” (O'Reilly ONJava, 2002).
The DADS definition specifies expiration by adding a fresh table at the head
and dropping the oldest table, and lookup by searching the tables; its note
also describes promotion of a hit to the newest table for an LRU use. The
bounded profile fixes four generations and eight separate-chaining buckets
per generation, with integer keys `0..31`, values `-1000..1000`, and at most
64 operations. `PUT` inserts or moves an existing key to the newest generation,
`GET` searches newest to oldest and moves an older hit to the newest generation,
and `AGE` discards and clears the oldest generation. PUT and GET promotion
remove any older copy so each key has at most one live entry. Each operation
emits one little-endian i64: `PUT` emits whether the key was previously absent,
`GET` emits its value or the miss sentinel, and `AGE` emits the number of live
entries dropped. This is distinct from the existing FIFO/LRU/MRU cache profiles,
which evict or order individual entries, and from ordinary hash-table
benchmarks, which do not expire entries by rotating whole table generations.
The primary reference uses bucket chains and a circular generation index; the
independent reference uses per-generation key/value maps and a direct
newest-to-oldest scan. Ten language ports, workload fixtures, provenance and
rights, package inventory, static checker, and reference/workload verifier are
integrated under `benchmarks/h/hashbelt_aging_hash_table/`; the shared
`i64_array_bytes_output` runner/verifier and catalog are wired. No code, task
text, or fixtures are reused, and no programs, tests, scripts, checkers,
builds, compilers, profilers, or benchmarks were run.

## Guy E. Blelloch parallel prefix scan integrated (2026-11-18)

Added `blelloch_parallel_prefix_scan` for the work-efficient exclusive
prefix-sum algorithm in Blelloch's *Prefix Sums and Their Applications*,
CMU-CS-90-190 (1990), Section 1.2. The repository's [`prefix_sum`](p/prefix_sum/README.md)
builds inclusive prefixes by the serial running-sum recurrence; it does not
perform the padded balanced-tree upsweep/downsweep or return exclusive
prefixes. The bounded profile accepts `[N,a0,...,aN-1]`, `1<=N<=64`, with
values in `[-1,000,000,1,000,000]`, pads to the next power of two with additive
identity zero, performs disjoint level-synchronous upsweep steps, sets the
root to zero, then performs disjoint downsweep steps in reverse level order.
It emits `N` little-endian i64 values where `out[0]=0` and
`out[i]=sum(a[0..i))`. Intermediates are bounded by 64,000,000; valid and
parseable input lengths are 65 and 66 i64 words, maximum output is 512 bytes,
and the workspace cap is 2,048 bytes. A direct serial prefix recurrence is
the independent reference. Primary source: Blelloch's [CMU technical report
page](https://www.cs.cmu.edu/afs/cs.cmu.edu/project/scandal/public/papers/CMU-CS-90-190.html)
and [report text](https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~guyb/papers/Ble93.pdf). The ten-port
package, workload, references, provenance/rights, static inventory/checker,
and workload/reference verifier are integrated under
`benchmarks/b/blelloch_parallel_prefix_scan/`; the shared
`i64_array_bytes_output` runner/verifier and catalog are wired. No code, text,
or fixtures are reused, and no programs, tests, scripts, checkers, builds,
compilers, profilers, or benchmarks were run.

## Encyclopedia of Algorithms Chapter 202: BLR linearity-test package implemented (2026-11-18)

Implemented `blr_linearity_test` for the Blum–Luby–Rubinfeld three-query homomorphism test over `GF(2)^n`: for each independently uniform pair `(x,y)`, query `f(x)`, `f(y)`, and `f(x xor y)`, rejecting when `f(x) xor f(y) != f(x xor y)`. The repository has exact linear-system solvers and the fast Walsh–Hadamard transform, but no query-based Boolean-function linearity tester; those solve different problems and do not replay this test's three-point consistency condition. The bounded deterministic profile accepts a complete Boolean truth table for `1<=n<=6`, then a fixed tape of `1<=q<=32` explicit pairs. Each pair must lie in `[0,2^n)^2`. It evaluates pairs in tape order and halts at the first rejection, or accepts after all `q` tests pass. Output is `[accept_bit, rounds_executed, oracle_query_calls]`, with exactly three query calls counted per executed round, including repeated points. The pair tape represents the random choices; because the tape may be arbitrary and `q` is fixed, the package makes no soundness or epsilon-to-query-count claim. Maximum frame is 130 i64 words, output is 24 bytes, and workspace is bounded to 1,024 bytes. Primary reference: Blum, Luby, and Rubinfeld, “Self-testing/correcting with applications to numerical problems,” *Journal of Computer and System Sciences* 47(3), 1993, DOI [10.1016/0022-0000(93)90044-W](https://doi.org/10.1016/0022-0000(93)90044-W), as summarized in Raskhodnikova and Rubinfeld, Encyclopedia of Algorithms Chapter 202, DOI [10.1007/978-1-4939-2864-4_202](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4939-2864-4_202); the operational test is also printed in the parity-encoding section of the [Arora–Lund–Motwani–Sudan–Szegedy paper](https://madhu.seas.harvard.edu/papers/1992/almss-journ.pdf), §4. The package-local ten ports, primary and independent references, workload, provenance/rights, inventory, static checker, and fixture verifier are complete under `benchmarks/b/blr_linearity_test/`; the shared `i64_array_bytes_output` suite and repository catalog are wired. No code, task text, or fixtures are reused. No programs, tests, scripts, checkers, builds, compilers, profilers, or benchmarks were run.

## Felzenszwalb–Huttenlocher 1D squared distance transform integrated (2026-11-18)

Added `felzenszwalb_huttenlocher_1d_squared_distance_transform` for the
linear-time lower-envelope algorithm for
`D[x] = min_i((x-i)^2 + f[i])` from Felzenszwalb and Huttenlocher,
[*Distance Transforms of Sampled Functions*](https://www.cs.cornell.edu/dph/papers/dt.pdf),
Cornell TR2004-1963. A repository search found no sampled-function/parabola
envelope package; [`infinite_knight_distance`](i/infinite_knight_distance/README.md)
computes a chess-knight metric and is unrelated. The bounded profile accepts
`[N,f0,...,f(N-1)]`, `1<=N<=128`, `0<=fi<=1,000,000`, and emits interleaved
`(D[x],argmin[x])` i64 pairs, where the label is the least site index attaining
the minimum. Output is at most 2,048 bytes; the workspace cap is 4,096 bytes.
Build the lower envelope in increasing seed index with integer breakpoint
comparisons; a new parabola becomes active at the first integer coordinate
where it strictly improves the current envelope, so ties remain with the
lower-index seed. The scan is O(N), uses O(N) bounded workspace, and all
results fit i64. An independent O(N^2) direct minimization reference checks
both values and minimizing-site labels. Ten language ports, workload,
references, provenance/rights, and static inventory/checker are integrated
under `benchmarks/f/felzenszwalb_huttenlocher_1d_squared_distance_transform/`;
the shared `i64_array_bytes_output` runner/verifier and catalog are wired.
Only the mathematical method is used; no code, prose, or fixtures are reused.
No programs, tests, scripts, checkers, builds, compilers, profilers, or
benchmarks were run.

## NIST DADS hash-index follow-up: multiply-shift universal hash trace integration (2026-11-18)

`multiply_shift_universal_hash_trace` implements Dietzfelbinger, Hagerup,
Katajainen, and Penttonen's odd-multiplier family
`h_a(x) = (a*x mod 2^32) div 2^(32-s)` with `a` selected from the odd
32-bit multipliers and `1<=s<=16`. This is distinct from DADS's
[multiplication method](https://xlinux.nist.gov/dads/HTML/multiplicationMethod.html),
which multiplies a key by an irrational constant modulo one, and from local
[`pearson_hash`](p/pearson_hash/README.md), [`zobrist_position_hash_trace`](z/zobrist_position_hash_trace/README.md),
and rolling-hash profiles, which use different update families; existing
hash-map packages benchmark collision resolution rather than this hash function family.
The bounded deterministic trace accepts `[s,q,(a,x)*q]`, with `1<=s<=16`,
`0<=q<=32`, odd `1<=a<=2^32-1`, and `0<=x<=2^32-1`; each output is one
little-endian i64 hash value. Callers supply multipliers, so the workload
makes no PRNG or random-seed claim. The primary uses a widened product,
low-word mask, and high-bit extraction; an independent 32-step modular
add-and-double reference computes the product. The ten-port package,
workload, references, provenance/rights, and static inventory are integrated
under `benchmarks/m/multiply_shift_universal_hash_trace/`; the shared
byte-output suite registers the primary and independent references, bounded
fixtures, and package metadata. Primary source: Dietzfelbinger et al., “A
Reliable Randomized Algorithm for the Closest-Pair Problem,” *Journal of
Algorithms* 25(1), 19–51 (1997), DOI
[10.1006/jagm.1997.0873](https://doi.org/10.1006/jagm.1997.0873); DADS's
universal-hashing and multiplication-method entries were discovery sources.
Only the method is used, with clean-room code and fixtures. No programs,
tests, scripts, checkers, builds, compilers, profilers, or benchmarks were
run.

## Samuelson–Berkowitz characteristic polynomial integration (2026-11-18)

Completion status: all ten ports, primary and independent references, workload, rights/provenance, inventory checker, and shared `i64_array_bytes_output` runner/verifier plus catalog registration are complete. No executable checks were run.

Added `berkowitz_characteristic_polynomial` for the division-free
Toeplitz-recursive characteristic-polynomial algorithm of Stuart J. Berkowitz,
“On computing the determinant in small parallel time using a small number of
processors,” *Information Processing Letters* 18(3), 147–150 (1984),
[DOI 10.1016/0020-0190(84)90018-8](https://doi.org/10.1016/0020-0190(84)90018-8).
The local [`characteristic_polynomial`](m/characteristic_polynomial/README.md)
uses similarity reduction to Hessenberg form and a prime-field leading-minor
recurrence; this package instead performs the Samuelson–Berkowitz recursion
without divisions and admits composite moduli. The bounded input is
`[N,modulus,row-major matrix]`, `1<=N<=7`, `2<=modulus<=1,000,000,000`,
with entries in `[-1,000,000,1,000,000]`. Output is the descending coefficient
vector of `det(xI-A)` modulo the supplied modulus, with the monic coefficient
first. The primary recursively multiplies the lower-triangular Toeplitz
coefficient transform built from `a_00`, `R M^k S`, and the characteristic
polynomial of the trailing principal submatrix. An independent reference
expands the polynomial determinant by permutations. The ten-port package,
workload, references, provenance/rights, static inventory/checker, and
`i64_array_bytes_output` runner/verifier plus catalog integration are complete
under `benchmarks/b/berkowitz_characteristic_polynomial/`. Only the
mathematical method is used; no code, prose, or fixtures are reused. No
programs, tests, scripts,
checkers, builds, compilers, profilers, or benchmarks were run.

## Encyclopedia of Algorithms Chapter 713: Crust opposite-pole selection integrated (2026-11-18)

`crust_opposite_pole_selection` profiles the explicit pole-selection stage in
Nina Amenta, Marshall Bern, and Manolis Kamvysselis, “A New Voronoi-Based
Surface Reconstruction Algorithm,” §4, Algorithm steps 2(a,c), pp. 4–5.
Given each non-convex-hull sample and the complete finite-vertex list of its
supplied Voronoi cell, select the farthest vertex as the positive pole, then
the farthest vertex whose displacement has negative dot product with the
positive-pole displacement. The package uses integer 3D coordinates in
[-16,16], 1–8 sample rows, 1–8 supplied cell vertices per row, and lowest
row-local ordinal for equal-distance ties; no eligible opposite vertex is
reported with ordinal -1. It measures pole selection only: Voronoi-cell
construction, convex-hull normal estimation, augmented Delaunay construction,
and triangle filtering are excluded. This is distinct from the existing
[`crust_pole_triangle_filter`](s/crust_pole_triangle_filter/README.md), which
accepts pole IDs and supplied augmented-Delaunay facets and performs only the
sample-only facet filter. Ten clean-room ports, independent scoring
references, bounded workload, provenance/rights, and static inventory are
complete under `benchmarks/c/crust_opposite_pole_selection/`; shared byte-output
runner/verifier and catalog integration are complete. Primary references: Amenta, Bern, and
Kamvysselis, *Proceedings of the 14th Annual ACM Symposium on Computational
Geometry* (1998), [author-hosted paper](https://people.eecs.berkeley.edu/~sequin/CS284/PAPERS/AmentaBernKamvysselis.pdf),
and Amenta, *Encyclopedia of Algorithms*, Chapter 713, [DOI
10.1007/978-1-4939-2864-4_713](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4939-2864-4_713).
Only mathematical ideas are used; no source code, prose, or fixtures are
reused. No programs, tests, scripts, checkers, builds, compilers, profilers,
or benchmarks were run.

## NIST DADS adjacent approximate-membership structure: Cuckoo Filter integrated (2026-11-18)

`cuckoo_filter_operation_trace` implements a deterministic fingerprint-only
Cuckoo Filter core from Fan, Andersen, Kaminsky, and Mitzenmacher, “Cuckoo
Filter: Practically Better Than Bloom,” CoNEXT 2014, Sections 3.1–3.3. NIST
DADS entries for [Bloom filters](https://xlinux.nist.gov/dads/HTML/bloomFilter.html)
and [cuckoo hashing](https://xlinux.nist.gov/dads/HTML/cuckooHashing.html)
provided adjacent discovery context. Existing [`bloom_filter`](b/bloom_filter/README.md)
stores membership bits without deletions, [`xor_filter_peeling`](x/xor_filter_peeling/README.md)
peels a static graph to assign fingerprints, and [`hash_map_cuckoo_hashing`](h/hash_map_cuckoo_hashing/README.md)
stores full keys; none has this fingerprint-only two-bucket eviction and deletion profile.

The bounded replay accepts 1–32 records `[opcode,primary_bucket,fingerprint]`
after a count word. It uses eight four-slot buckets,
`delta(f)=1+((5*f+3) mod 7)`, and alternate bucket `i xor delta(f)`. Insertion
prefers primary then alternate empty slots; otherwise it starts at the primary
bucket, evicts the lowest-numbered slot, and continues for at most eight kicks.
Failure aborts the trace with `-3` and no output. Lookup and deletion scan the
primary then alternate bucket and report misses as zero. Output is one LE i64
status per operation; inputs are capped at 97 valid and 98 parseable words,
output at 256 bytes, and workspace at 1,024 bytes. The deterministic tie policy
is a bounded replay adaptation and makes no probabilistic success or
false-positive claim. Ten ports, independent references, workload,
provenance/rights, static inventory, and shared `i64_array_bytes_output`
runner/verifier plus catalog registration are complete under
`benchmarks/c/cuckoo_filter_operation_trace/`. No source code, prose, or
fixtures were reused. No programs, tests, scripts, checkers, builds,
compilers, profilers, or benchmarks were run.

§§2.2 and 2.4. No upstream code, book prose, or examples were reused. No

## Source-backed reservations and completed integrations (2026-11-18)

The 2-left hashing reservation has been completed and integrated. The
`bagwell_varray_growth_index` is complete and integrated from Bagwell's
[report](https://lampwww.epfl.ch/papers/techlists.pdf), §4, Fig. 7. Its ten
ports and primary reference create linked level headers at 64 and 320 values,
then follow previous-level links for indexed lookup. This is separate from
`dynamic_array`'s contiguous resize/copy strategy and from
`vlist_persistent_sequence`'s persistent prepend/cdr operations. Package
references and workload, provenance/rights, static inventory, byte-output
runner/verifier registration, and catalog entry are in source. No programs,
tests, scripts, checkers, builds, compilers, profilers, or benchmarks were run.

`reverse_delete_mst` is complete and integrated from the NIST DADS/Codewars
lead. Starting from a connected simple weighted graph, it processes edges from
greatest to least weight and deletes an edge only when a traversal reaches
every vertex. This differs from the repository's Kruskal, Prim, and Borůvka
profiles, which grow a forest through union or frontier selection. The
clean-room profile follows Kruskal's Construction A′ in the [1956 paper](https://www.cs.yale.edu/homes/lans/readings/routing/kruskal-1956.pdf)
and pins deterministic equal-weight behavior. Ten ports, 17 fixtures, package
references, provenance/rights, static inventory, byte-output runner/verifier
registration, and catalog entry are in source. No programs, tests, scripts,
checkers, builds, compilers, profilers, or benchmarks were run.

`bagwell_functional_hash_list` is complete and integrated from Bagwell's
[report](https://lampwww.epfl.ch/papers/techlists.pdf), §3 and Fig. 6.
It combines persistent geometrically growing VList blocks with a block-local
hash table and chain offsets, so lookup searches only entries visible in the
selected snapshot before following earlier blocks. This differs from
[`immutable_hash_map`](i/immutable_hash_map/README.md), which searches a
newest-first persistent history, and from mutable separate-chaining maps,
which do not retain snapshot roots. The bounded profile uses up to 32
front-cons insertions and 32 lookups against saved prefix roots, signed-i32
keys/values, geometric block sides 8/16/32, and Euclidean `key mod side`
bucket selection. Its independent reference scans the visible newest-first
history. The primary now keeps each snapshot's current block and local offset
and follows explicit `Prev` links during lookup. All ten native ports,
references, 13 workload fixtures, docs, rights, and inventory are present. A
primary-reference entry offset was corrected during source review. A manual
cross-port and fixture reconciliation found no further mismatch. Byte-output
runner/verifier registration and a catalog entry are integrated. No helpers or
suite machinery were run.

`k2_tree_compact_graph` is reserved to the Algorithm Archive/NIST lane. It
stores a padded binary adjacency matrix in the `T` and `L` bitmaps of a
recursive k²-tree and answers edge-membership and bounded successor queries
through rank-based navigation. This is distinct from the repository's LOUDS
ordered-tree navigation and quadtree spatial indexes: the candidate encodes a
directed graph relation with a succinct matrix hierarchy. The discovery index
is [NIST DADS](https://xlinux.nist.gov/dads/HTML/k2tree.html); the operational
layout is cross-referenced with Brisaboa, Ladra, and Navarro,
[*k²-trees for Compact Web Graph Representation*](https://lbd.udc.es/Repository/Publications/Drafts/K2treforCom.pdf).
The package is complete and integrated. It has primary and independent
references, README, rights, inventory metadata, all ten language ports, a
full N=32, Q=128 fixture (418 input words and 1,032 output bytes), byte-output
runner/verifier registration, and a catalog entry. Static source review caught
and corrected a Mojo row-mask offset. No helpers or suite machinery were run.

`pagoda_meldable_priority_queue` is complete and integrated from the NIST DADS
lead. The bounded `i64_array_scalar` trace uses
`[q,m,(op,a,b,key)*m]`, `1<=q<=8`, and at most 64 operations. It covers
INSERT, destructive UNION/MELD, MIN, and EXTRACTMIN with globally unique
priorities, as assumed by the original paper. The primary stores the pagoda's
parent and extreme-descendant links and melds by bottom-up merging the right
branch of the first queue and the left branch of the second; EXTRACTMIN melds
the removed root's right and left subtrees in that order. The independent
reference uses ordinary sorted priority collections. This merge procedure is
distinct from the local leftist, skew, pairing, binomial, Fibonacci,
rank-pairing, and hollow heaps. The discovery and pointer-layout index is
[NIST DADS](https://xlinux.nist.gov/dads/HTML/pagoda.html); the algorithm is
cross-referenced with Francon, Viennot, and Vuillemin,
[*Description and Analysis of an Efficient Priority Queue Representation*](https://www.xavierviennot.org/xavier/articles_files/FrViVu78.pdf).
All ten language ports, two references, 258-word and 64-node stress fixtures,
docs, rights, and static inventory are present. The scalar bound is 4,160,079,
attained by inserting priority 1,000 then querying it for the remaining
operations. Scalar runner/verifier registration and a catalog entry are
integrated. This remains distinct from local leftist, skew, pairing, binomial,
Fibonacci, rank-pairing, and hollow heaps. The paper defines the queue
primitives and the simplifying distinct-priority assumption (pp. 1, 3–6).
No programs, tests, scripts, checkers, builds, compilers, profilers, or
benchmarks were run.

The same NIST pass excluded Schorr–Waite marking because
[`schorr_waite_graph_marking`](s/schorr_waite_graph_marking/README.md) already
implements it. The “huge sparse array” lead was not reserved because its
dense/sparse inverse-array representation is close to
[`sparse_set_dense_array`](s/sparse_set_dense_array/README.md). The initial
“Hash heap” lead was deferred because NIST DADS does not specify bucket-full
behavior. A later bounded profile caps insertions below a fixed per-bucket
arena limit, so bucket overflow cannot occur; see the dated implementation
follow-up below.

`minimum_weight_cycle_floyd` is complete and integrated from the OI Wiki
minimum-cycle method. Before each Floyd–Warshall update for vertex `k`, it
checks cycles whose greatest-numbered vertex is `k`, combining the current
shortest path between two lower-numbered vertices with their two original
edges to `k`. This differs from
[`minimum_cycle_basis_horton`](m/minimum_cycle_basis_horton/README.md), which
finds a minimum-weight basis of the cycle space, and from directed girth.
The profile uses an undirected simple graph with `3<=n<=9`, positive weights
at most 1,000, and outputs the minimum cycle weight or a valid `-1` payload
when acyclic; an exhaustive simple-cycle enumerator is the independent
reference. Ten ports, fixtures, package references, provenance/rights, static
inventory, byte-output runner/verifier registration, and catalog entry are in
source. Discovery and method description: OI Wiki's [minimum-cycle page](https://oi-wiki.org/graph/min-cycle/).
No programs, tests, scripts, checkers, builds, compilers, profilers, or
benchmarks were run.

`all_pairs_directed_random_walk_hitting_times` is complete and integrated from
the OI Wiki lead. The bounded contract is a strongly connected simple digraph
with `3<=n<=8`, no self-loops or parallel arcs, and input `[n,m,(u,v)*m]`. It
emits the full ordered-pair expected hitting-time matrix modulo `1,000,000,007`
as little-endian i64 values; diagonal entries are zero. At this bound,
directed-tree cofactors and their normalization stay below the prime, so the
stationary distribution and absorbing-chain systems remain invertible in the
field. The primary computes the stationary distribution, uses `g_i=1/pi_i`
in the rank-deficient matrix equation, fixes one free row, then shifts each
column to make its target diagonal zero. An independent reference solves a
separate absorbing-chain system for each target. This is distinct from
[`tree_random_walk_edge_hitting_cost`](t/tree_random_walk_edge_hitting_cost/README.md),
which uses a tree-specific rerooting recurrence for adjacent endpoints.
Discovery and method description: OI Wiki's [graph random-walk page](https://oi-wiki.org/graph/graph-random-walk/),
§ “General graph.” Ten ports, both references, 15 fixtures including the
114-word/512-byte valid maximum case and the 115-word parseable trailing-word
rejection, provenance/rights, static inventory,
`i64_array_bytes_output` runner/verifier integration, and catalog entry are
complete under
[`all_pairs_directed_random_walk_hitting_times`](a/all_pairs_directed_random_walk_hitting_times/README.md).
No upstream code, prose, or fixtures were reused. No programs, tests, scripts,
checkers, builds, compilers, profilers, or benchmarks were run.

The OI Wiki pass also matched its tree Mo method to

in linear time. The NIST DADS [unranking entry](https://xlinux.nist.gov/dads/HTML/unrank.html)
identifies the operation and cites the linear-time method; the pinned method
is Algorithm 1 in Myrvold and Ruskey, “Ranking and Unranking Permutations in
Linear Time,” *Information Processing Letters* 79 (2001),
[DOI 10.1016/S0020-0190(01)00141-7](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0020-0190(01)00141-7),
[author PDF](https://webhome.cs.uvic.ca/~ruskey/Publications/RankPerm/MyrvoldRuskey.pdf).
The bounded byte-output contract is `[n,r]`, `0<=n<=8`, with `r=0` for
`n=0` and `0<=r<n!` otherwise; output is the `n` labels as little-endian
signed-i64 values. The valid input frame is two words, maximum parseable
length is three words, maximum output is 64 bytes, and workspace is capped at
256 bytes. Ten language ports, primary and inverse-rank references, workload
fixtures, provenance/rights, and static inventory/checker are present under
[`myrvold_ruskey_permutation_unrank`](m/myrvold_ruskey_permutation_unrank/README.md).

## NIST DLMF Stieltjes quotient-difference conversion integrated (2026-11-18)

Added `stieltjes_quotient_difference_transform` from NIST DLMF
[§3.10(ii), Eqs. 3.10.8–3.10.10](https://dlmf.nist.gov/3.10#E8). It converts
power-series coefficients to the coefficients of an S-fraction by the
quotient-difference rhombus recurrence. This is distinct from the local
[`continued_fraction_convergents`](c/continued_fraction_convergents/README.md),
which consumes already-supplied continued-fraction coefficients to emit
approximants. Proposed exact profile uses `F_998244353`, input
`[N,c0,...,c_(N-1)]` with `2<=N<=9` and canonical nonzero residues, and output
`[N,a0,...,a_(N-1)]` as little-endian i64 words. It retains q cells
`q_1^k` for `0<=k<N-1`, then for each `j>=1` the triangular cells
`e_j^k` for `0<=k<=N-2j-1` and `q_(j+1)^k` for `0<=k<=N-2j-2`; output
coefficients are `a0=c0`, `a_(2j-1)=q_j^0`, and `a_(2j)=e_j^0` when the index
is below N. Any zero divisor pivot required by the q updates makes the full
input invalid before output-capacity handling. Maximum input is 10 valid / 11
parseable words; maximum output is 10 words / 80 bytes. The primary uses two
fixed 5x9 i64 rhombus tables (720 bytes total); the independent reference uses
Hankel-minor determinant ratios. Ten ports, workload, provenance/rights, static
inventory, and `i64_array_bytes_output` runner/verifier and catalog
registration are integrated under
[`stieltjes_quotient_difference_transform`](s/stieltjes_quotient_difference_transform/README.md).

## NIST DLMF continued-fraction forward-series recurrence integrated (2026-11-18)

`continued_fraction_forward_series_recurrence` follows NIST DLMF
[§3.10(iii), Eq. 3.10.15](https://dlmf.nist.gov/3.10#E15). It evaluates the
continued fraction with unit denominators through the forward series state

`[N,S1,...,SN]` for `S_m=sum(t_0,...,t_(m-1))`; a zero divisor in any rho
update is invalid before capacity handling. This finite-field profile preserves

is limited to unit denominators. Proposed bounded profile uses

before capacity handling. The profile accepts 18 valid / 19 parseable words,
