tree-construction problem but focuses on galled networks and does not provide a
canonical network serialization; this profile instead benchmarks the separately
specified BUILD tree procedure from Aho et al., “Inferring a Tree from Lowest
Common Ancestors with an Application to the Optimization of Relational
Expressions,” *SIAM Journal on Computing* 10(3), 1981, pp. 405–421,
[DOI 10.1137/0210030](https://doi.org/10.1137/0210030). The book context is
[DOI 10.1007/978-1-4939-2864-4_92](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4939-2864-4_92).
For each recursive leaf set, BUILD creates the undirected Aho graph with edge
`{a,b}` for every input constraint `ab|c` wholly inside that set; a connected
graph means incompatibility, otherwise BUILD recurses on each connected
component and joins the returned trees below a new root. The result is the
particular BUILD/Aho tree when compatible, not a claim of a globally
least-resolved tree. A deterministic serialization sorts child components by
minimum taxon label.

No exact rooted-triplet consistency or BUILD package/reservation was found.
Local `directed_perfect_phylogeny` handles binary-character laminar
compatibility, `phylogenetic_tree_from_distance_matrix` constructs trees from
pairwise distances, and `nni_phylogeny_distance` computes a distance between
trees; none decides or constructs a tree from rooted-triplet constraints.
Proposed `i64_array_bytes_output` frame is `[n,q,(a,b,c)*q]`, with `1<=n<=7`,
`0<=q<=3*C(n,3)`, zero-based labels, distinct labels per triple, and duplicate
oriented triplets rejected after treating the clustered pair as unordered.
The maximum valid and parseable inputs are 317 and 318 words. A compatible
output is `[node_count, preorder_tokens...]`, with leaf token `-(label+1)` and
internal token equal to its child count; incompatibility is `[0]`. At most 13
tree nodes fit for seven leaves, so output is at most 112 bytes. Ten language
ports, references, workload, rights/provenance, and static inventory are
integrated into the shared runner, independent verifier, README, and catalog.
The package source crosswalk records the method and chapter roles. No source
code, prose, examples, tests, or submissions are copied, and no programs,
tests, scripts, checkers, builds, compilers, profilers, or benchmarks are run.

## Butz Hilbert coordinate-to-index encoding integrated (2026-11-18)

`hilbert_curve_index_encode` implements the iterative 2D Hilbert coordinate
to distance mapping described by Butz, “Alternative Algorithm for Hilbert's
Space-Filling Curve,” *IEEE Transactions on Computers* 20(4), 1971, pp.
424–426, [DOI 10.1109/T-C.1971.223258](https://doi.org/10.1109/T-C.1971.223258).
This maps one bounded integer grid point to its scalar path index through
successive quadrant digits and orientation changes. The existing
[`hilbert_curve`](h/hilbert_curve/README.md) recursively materializes every
point of a curve with configurable starting rotation; it does not map one
coordinate to its index. Local [`morton_sort`](m/morton_sort/README.md) sorts
points by interleaved coordinate bits and uses a different Z-order mapping.
No Hilbert point-to-index package or reservation was found.

The byte-output profile accepts `[order,x,y]` for `1<=order<=8`
and `0<=x,y<2^order`, and emits one little-endian signed-i64 Hilbert index.
The canonical orientation starts at `(0,0)` and visits `(0,1),(1,1),(1,0)`
at order one. The primary iterates over coordinate bits with the Butz-style
quadrant/orientation transform; an independent recursive quadrant traversal
computes the same index. Maximum valid/parseable inputs are 3/4 words, output
is 8 bytes, and native scratch is zero. Ten ports, references, workload,
rights/provenance, static inventory, and `i64_array_bytes_output`
runner/verifier and catalog integration are present. No external code, prose,
examples, or tests are copied; no programs, tests, scripts, checkers, builds,
compilers, profilers, or benchmarks are run.

## Encyclopedia Chapter 423: CL complementary-pair bucket chooser integrated (2026-11-18)

Added `random_3sat_cl_bucket_heuristic` for the Chapter 423 CL profile.
The existing [`random_3sat_greedy_dpll`](r/random_3sat_greedy_dpll/README.md)
uses unit-first no-backtrack DPLL, while
[`random_3sat_hajiaghayi_sorkin_algorithm_a`](r/random_3sat_hajiaghayi_sorkin_algorithm_a/README.md)
selects a variable directly by the paper's degree-difference/sum rule. CL
instead buckets each unset literal by the capped degree of it and its
complement, simulates one deterministic-refinement round for each nonempty
bucket, and chooses the bucket maximizing the change ratio between the
two-to-one and three-to-two clause flows. Its bucket scoring and free-step
selection therefore add a distinct procedure rather than another encoding of
either local DPLL profile. The operational source is Kaporis, Kirousis, and
Lalas, “Selecting Complementary Pairs of Literals,” Algorithm CL and
Definitions 1–2, *Electronic Notes in Discrete Mathematics* 16 (2003),
47–70, [DOI 10.1016/S1571-0653(04)00462-7](https://doi.org/10.1016/S1571-0653(04)00462-7),
with the detailed flow definitions in “The Probabilistic Analysis of a Greedy
Satisfiability Algorithm,” §5. The bounded profile uses `h=10`, lowest
literal-ID deterministic selection within buckets/unit clauses, and explicitly
supplied formulas; it makes no random-process or threshold-guarantee claim.
Ten native ports, mutable and immutable references, boundary fixtures, rights
and provenance, static inventory, and `i64_array_bytes_output` runner/verifier
and catalog registration are integrated. No source code, prose, examples, or
tests are copied, and no programs, tests, scripts, helpers/checkers, builds,
compilers, profilers, or benchmarks are run.

## RFC 3492 Punycode scalar-sequence encoder integrated (2026-11-18)

Added `punycode_codepoint_sequence_encode` for RFC 3492's Punycode instance
of Bootstring, sections 3–6: preserve basic code points, encode the
non-basic-point insertion deltas as generalized variable-length integers, and
adapt the bias between insertions. Local catalog, coverage, and path searches
found no Punycode/Bootstring package or reservation. Base64/Base58Check encode
bytes in different radices, while URL percent encoding escapes UTF-8 bytes;
none implements this code-point algorithm. The proposed bounded profile takes
`[count,codepoint...]` for 0–32 Unicode scalar values, rejecting surrogates
and values above U+10FFFF, and emits only the RFC Punycode payload. It excludes
the IDNA `xn--` prefix, normalization, label splitting, and domain rules. A
320-byte output cap covers the bound: every non-basic point needs at most nine
generalized digits because its delta stays below 10^8 and every continuation
divides by at least 10. With 32 total points, all-non-basic input emits at
most 288 digits; mixed input emits at most `9k+(32-k)+1 = 33+8k <= 281`
bytes for `k<=31`, and all-basic input emits at most 33 bytes including its
required delimiter. The primary is an RFC encoder; the independent reference
uses Python's built-in Punycode codec and a structurally separate insertion
decoder. Ten ports, original fixtures, rights/provenance, static inventory,
and `i64_array_bytes_output` runner/verifier and catalog registration are
integrated. Discovery repository:
[`mathiasbynens/punycode.js`](https://github.com/mathiasbynens/punycode.js).
Normative source: [RFC 3492](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3492.html),
sections 3–6. No code, prose, examples, or tests are copied; no programs,
tests, scripts, checkers, builds, compilers, profilers, or benchmarks are run.

[§3.10(iii)](https://dlmf.nist.gov/3.10.iii), which names Lentz's and modified
Lentz's algorithms as alternatives to Steed's algorithm, with the explicit

Complex Arguments and Order,” *Journal of Computational Physics* 64 (1986),

pairs and rejects the same zero-divisor domain. Ten language ports, both
references, workload, rights/provenance, static inventory, and
`i64_array_bytes_output` runner/verifier and catalog registration are

and [Thompson–Barnett (1986), Appendix III](https://csclub.uwaterloo.ca/~pbarfuss/thompson1986.pdf).

## NIST DLMF Lanczos symmetric tridiagonalization integrated (2026-11-18)

Added `lanczos_symmetric_tridiagonalization` from NIST DLMF §3.2(vi),
[Eqs. 3.2.21–3.2.22](https://dlmf.nist.gov/3.2.vi). Local `qr_eigen_values`,
`mccat_05_eks`, and `power_iteration` compute eigenvalues, eigensolutions, or
spectral estimates; no local profile returns the Lanczos three-term recurrence
coefficients for a supplied symmetric matrix and start vector. The bounded
profile fixes the normalized start vector to `e_1`, accepts a symmetric
integer-valued matrix of order `1..4` with entries in `[-4,4]`, and requests
`1<=k<=n` recurrence vectors. It returns only the length-`k` coefficient trace
`[k,alpha_1..alpha_k,beta_2..beta_k]`; a zero/nonfinite required beta before
the requested length is a numerical breakdown. The primary follows DLMF's
three-term recurrence; the independent reference builds the Krylov basis from
matrix powers with two-pass modified Gram–Schmidt and forms its projected
matrix. The float64 frame `[n,k,A_row_major]` has exact length `2+n^2`, maximum
valid/parseable lengths 18/19, and output/workspace capacity 8 elements. Ten
ports, references, fixtures, rights/provenance, and static inventory are
integrated with `float64_slice_io` runner/verifier and catalog registration.
Both references and all ports use the `2^-40` breakdown guard. The accepted
integer-matrix domain has a proven lower bound of `1/256` for every exact
nonzero beta, so a threshold-boundary fixture cannot occur; the diagonal
fixture covers exact breakdown. No code, examples, or prose are copied; no
programs, tests, scripts, helpers/checkers, builds, compilers, profilers, or
benchmarks were run.

## RosettaGit Farey sequence ordered enumeration integrated (2026-11-18)

Added `farey_sequence_ordered_enumeration` from the RosettaGit [Farey
sequence task](https://rosettagit.org/tasks/farey-sequence/), identified in the
pinned RosettaCodeData popular-title index at commit
`1d475861d7141ef2fafff293d9339f56e4b0f5db`. The local
[`farey_approximation`](f/farey_approximation/README.md) performs a fixed number
of mediant refinements toward one decimal target; [`stern_brocot_tree`](s/stern_brocot_tree/README.md)
provides path and navigation queries. Neither generates the complete ordered
set of reduced fractions with denominator at most `N`. The profile accepts
`[N]`, `1<=N<=32`, and emits `[count,p_0,q_0,...,p_(count-1),q_(count-1)]`
for `0/1` through `1/1` in increasing rational order. Its primary successor
state emits the initial left endpoint `0/1`, starts at the adjacent pair
`(0/1,1/N)`, and advances by `k=floor((N+b)/d)`,
`(p',q')=(k*c-a,k*d-b)`; each resulting right term is emitted once, through
the terminal `1/1`. The independent reference
enumerates `0<=p<=q<=N` with `gcd(p,q)=1` and sorts by exact cross-products.
Maximum valid/parseable input lengths are 1/2 words. Farey sequences are
nested by order and OEIS [A005728](https://oeis.org/A005728) gives
`|F_32|=325`, so output is at most 651 signed-i64 words (5,208 bytes).
Ten ports, two references, workload, rights/provenance, and static inventory
are integrated with `i64_array_bytes_output` runner/verifier and catalog
registration. The two large valid payloads use oracle-derived fixture markers
with pinned byte lengths; the verifier constructs expected bytes from the
independent gcd-and-sort reference. Mathematical definition and successor
properties are cross-checked with [MathWorld's Farey Sequence entry](https://mathworld.wolfram.com/FareySequence.html)
and Pătrașcu and Pătrașcu's [ordered-generation discussion](https://people.csail.mit.edu/mip/papers/farey/farey.pdf).
RosettaGit and RosettaCodeData are discovery/specification context only; no
task code, wording, examples, tests, or output lists are copied. No programs,
tests, scripts, helpers/checkers, builds, compilers, profilers, or benchmarks
were run.

## Encyclopedia of Algorithms Chapter 225: randomized Tutte-matrix perfect matching integrated (2026-11-18)

Added `tutte_matrix_randomized_perfect_matching` from Marcin Mucha,
“Maximum Matching,” [Encyclopedia of Algorithms Chapter 225](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4939-2864-4_225), following Mucha and Sankowski,
“Maximum Matchings via Gaussian Elimination,” §3 Algorithm 2,
[DOI 10.1109/FOCS.2004.40](https://doi.org/10.1109/FOCS.2004.40). The local
[`edmonds_blossom_algorithm`](e/edmonds_blossom_algorithm/README.md) uses
deterministic odd-cycle contraction for unweighted maximum cardinality, while
[`general_weighted_matching`](g/general_weighted_matching/README.md) uses
subset DP for maximum total weight; neither performs the chapter's algebraic
perfect-matching construction. The bounded profile accepts an even simple
undirected graph with `2<=n<=8`, ordered normalized edges, and one supplied
nonzero finite-field substitution per edge in `F_65521`. It computes the
skew-symmetric Tutte matrix inverse, scans uneliminated vertices in ascending
order, chooses the lowest eligible endpoint with nonzero edge value and
inverse entry, then eliminates the corresponding row/column pair twice as in
Algorithm 2. The substitution is replayed input; singular matrices return a
negative instance/inconclusive profile result, and no random process or
probability guarantee is measured. Maximum valid/parseable input lengths are
86/87 i64 words; output is `[status,pair_count,pairs...]` in at most 80 bytes;
the 8,192-byte workspace bound includes fixed matrices and staged output. The
independent reference uses determinant/cofactor expansion and direct residual
recomputation rather than inverse updates. Ten ports, workload,
rights/provenance, static inventory, and `i64_array_bytes_output`
runner/verifier and catalog registration are integrated. No code, examples,
tests, or prose are copied; no programs, scripts, helpers/checkers, tests,
builds, compilers, profilers, or benchmarks were run.

## NIST DLMF modified Newton correction for known multiplicity integrated (2026-11-18)

Added `modified_newton_multiple_root` from the multiplicity correction described in NIST DLMF [§3.8(ii), following Eq. 3.8.4](https://dlmf.nist.gov/3.8#E4). The profile uses `f(x)=(x-1)^2(x+2)`, a known double root at 1, and updates `x <- x - 2*f(x)/f'(x)` for a bounded number of steps. Ordinary Newton's update and Halley's second-derivative update are different; the local Aitken Δ² package transforms supplied triples and does not generate this root iteration. ## Encyclopedia of Algorithms Chapter 24: efficient K-run construction audit (excluded)

Audited whether Chapter 24's efficient maximal-run method could be added as a distinct profile beside [`approximate_tandem_k_runs`](a/approximate_tandem_k_runs/README.md), which directly enumerates every factor satisfying the K-run window definition. The chapter and accessible Kolpakov–Kucherov paper provide a three-stage outline and explored-interval bounds, but defer full pseudocode to INRIA RR-4163. The available description does not specify how Algorithm 1 results become subrun intervals, the modified second-stage list updates/merges, or the third-stage boundary split/copy/relink transitions. ## Rosetta Code audit: Rice coding excluded as a duplicate (2026-11-19)

Rice coding with parameter `k` is Golomb coding with divisor `b=2^k`: both emit the same unary quotient and fixed-width `k`-bit remainder when the divisor is a power of two. The local [`integer_sequence_codes`](i/integer_sequence_codes/README.md) benchmark already includes Golomb mode 4, so no separate Rice-coding benchmark was added.

## NIST DADS Shannon–Fano–Elias coding integrated (2026-11-19)

Added `shannon_fano_elias_symbol_codes` after package/path/README/coverage searches found no Shannon–Fano–Elias or Gilbert–Moore midpoint-code profile. The existing [`shannon_fano`](s/shannon_fano/README.md) recursively balances frequency-sorted contiguous partitions; [`shannon_fano_compressor`](s/shannon_fano_compressor/README.md) uses a separately pinned greedy splitter; Huffman profiles build merge trees; [`arithmetic_coding`](a/arithmetic_coding/README.md) encodes a whole message through nested intervals. This package assigns each ordered symbol an independent codeword from the first `L_i = ceil(log2(W/w_i))+1` bits of its cumulative-probability interval midpoint, a distinct construction.

The `i64_array_bytes_output` profile accepts `[n,w_0,...,w_(n-1)]`, with `1<=n<=8`, positive weights `1..15`, and total weight `W<=120`; valid/parseable frames are 9/10 words. For symbol `i`, set `P_i=sum(w_j for j<i)`, `L_i` to the smallest positive integer satisfying `2^(L_i-1)*w_i>=W`, and `C_i=floor((2*P_i+w_i)*2^(L_i-1)/W)`. Emit `n` followed by `(L_i, C_i << (8-L_i))` byte pairs, with code bits MSB-first and zero padding at the low end; maximum output is 17 bytes. Malformed input returns `-1`; output-null or capacity-short returns `-2` after full input validation. Workspace is 1,024 bytes. The primary uses the exact integer midpoint formula; the independent reference generates each binary fractional bit by repeated rational doubling. All ten language ports, workload, rights/provenance, static inventory, and byte-output runner/verifier/catalog registration are integrated. Discovery: NIST's [Shannon–Fano coding entry](https://xlinux.nist.gov/dads/HTML/shannonFano.html); operational primary: Gilbert and Moore, “Variable-Length Binary Encodings,” *Bell System Technical Journal* 38(4), 1959, [DOI 10.1002/j.1538-7305.1959.tb01583.x](https://doi.org/10.1002/j.1538-7305.1959.tb01583.x). Algorithm descriptions only; no code or source text reused. No programs, tests, helpers/checkers, builds, compilers, profilers, or benchmarks were run.

implicit unweighted graph over array positions. Adjacent positions are linked,
and positions with equal values form implicit cliques. The primary groups
indices by bounded value and clears each group after its first BFS expansion,
so every vertex and group member is scanned only O(1) times. The independent
oracle checks all possible destinations pairwise. This is distinct from
[`jump_game`](j/jump_game/README.md), which tracks reachability bounds, and
[`jump_game_ii`](j/jump_game_ii/README.md), which uses supplied jump lengths.
The bounded profile uses arrays of length at most 64 and values in `[-64,64]`.
Ten language ports, two references, workload, rights/provenance, static
inventory, and scalar runner/verifier/catalog registration are integrated.
LeetCode supplied discovery and transition semantics only; shortest-path
semantics follow the generic [CP-Algorithms BFS description](https://cp-algorithms.com/graph/breadth-first-search.html).
No problem text, source code, examples, tests, or submissions were copied. No
programs, tests, scripts, helpers, checkers, builds, compilers, profilers, or
benchmarks were run.

Added [`weiler_atherton_polygon_intersection`](w/weiler_atherton_polygon_intersection/README.md)

## Encyclopedia of Algorithms Chapter 410: succinct BP pioneer matching integrated

Added [`succinct_bp_pioneer_match_index`](s/succinct_bp_pioneer_match_index/README.md)
for recursive pioneer-family matching on balanced-parenthesis strings. Local
`rank_select_bitstring` implements bit-vector rank/select, while
`bp_ordered_tree_navigation` uses direct bounded scans; neither builds this
index. The profile fixes block size 8 and a direct base table at 16 symbols.
Transient stack matches and destination blocks are discarded after index
construction. Far queries recurse through the nearest directional pioneer and
use ordered source/target/depth groups to select the opposite parenthesis; no
far mate is retained. The independent reference directly uses a stack. This
finite profile makes no succinct-space or constant-time claim. Ten language
ports, bounded fixtures, rights/provenance, static inventory, and
`i64_array_bytes_output` runner/verifier/catalog registration are integrated.
Sources: He, *Encyclopedia of Algorithms*, [Chapter 410](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4939-2864-4_410),
and Geary, Rahman, Raman, and Raman, [“A Simple Optimal Representation for
Balanced Parentheses,” §§2.1–2.3](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.tcs.2006.09.014).
No source code, prose, examples, or tests were copied. No programs, tests,
helpers/checkers, builds, compilers, profilers, or benchmarks were run.

## Standard quotient-filter operation trace integrated (2026-11-19)

Added `quotient_filter_operation_trace` for the standard quotient filter
(SQF), specifically the three-bit `is_occupied` / `is_continuation` /
`is_shifted` representation. This is distinct from the repository's Bloom,
cuckoo, XOR, and invertible Bloom filters: SQF stores ordered remainder runs
in a circular slot array and maintains them by local shifting. The bounded
profile supplies 8-bit fingerprints directly, uses three quotient bits and
five remainder bits, caps occupancy at six of eight slots, and replays insert,
lookup, and one-copy delete operations. It follows Bender et al.'s multiset
semantics (equal fingerprints occupy adjacent copies); insertion at the cap
returns a non-mutating full status. A successful operation emits one status
byte; slot-state bytes are not part of the output. Malformed input and
insufficient output capacity use the byte-suite error statuses. The workload
pins duplicate placement/removal, wraparound traversal, and local
continuation/shifted metadata updates. The independent reference is an abstract
fingerprint multiset, separate from the physical slot representation.

Primary source: Bender et al., [“Don't Thrash: How to Cache Your Hash on
Flash”](https://doi.org/10.14778/2350229.2350275), §3 and Figure 3. The
standard-QF invariants and serial insert/delete traversal are cross-checked
against Geil, Farach-Colton, and Owens, [“Quotient Filters: Approximate
Membership Queries on the GPU”](https://doi.org/10.1109/IPDPS.2018.00055),
§III-A and Algorithms 1 and 3. Bloom, cuckoo, XOR, and IBLT profiles remain
separate algorithm families. NIST DADS's Bloom-filter entry was only adjacent
discovery context; the QF procedure itself is sourced from the cited papers.
Ten native ports, primary and independent references, bounded fixtures,
rights/provenance, static inventory, and `i64_array_bytes_output`
runner/verifier/catalog registration are integrated. No programs, tests,
scripts, helpers/checkers, builds, compilers, profilers, or benchmarks were
run.

## Source-backed reservation and integration status (2026-11-19)

- **Counting Bloom filter operation trace** — `counting_bloom_filter_operation_trace`
  is implemented and integrated. The accepted scope is a
  bounded counter-based Bloom filter with increment/decrement updates and
  Bloom membership queries (`all k counters are nonzero`), compared against
  an abstract multiset reference. Deletes are valid-operation preconditions;
  no exact-membership guard is added. This is distinct from the local bit
  Bloom filter, quotient filter, cuckoo filter, XOR filter, and IBLT. Source:
  Fan et al., “Summary Cache: A Scalable Wide-Area Web Cache Sharing
  Protocol,” §4.3, [DOI 10.1145/285243.285287](https://doi.org/10.1145/285243.285287).
  Ten ports, a bounded workload, two references, rights/provenance, static
  inventory, and `i64_array_bytes_output` runner/verifier/catalog registration
  are present. No code, prose, examples, or fixtures were copied.
- **Routh–Hurwitz stability predicate** — `routh_hurwitz_stability_predicate`
  is now implemented and integrated. For degree at most four and integer
  coefficients in `[-3,3]`, an exact rational Routh table returns whether all
  roots have strictly negative real part; an independent reference checks
  leading principal Hurwitz minors. Zero pivots and zero rows fail the strict
  predicate; no epsilon substitution or non-strict claim is made. Ten ports,
  18 fixtures, rights/provenance, static inventory, and scalar
  runner/verifier/catalog registration are present. The candidate was found
  through the RosettaCodeData popular-title index, whose task text and code
  were not reused. Sources: Routh's [1877 treatise](https://archive.org/details/treatiseonstabil00routuoft),
  Hurwitz's [1895 paper](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01446812), and the
  [Encyclopedia of Mathematics criterion entry](https://encyclopediaofmath.org/wiki/Routh-Hurwitz_criterion).
  No programs, tests, helpers, checkers, builds, compilers, profilers, or
  benchmarks were run.
- **Jury discrete-time stability predicate** — `jury_discrete_time_stability_predicate`
  is implemented and integrated. The bounded profile tests
  whether all polynomial roots lie strictly inside the unit circle using the
  1961 Jury–Blanchard table form, with a structurally different Schur–Cohn
  determinant reference. This differs from the integrated Routh–Hurwitz
  left-half-plane test. Ten ports, bounded fixtures, exact arithmetic limits,
  rights/provenance, static inventory, and `i64_array_scalar`
  runner/verifier/catalog registration are present. Sources: Jury and Blanchard,
  “A Stability Test for Linear Discrete Systems in Table Form,” *Proceedings
  of the IRE* 49 (1961), 1947–1948
  ([original issue scan](https://www.worldradiohistory.com/Archive-IRE/60s/IRE-Proceedings-1961-12-R.pdf));
  Jury, “A Simplified Stability Criterion for Linear Discrete Systems,” 1962,
  [DOI 10.1109/JRPROC.1962.288193](https://doi.org/10.1109/JRPROC.1962.288193).
  The task index was discovery-only; task text and code were not reused. No
  programs, tests, helpers, checkers, builds, compilers, profilers, or
  benchmarks were run.
- **RNA pair-activity partition function** — `rna_pair_activity_partition_function`
  is implemented and integrated as an exact bounded sum-product DP
  over noncrossing pair sets with supplied integer pair activities. This is
  distinct from the local Nussinov maximum-pair-count and RNA MFE
  minimum-energy objectives. It uses the context-independent pair-energy
  specialization of the McCaskill partition function; it does not claim full
  nearest-neighbor thermodynamics or base-pair probabilities. Source:
  Encyclopedia of Algorithms Chapter 345 and McCaskill, “The Equilibrium
  Partition Function and Base Pair Binding Probabilities for RNA Secondary
  Structure,” [DOI 10.1002/bip.360290621](https://doi.org/10.1002/bip.360290621).
  The contract bounds `n<=16`, pair activity `0..3`, input to 121 valid and
  122 parseable words, and workspace to 2,048 bytes. Ten ports, two interval
  references, workload, rights/provenance, static inventory, and
  `i64_array_scalar` runner/verifier/catalog registration are integrated.

Counting Bloom, Routh–Hurwitz, Jury stability, and RNA pair-activity

## RosettaCodeData Kirkpatrick–Seidel hull implementation (2026-11-20)

Implemented `kirkpatrick_seidel_convex_hull` as a distinct planar hull kernel.
The primary uses Kirkpatrick–Seidel marriage-before-conquest: recursively
find upper and lower bridges across median-x separators, prune points strictly
interior to each bridge, and recurse on the remaining sides. This is distinct
from local Chan wrapping (group hulls plus tangent searches and retries) and
divide-and-conquer tangent merging (construct child hulls, then merge them).
The bounded `i64_array_bytes_output` contract accepts
`[n,x0,y0,...]`, `3<=n<=32`, unique x-coordinates, coordinates in
`[-1000,1000]`, and at least one non-collinear triple; collinear boundary
points are permitted. It emits strict convex-hull vertices in CCW order from
the lexicographically least point as little-endian `i64` coordinate pairs.
Malformed input returns `-1`; valid output with null/short capacity returns
`-2`. Median selection is deterministic linear-time selection; bridge slopes,
support values, orientation, and canonicalization use exact cross-products.
Tie rules pin candidate order to input order, pair consecutive candidates,
orient each pair by x, use lower medians, select the extreme-x support
contacts, and treat a separator crossing as `x(left)<=a<x(right)`. The
independent oracle enumerates support edges in `O(n^3)` and collapses collinear
contacts to extreme endpoints. Ten native-language ports, bounded fixtures,
primary/reference implementations, rights/provenance, static inventory, and
byte-output runner/verifier registration are present. No programs, tests,
scripts, checkers, builds, compilers, profilers, or benchmarks were run. Sources:
Kirkpatrick and Seidel, “The Ultimate Planar Convex Hull Algorithm?”, SIAM J.
Comput. 15(1), 1986, [DOI 10.1137/0215021](https://doi.org/10.1137/0215021);
the RosettaCodeData “Kirkpatrick-Seidel algorithm” title is discovery only.
No upstream code, prose, examples, tests, or fixtures will be reused.

## OI Wiki degree-ordered four-cycle counter implementation (2026-11-20)

Implemented `undirected_four_cycle_count_degree_order` after comparing the
[OI Wiki ring-counting article](https://oi-wiki.org/graph/rings-count/)
against local graph-counting packages. Local [`counting_c4`](c/counting_c4/README.md)
counts four-edge-ID cycles per input edge in an undirected multigraph using
length-three paths through an edge-multiplicity matrix; this package instead
returns one aggregate count of simple-graph four-cycle edge sets using
degree-rank orientation and `O(m sqrt(m))` work. Existing triangle and
five-cycle profiles count different fixed lengths. This bounded
`i64_array_scalar` profile accepts a canonical simple undirected edge list with
`1<=n<=16` and `0<=m<=64`; it returns the exact number of distinct four-cycle
edge sets.
The primary orders vertices by the strict key `(degree,vertex_id)`, then for
each pivot `a` counts pairs of lower-ranked common neighbors for every
lower-ranked opposite vertex `c`. The unique maximum-ranked vertex is the
pivot, `c` is its unique opposite vertex, and the remaining two vertices are
counted as an unordered pair, so each four-cycle contributes once; `K4`
contributes three. The independent reference enumerates canonical cycles
directly. Ten language ports, bounded workload, README/RIGHTS/INVENTORY, a
static checker, and `i64_array_scalar` runner/verifier registration are
present. Only the article's algorithm description is used; no code, prose,
fixtures, examples, or tests were reused. No programs, tests, scripts,
checkers, builds, compilers, profilers, or benchmarks were run.

## OI Wiki tree-center rerooting-DP implementation (2026-11-20)

Implemented `tree_center_rerooting_dp` after the current
[OI Wiki tree-center article](https://oi-wiki.org/graph/tree-center/)
showed a method distinct from local [`tree_center`](t/tree_center/README.md),
which peels leaf layers. The bounded `i64_array_bytes_output` input is
`[n,(u,v)*(n-1)]` for a simple unweighted tree with `1<=n<=64`. The result is
the same one or two center vertex IDs, sorted ascending; invalid input returns
`-1`, and null or short output returns `-2` without writes. The primary uses a
rooted postorder to retain each node's two best downward heights, followed by
a preorder that propagates the best height outside each subtree; the
eccentricity is the maximum of the downward and outside heights. The
independent reference computes every vertex's eccentricity with BFS. Ten
language ports, bounded workload, README/RIGHTS/INVENTORY, a static checker,
and byte-output suite registration are present. Only the OI Wiki method
description is used; no source code, prose, examples, or fixtures were reused.
No programs, tests, scripts, checkers, builds, compilers, profilers, or
benchmarks were run.

## OI Wiki undirected simple-cycle subset-DP implementation (2026-11-20)

Implemented `undirected_simple_cycle_subset_dp_count` after the OI Wiki ordinary
ring-counting section was compared against the local inventory. Local
[`gbbs_five_cycle_count`](g/gbbs_five_cycle_count/README.md) counts only
length-five cycles; [`directed_simple_cycles`](d/directed_simple_cycles/README.md)
enumerates directed cycles and returns a cycle list; and minimum-cycle,
cycle-basis, and Hamiltonian profiles optimize weights, construct a basis, or
test existence rather than count every undirected simple cycle. This profile
counts all simple cycles of length at least three once up to rotation and
reversal.

The bounded `i64_array_scalar` contract is `[n,m,(u,v)*m]` for a simple
undirected graph, with `1<=n<=14`, `0<=m<=min(91,n(n-1)/2)`, zero-based IDs,
`u<v`, and strictly lexicographically increasing edge pairs. A valid frame is
at most 184 words; 185 words are parseable to reject one trailing value.
Malformed or null input returns `-1`; valid input returns the exact scalar
count, which fits signed 64-bit output.

The primary assigns each cycle to its least-numbered vertex `s` and performs
subset DP over paths beginning at `s`, using only vertices greater than `s`.
For every state with at least three vertices, an edge from its endpoint back to
`s` contributes one oriented cycle; summing both directions and dividing by
two counts each undirected cycle once. The independent reference canonically
enumerates cycles by fixing the least vertex, requiring the second vertex to
be smaller than the last, and directly checking cycle edges. Source:
the [OI Wiki ring-counting article](https://oi-wiki.org/graph/rings-count/),
ordinary-cycle subset-DP section. Ten language ports, bounded workload,
README/RIGHTS/INVENTORY, a package-local static checker, and `i64_array_scalar`
runner/verifier registration are integrated. The fixed table bound is 2 MiB.
Only the article's algorithm description is used; no code, prose, examples,
fixtures, or tests are reused. No programs, tests, scripts, checkers, builds,
compilers, profilers, or benchmarks were run.

## LeetCode official-title audit: graph, geometry, advanced DP (2026-11-20)

The official [Graph Theory Study Plan](https://leetcode.com/studyplan/graph-theory/),
[Dynamic Programming Study Plan](https://leetcode.com/studyplan/dynamic-programming/),
and current [problemset index](https://leetcode.com/problemset/) were used as
title/topic discovery indexes. LeetCode material is not used as implementation
text: no problem prose, examples, test cases, submissions, editorials, or site
code are copied. The following exact local-method comparisons led to three
separate reservations:

- **Package complete under reserved name `minimum_area_rectangle_arbitrary_orientation` (LeetCode 963,
  Minimum Area Rectangle II).** The local
  [`minimum_area_enclosing_rectangle`](m/minimum_area_enclosing_rectangle/README.md)
  finds a smallest rectangle containing a convex polygon by supporting-line
  calipers; [`rectangle_union_area`](r/rectangle_union_area/README.md) and
  [`rectangle_union_area_sweep`](g/rectangle_union_area_sweep/README.md)
  measure unions of axis-aligned rectangles. Neither selects four points from
  an arbitrary point set to minimize the area of an arbitrary-orientation
  rectangle. The bounded `i64_array_scalar` contract is `[n,(x,y)*n]`,
  `4<=n<=16`, unique integer points with coordinates in `[-32,32]`, and exact
  length `1+2*n`; return twice the minimum rectangle area as an integer,
  `0` if no rectangle exists, or `-1` for malformed input. The primary forms
  all unordered point pairs and compares disjoint pair pairs, requiring equal
  doubled midpoints and squared diagonal lengths; doubled area is the absolute
  cross product of the diagonal vectors. It takes `O(n^4)` time and `O(n)`
  space for bounded point storage.
  The independent oracle enumerates every 4-point subset and every cyclic
  ordering, checking equal diagonal midpoints and perpendicular adjacent
  sides directly. Sources: [official title/specification page](https://leetcode.com/problems/minimum-area-rectangle-ii/)
  and the [Hong Kong Olympiad in Informatics computational-geometry notes](https://assets.hkoi.org/training2023/geom.pdf)
  for the equal-midpoint/equal-length diagonal characterization.
- **Package complete under reserved name `secret_sharing_time_batched_dsu` (LeetCode 2092, Find All People
  With Secret).** Static inventory search found DSU, offline dynamic
  connectivity, and graph traversal packages, but no method that applies
  instantaneous transitive sharing within each timestamp and discards
  timestamp-local connectivity that is not connected to the already-informed
  set. The `i64_array_scalar` contract is `[n,first_person,m,(u,v,time)*m]`,
  `2<=n<=16`, `1<=first_person<n`, `0<=m<=20`, distinct endpoints in
  `[0,n)`, timestamps in `[1,20]`, and exact length `3+3*m`; duplicate
  meetings are allowed. Return the bitmask of all informed people after
  processing timestamps in increasing order, or `-1` for malformed input.
  The primary scans the bounded timestamp range, unions every meeting in one
  batch, preserves components reaching person 0, and resets the batch's other
  participants. It takes `O(T(m+n) + m alpha(n))` time for `T<=20` and
  `O(n+m)` space.
  The independent reference constructs each timestamp's meeting graph and
  BFSes from the informed set at that time, without DSU state. Sources:
  [official title/specification and method hints](https://leetcode.com/problems/find-all-people-with-secret/)
  and [CP-Algorithms DSU reference](https://cp-algorithms.com/data_structures/disjoint_set_union.html).
- **Package complete under reserved name `redundant_directed_connection_repair` (LeetCode 685,
  Redundant Connection II).** Local [`redundant_connection`](r/redundant_connection/README.md)
  processes undirected edges with DSU and does not diagnose a two-parent
  conflict in a directed rooted tree. The bounded `i64_array_scalar` contract
  is `[n,(u,v)*n]`, `3<=n<=16`, labels in `[0,n)`, exact length `1+2*n`,
  and a valid directed rooted tree plus one additional previously absent
  directed edge. Return the zero-based index of the last input edge whose
  removal leaves one rooted arborescence, or `-1` for malformed input. The
  primary records any child with two incoming edges, tentatively skips the
  later incoming edge, and uses DSU cycle detection to resolve the one-parent,
  two-parent-without-cycle, and two-parent-with-cycle cases. DSU repair takes
  `O(n alpha(n))`; total time is `O(n^2)` because duplicate directed pairs are
  rejected during input validation, with `O(n)` space. The independent oracle tries edges
  from last to first and validates indegrees, unique-root reachability, and
  edge count after each deletion. Sources: [official title/specification page](https://leetcode.com/problems/redundant-connection-ii/),
  [GeeksforGeeks method explanation](https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/dsa/extra-edge-in-a-directed-rooted-tree/),
  and [CP-Algorithms DSU reference](https://cp-algorithms.com/data_structures/disjoint_set_union.html).

Other high-signal title-index outcomes in the same review:

- **Implemented:** [Find Critical and Pseudo-Critical Edges in MST, LC 1489](https://leetcode.com/problems/find-critical-and-pseudo-critical-edges-in-minimum-spanning-tree/)

## Algorithm Archive remaining partial/open chapter-body audit (2026-11-20)

Rechecked the Archive pages still labeled incomplete, work in progress, or
open-ended against package contracts rather than relying on chapter titles.
The [Taylor-series page](https://www.algorithm-archive.org/contents/taylor_series_expansion/taylor_series_expansion.html)
remains explicitly incomplete. Its generic expansion and constant-acceleration
example do not prescribe a function family, derivative input format, finite
term rule, stopping criterion, or numerical domain. Local
[`maclaurin_series`](m/maclaurin_series/README.md), [`maclaurin`](m/maclaurin/README.md),
[`exponential_function`](e/exponential_function/README.md), and
[`trig_functions`](t/trig_functions/README.md) cover concrete Taylor/Maclaurin
approximations under distinct contracts. A general finite expansion with
derivative values supplied as coefficients is polynomial evaluation after
coefficient scaling; an input-function evaluator would need more specification.
Disposition: specialized profiles are implemented; the general chapter is
excluded as underspecified, with no confirmed missing kernel.

The [Computer Graphics overview](https://www.algorithm-archive.org/contents/computer_graphics/computer_graphics.html)
is marked as a work in progress and names Canny edge detection as a future
topic without defining its pipeline. The repository already has
[`sobel_filter`](s/sobel_filter/README.md) for normalized Sobel-gradient output
and [`canny`](c/canny/README.md) for Gaussian smoothing, Sobel derivatives,
gradient normalization, directional non-maximum suppression, thresholding,
and hysteresis. Canny therefore classifies as implemented, distinct from the
Sobel-only result; the bounded profile follows its pinned source and is
cross-checked against Canny's original method paper
([DOI 10.1109/TPAMI.1986.4767851](https://doi.org/10.1109/TPAMI.1986.4767851)).
No additional graphics kernel is specified by the open overview. The plotting
chapter is a data-export/visualization guide, and the quantum-information page
is a survey that explicitly declines code contributions; both remain excluded
as nonportable workflow/background material.

The [Cryptography overview](https://www.algorithm-archive.org/contents/cryptography/cryptography.html)
marks symmetric and asymmetric sections as works in progress. Its named
families map to local contracts: Caesar, fixed-shift ROT13, permutation, and
repeating-key XOR; DES; AES/Rijndael; Blowfish; RSA key generation and
supplied-key transforms; and elliptic-curve Diffie–Hellman. ROT13 is a fixed
shift specialization of Caesar, while block modes and key-generation versus
transform operations remain separate profiles where their workloads differ.
Beyond those family names, the page supplies no specific block mode, round
schedule, signature, or operational ECC key-exchange procedure. Disposition:
named families are implemented, the ROT13 lead is a
duplicate specialization, and the unfinished overview is excluded from new
package requests. The Archive homepage states code examples use MIT terms and
text uses CC BY-SA 4.0 with attribution; the crosswalk uses descriptions only.

The broad Data Structures chapter and Complexity Notation chapter do not name
one additional bounded kernel; concrete stack, queue, tree, and traversal
profiles are crosswalked separately. No genuinely missing candidate emerged
from this partial/open-page pass, so nothing was reserved. This is a static
article and contract comparison only; no programs, scripts, tests, checkers,
builds, compilers, profilers, or benchmarks were run.

## RosettaCodeData lower-rank popular-title crosswalk and reservation (2026-11-20)

This focused static pass crosswalks selected algorithm-bearing titles from the
pinned [RosettaCodeData popular-task index](https://github.com/acmeism/RosettaCodeData/blob/1d475861d7141ef2fafff293d9339f56e4b0f5db/popular-tasks)
against package names, README method descriptions, and earlier ledger entries.
The index supplies discovery titles and scores only. The Rosetta Code
[copyright note](https://rosettacode.org/wiki/Rosetta_Code:Copyrights) describes
submitted task content as GFDL 1.2 (with possible more permissive contributor
licenses); this pass does not use task prose, submissions, code, tests, or
examples. Local package guides and the independent mathematical source below
provide method context.

| Index score and title | Disposition after local method comparison |
|---|---|
| 157, Mandelbrot set | Covered by [`mandelbrot`](m/mandelbrot/README.md), which iterates the complex quadratic recurrence and tests escape. |
| 157, Count occurrences of a substring | Covered by [`count_substrings`](c/count_substrings/README.md), including overlapping occurrence positions. |
| 154, Binary search | Covered by [`binary_search`](b/binary_search/README.md); recursive and ordering-specific search packages are also present. |
| 151, Pascal's triangle | Covered by [`pascal_triangle`](p/pascal_triangle/README.md) and [`pascal_triangle_row`](p/pascal_triangle_row/README.md). |
| 147, Knuth shuffle | Same Fisher–Yates descending-swap kernel as [`fisher_yates_shuffle`](f/fisher_yates_shuffle/README.md); no second package. |
| 146, Catalan numbers | Covered by [`catalan_number`](c/catalan_number/README.md); alternate recurrence and combinatorial profiles do not add another Catalan algorithm. |
| 142, N-queens problem | Covered by [`queens`](q/queens/README.md), [`n_queens_solution_count`](n/n_queens_solution_count/README.md), and the separately named solver profile. |
| 141, Conway's Game of Life | Covered by [`game_of_life`](g/game_of_life/README.md), a finite-grid cellular automaton update. |
| 140, Averages: median | Covered by [`calculate_median`](c/calculate_median/README.md) and the order-statistic/streaming median variants. |
| 139, Look-and-say sequence | The per-term transformation is covered by [`conway`](c/conway/README.md); repeatedly applying that transition does not justify another algorithm package. |
| 138, Horner's rule for polynomial evaluation | Covered by [`polynomial_evaluation`](p/polynomial_evaluation/README.md), whose primary routine is Horner's recurrence. |
| 137, Haversine formula | Covered by [`haversine_distance`](h/haversine_distance/README.md). |
| 120, Josephus problem | Covered by [`josephus_problem`](j/josephus_problem/README.md), with recursive and simulation profiles alongside it. |
| 103, Hamming numbers | Covered by [`hamming_numbers`](h/hamming_numbers/README.md), generating the smooth-number sequence. |
| 97, Euler method | Covered by [`euler_method`](e/euler_method/README.md), the first-order explicit ODE stepper. |
| 92, Damm algorithm | Covered by [`damm`](d/damm/README.md), the quasigroup-based decimal check-digit procedure. |
| 91, Pythagorean triples | Covered by [`pythagorean_triple`](p/pythagorean_triple/README.md), with separate bounded triple-generation profiles. |
| 90, Bell numbers | Covered by [`bell_numbers`](b/bell_numbers/README.md). |
| 88, Van der Corput sequence | Covered by [`van_der_corput_sequence`](v/van_der_corput_sequence/README.md), using radical-inverse digit reversal. |
| 86, Stern–Brocot sequence | Covered by [`stern_brocot_tree`](s/stern_brocot_tree/README.md); adjacent Stern-diatomic values are also exposed by `calkin_wilf_index`. |
| 81, Egyptian division | Method duplicate of [`divide_two_integers`](d/divide_two_integers/README.md): both form power-of-two divisor multiples and subtract them to build the quotient. |

One genuinely distinct title was implemented as a bounded combinatorial count:
`random_permutation_cycle_cap_count` (RosettaCodeData score 95, “100
prisoners”). Its `i64_array_scalar` contract is `[n,k]`, with
`1<=n<=20` and `1<=k<=n`; return the number of permutations of `n` labels
whose every cycle has length at most `k`. This is the success count for the
cycle-following locker strategy with a per-prisoner limit of `k` openings; its
success probability is that count divided by `n!`. The primary recurrence
decomposes by the cycle containing a fixed label:
`C(0,k)=1` and
`C(n,k)=sum(j=1..min(n,k), (n-1)!/(n-j)! * C(n-j,k))`.
The maximum result is `20!`, which fits signed 64-bit output. Local
[`permutations`](p/permutations/README.md) enumerates permutations,
[`permutation_count`](p/permutation_count/README.md) counts unrestricted
partial permutations, [`functional_graph_cycle_parameters`](f/functional_graph_cycle_parameters/README.md)
examines one supplied successor map, and [`problem95`](p/problem95/README.md)
analyzes aliquot-sequence orbits; none counts permutations under a maximum
cycle-length cap. Method context is Curtin and Warshauer, “The Locker Puzzle,”
*The Mathematical Intelligencer* 28(1), 2006, [DOI 10.1007/BF02986999](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02986999),
and their [article PDF](https://www.cl.cam.ac.uk/~gw104/Locker_Puzzle.pdf).
RosettaCodeData remains title discovery only; no task text, code, examples,
tests, or fixtures are reused. Ten native ports, two exact references, bounded
fixtures, rights notes, and `i64_array_scalar` runner/verifier registration
are present; see [`random_permutation_cycle_cap_count`](r/random_permutation_cycle_cap_count/README.md).
No programs, scripts, checkers, tests, builds, compilers, or benchmarks were run.

**Library Checker proposal follow-up (2026-11-20):** proposal [#1380, “O(V)-O(1) gcd”](https://github.com/yosupo06/library-checker-problems/issues/1380)
is implemented as [`batch_gcd_small_range_precomputed`](b/batch_gcd_small_range_precomputed/README.md).
The bounded-domain sieve and fixed-step pair-query behavior differs from local
per-pair Euclid, binary GCD, and list-fold GCD. Ten native ports, an independent
Euclidean reference, clean-room rights notes, fixtures, and byte-output suite
registration are present. Proposal [#1373, “Strongly Connected Components
(Dense)”](https://github.com/yosupo06/library-checker-problems/issues/1373)
is implemented as [`kosaraju_dense_bitset_scc`](k/kosaraju_dense_bitset_scc/README.md),
a packed-row neighbor-discovery workload. The local Kosaraju package also
stores rows as bitmasks but examines every possible neighbor index; this profile
selects neighbors through row/unvisited word intersections and is bounded to a
dense matrix contract. Ten ports, an independent adjacency-list Tarjan
reference, bounded fixtures, rights notes, and byte-output suite registration
are present. The package pins the issue's open encoding and scale details and
accounts for transpose construction in the full complexity. The proposal and
cited community implementations are idea indexes only; no source code or task
content is reused. Ports remain uncompiled and unexecuted.

**Algorithm Archive chapter-body follow-up (2026-11-20):** the [Approximate
Counting chapter](https://www.algorithm-archive.org/contents/approximate_counting/approximate_counting.html)
specifies Morris's tunable parameter `a`, including `a=1/2`. The local
[`morris_approximate_counter`](m/morris_approximate_counter/README.md) fixes
`a=1`, producing a dyadic transition threshold and estimate. The `a=1/2`
setting uses transition probability `3^-v` and estimate `(3^v-1)/2`; its
different per-state probabilities and estimator justify a separate workload
variant within the Morris family. Implemented as
[`morris_approximate_counter_base_three`](m/morris_approximate_counter_base_three/README.md)
with exact finite draw thresholds, `Q<=30`, and a byte-output contract. Ten
native ports, independent references, bounded draw tapes, rights notes, and
byte-output suite registration are present; ports remain uncompiled and
unexecuted. The Archive's top-level license notice gives code examples MIT
terms and text CC BY-SA 4.0 with attribution; this profile uses algorithm
descriptions only and includes no copied code, prose, examples, tests, or
fixtures.

**Codewars title-only follow-up (2026-11-20):** the expanded public title/tag
crosswalk found two distinct bounded scalar workloads. `factorial_last_nonzero_digit`
returns the last nonzero decimal digit of `n!`, unlike local factorial
evaluation, trailing-zero counting, and prime-factorial profiles. Its
logarithmic base-five recurrence is documented in
[`README.md`](f/factorial_last_nonzero_digit/README.md), with Dresden's paper
and OEIS A008904 as independent method references. `nmea_xor_checksum`
folds an NMEA sentence payload with bytewise XOR; it is distinct from
[`hash_xor8`](h/hash_xor8/README.md), which sums and two's-complement-finalizes
bytes, and from Internet, Fletcher, Adler, and CRC checksums. Its payload-only
ABI and 76-byte bound are documented in
[`README.md`](n/nmea_xor_checksum/README.md), using GPSD's NMEA protocol
description. Both have ten native ports, independent references, bounded
fixtures, rights notes, and scalar-suite registration. Codewars digit-counting
and binary-divisibility titles remain excluded from the new-work queue because
their visible titles/tags do not specify a unique bounded contract or method;
they may map to generic local operations. Catalog titles are discovery labels
only; no community task text, source code, tests, examples, or fixtures are

## OI Wiki current source-navigation follow-up and Eulerian-number reservation (2026-11-20)

Compared algorithm-bearing headings in the current OI Wiki
[`mkdocs.yml` navigation](https://github.com/OI-wiki/OI-wiki/blob/master/mkdocs.yml)
and its [algorithm page index](https://oi-wiki.org/pages/) against local
package contracts and active reservations. This is an index/title crosswalk,
not an article-by-article audit.

| OI Wiki heading family | Local comparison and disposition |
|---|---|
| Sorting, search, string matching, and common DP headings | Covered by the repository's named sort/search/string packages and task-specific dynamic-programming contracts, including suffix automata/arrays, prefix-function matching, knapsack, digit DP, plug DP, and tree DP. Broad design headings remain excluded unless they name one operation and return value. |
| Number theory, polynomial operations, sequences, and linear algebra | Sieve, summatory-function, factorial, recurrence, transform, interpolation, determinant, and integer-sequence profiles are already represented. The combinatorics heading **Eulerian Number** is implemented as [`eulerian_number`](e/eulerian_number/README.md): unlike [`entringer_number`](e/entringer_number/README.md), which counts alternating permutations by first element, or graph Eulerian path/circuit profiles, it computes the classical descent-count triangle. |
| Trees and data structures | B/B+ trees, WBLT, Sqrt Tree, block arrays/lists, nested Fenwick/segment trees, dynamic trees, PQ trees, finger trees, wavelet structures, and tournament structures map to local contracts or prior OI Wiki entries. The Persistent Block Array heading remains an empty/underspecified placeholder and is excluded. |
| Graph algorithms and combinatorial structures | Connectivity, shortest paths, arborescences, spanning trees, cycle counts, 2-SAT, flows, matching, Steiner trees, Prüfer coding, tree centers, and simple-cycle counting map to existing local profiles or prior OI Wiki reservations. Generic graph-concept headings do not define additional kernels. |
| Computational geometry and miscellaneous methods | Hulls, nearest pairs, clipping, triangulation, calipers, smallest enclosing circles, CDQ, parallel binary search, Mo variants, Josephus, Garsia–Wachs, Kahan summation, and hanging-line histograms are present or recorded in the prior crosswalk. Broad overviews, optimizations, and theory pages without one bounded operation are excluded. |

**Implemented — `eulerian_number`:** use `i64_array_scalar`
with input `[n,k]`, `0<=n<=20`, and `k=0` for `n=0` or `0<=k<n` otherwise.
Return `A(n,k)`, the number of permutations of `[n]` with exactly `k`
descents; malformed framing or an out-of-domain pair returns `-1`. The primary
row recurrence is `A(0,0)=1` and
`A(n,k)=(k+1)A(n-1,k)+(n-k)A(n-1,k-1)`, with out-of-range entries zero.
For `n>=1`, an independent reference uses the inclusion-exclusion formula
`sum(j=0..k+1, (-1)^j * binom(n+1,j) * (k+1-j)^n)` and big-integer
intermediates; it returns `A(0,0)=1` directly rather than evaluating the
formula at `n=0` (where its `0^0` term would need a special convention).
`20!` bounds every valid result below `INT64_MAX`.

Method context is the current OI Wiki [Eulerian Number article](https://oi-wiki.org/math/combinatorics/eulerian/),
the classic Eulerian triangle [OEIS A008292](https://oeis.org/A008292), and
Stanley's *Enumerative Combinatorics, Volume 1*, §1.4. OI Wiki's license
notice states [CC BY-SA 4.0 and SATA](https://oi-wiki.org/intro/faq/); only the
algorithm idea and standard mathematical definition are used. No OI Wiki code,
prose, examples, or test cases are reused. The package now has ten native
ports, a bounded workload, two structurally different Python references,
package-local rights/inventory/workload-checker sources, and the
`i64_array_scalar` runner/verifier and catalog registration are integrated.
No programs, scripts, checkers, tests, builds, compilers, or benchmarks were
run.

|---|---|
| Longest common subsequence; A* search; Barnsley fern; FFT; Runge–Kutta; Cholesky decomposition; Miller–Rabin; Dijkstra; move-to-front; Farey sequence; Quickselect; closest pair; shoelace area; topological sort; Huffman/LZW coding; K-means++; Boyer–Moore search; Christofides; CORDIC; flood fill | Implemented in existing local packages, including `longest_common_subsequence` / `hirschberg_lcs`, `a_star_search`, `barnsley_fern`, `fast_fourier_transform` and specialized FFTs, `runge_kutta`, `cholesky_decomposition`, `miller_rabin`, `dijkstra`, `move_to_front`, `farey_sequence_ordered_enumeration`, `quick_select`, closest-pair profiles, polygon-area profiles, topological-sort profiles, Huffman/LZW profiles, `kmeans_plus_plus_seeding`, `boyer_moore`, `metric_tsp_christofides`, `cordic_rotation_fixed_point`, and `flood_fill`. Earlier score-specific additions include Sutherland–Hodgman, VLQ, Penney probability, Gaussian prime classification, MRG32k3a, tanh–sinh, Sturmian words, Pritchard sieve, and the score-23 family crosswalk. |
| Knuth shuffle; Egyptian division; tree sort on a linked list | Duplicate methods of Fisher–Yates, `divide_two_integers`, and `tree_sort`, respectively; representation or naming differences do not introduce another kernel. |
| General Monte Carlo methods; custom-comparator sort; language-feature, system, GUI, and network-interface demonstrations; puzzle titles without one specified solver/heuristic; conjectural property searches | Excluded as broad or underspecified title leads: they do not define one bounded deterministic algorithm and output contract. |
| Schieber–Vishkin algorithm (score 21) | Implemented as `schieber_vishkin_lca` with ten language ports, a source-shaped inlabel/ascendant reference, an independent binary-lifting reference, bounded fixtures, rights/provenance, and static package inventory. Local LCA packages are path comparison, binary lifting, Tarjan offline DSU, and Farach–Colton–Bender Euler-tour ±1 RMQ; none uses Schieber–Vishkin's preorder inlabels, ascendant path-level bitsets, and path-head query jumps. Byte-output runner/verifier, README, and catalog integration are complete. |

Implemented contract for `schieber_vishkin_lca`: `i64_array_bytes_output` input `[n,root,m,q,(u,v)*m,(x,y)*q]`, with `1<=n<=256`, `m=n-1`, and `0<=q<=1024`; edge and query IDs are in `0..n-1`, and the edge list must describe one connected acyclic undirected tree. `n=1,m=0,q=0` is valid. Return one byte containing each query's LCA ID in query order; a valid empty query batch returns zero and accepts null output. Malformed framing, invalid IDs, self-edges, or a non-tree return `-1`; a valid nonempty query batch with null or undersized output returns `-2`, with no partial writes. Maximum valid input is 2,562 i64 words; the one-word trailing-frame probe is 2,563 words; maximum output is 1,024 bytes; fixed logical scratch is bounded to 32,768 bytes, including staged query answers. The primary uses Schieber–Vishkin inlabel/ascendant/head preprocessing and constant-operation queries; the independent reference uses binary lifting. Sources: Schieber and Vishkin, “On Finding Lowest Common Ancestors: Simplification and Parallelization,” *SIAM Journal on Computing* 17(6), 1253–1262 (1988), [DOI 10.1137/0217079](https://doi.org/10.1137/0217079); Schieber, “Parallel Lowest Common Ancestor Computation,” in *A Synthesis of Parallel Algorithms*, chapter 6 (1994), listed on [Schieber's publication page](https://sbarnjit.github.io/). Algorithm descriptions only; RosettaCodeData provides title discovery and no task prose, code, examples, tests, or fixtures are reused. No ports or validation checks were run.

compilers, or benchmarks were run.

**Implemented — [`fractional_programming_ratio_knapsack_binary_search`](f/fractional_programming_ratio_knapsack_binary_search/README.md):**
the OI Wiki [fractional-programming article](https://oi-wiki.org/misc/frac-programming/)
describes ratio bisection with a transformed additive objective, including a
minimum-denominator 0/1 knapsack feasibility check. This differs from local
[`dinkelbach_fixed_cardinality_ratio`](d/dinkelbach_fixed_cardinality_ratio/README.md),
which iterates Dinkelbach updates and selects exactly `K` items by top-`K`
residuals; the new profile uses a denominator-threshold DP and returns a
fixed-resolution ratio. Contract: `i64_array_scalar`, input
`[n,W,(a_i,b_i)*n]`, with `1<=n<=12`, `1<=W<=32`, `0<=a_i<=1000`,
`1<=b_i<=8`, and `W<=sum(b_i)`. Return
`floor(1,000,000 * max_{S: sum(b_i)>=W}(sum(a_i)/sum(b_i)))`. Invalid or
malformed input returns `-1`. The primary binary-searches the largest integer
threshold `q` for which a two-row 0/1 knapsack over denominator sums capped at
`W` has maximum transformed score
`sum(1,000,000*a_i-q*b_i)>=0`; its search range is `0..=1,000,000,000`.
The independent reference enumerates all subsets and computes the exact
maximum ratio with integer cross-products before flooring the scaled result.
All products, sums, and the maximum output fit signed 64-bit integers. The
profile is bounded to at most 26 valid and 27 parseable i64 words. The package
contains ten clean-room ports, two references, workload, README/RIGHTS/
INVENTORY, and package-local static checker sources; scalar runner/verifier,
README, and catalog integration are complete. OI Wiki supplies method discovery
under CC BY-SA 4.0/SATA; only the algorithm idea is used, with no source text,
code, examples, or tests reused.

| `multidimensional_newton_raphson` | `benchmarks/m/multidimensional_newton_raphson/` | ABI `i64_array_bytes_output`; input `[x0_milli,y0_milli,updates]`, exact length 3, with each start coordinate in `900..1500` and `updates` in `1..8`. Start from `(x0_milli/1000,y0_milli/1000)` and apply exactly `updates` binary64 Newton steps to `F1=x^2+y-3`, `F2=x+y^2-3`: solve `[[2x,1],[1,2y]]*[dx,dy]=[F1,F2]`, then set `(x,y)-=(dx,dy)`. Emit the two coordinates rounded to 1e-9, ties away from zero, as two little-endian signed i64 values (16 bytes); invalid input returns `-1`, insufficient output capacity `-2`. Local Newton profiles use one scalar variable; Gaussian elimination is only a linear-system primitive. This measures coupled Jacobian construction and correction rather than scalar derivative division. Method context: Chen and Strader, “A normalized multidimensional Newton-Raphson method,” *International Journal of Control* 12(2), 273–279 (1970), [NASA NTRS paper](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/19780021877/downloads/19780021877.pdf), whose section 2 presents the general simultaneous-equation Newton step. This bounded profile uses that standard step and does not claim to implement the paper's separate normalization transforms. Only the mathematical method is used; the article is copyrighted and no text, code, examples, or task content are reused. |
| `brace_range_expansion` | `benchmarks/b/brace_range_expansion/` | ABI `i64_array_bytes_output`; input `[length,ascii_bytes...]` is one printable-ASCII pattern of at most 64 bytes in the grammar `prefix{start..end[..step]}suffix`, with exactly one brace pair and one range. Endpoints are either unsigned decimal integers of at most four digits or single same-case ASCII letters. Integer ranges preserve width if either endpoint has a leading zero; omitted step follows endpoint direction, explicit nonzero step must point toward the endpoint; emit values within the inclusive bound without forcing the endpoint to occur. At most 16 items and at most 32 combined prefix/suffix bytes are accepted. Output expanded words in left-to-right order, NUL-separated; maximum output is 591 bytes. Malformed input or over-bound expansion returns `-1`; insufficient capacity returns `-2`. No local shell brace-expansion parser or range generator was found. This differs from numeric range iteration because it parses and expands an embedded string expression. Primary behavior reference: the [GNU Bash Reference Manual, §3.5.1](https://www.gnu.org/software/bash/manual/html_node/Brace-Expansion.html), defining integer/letter ranges, step direction, zero padding, and left-to-right output. Use documentation behavior only; no manual prose or implementation is reused. |
| `wave_function_collapse_simple_tiled` | `benchmarks/w/wave_function_collapse_simple_tiled/` | ABI `i64_array_scalar`; input `[width,height,k,domains[cells],weights[k],adjacency[4*k],draws[cells]]`, with `1<=width,height<=4`, `cells=width*height<=16`, `1<=k<=4`, nonempty domain masks within `0..(1<<k)-1`, tile weights `1..4`, directional adjacency masks within the tile mask, and one draw `0..65535` per cell. Require reciprocal N/S and E/W compatibility. Run FIFO support propagation over caller domains once, seeding every cell in row-major order, before observation; this makes the behavior defined for arbitrary nonempty input domains. Then repeatedly choose a nonsingleton cell with minimum candidate count (row-major tie), select a remaining tile in ascending ID by weighted cumulative rank `floor(draw*remaining_weight/65536)`, and FIFO-propagate adjacency support reductions without backtracking. Return success bit 32 plus two-bit tile IDs in row-major order; return `-2` for a valid contradiction and `-1` for malformed framing/domain/weights. Local Sudoku MRV uses domain-specific exact search/backtracking and does not implement stochastic tile observation or adjacency-wave propagation. Method context: Karth and Smith, “WaveFunctionCollapse is constraint solving in the wild,” FDG 2017, [DOI 10.1145/3102071.3110566](https://doi.org/10.1145/3102071.3110566), and their later [rational reconstruction](https://doi.org/10.1109/TG.2021.3076368). Only the algorithm description is used; the publications are copyrighted and no paper text, figures, code, examples, or task content are reused. |

The WFC initialization rule is explicit: seed one FIFO queue with every cell in
row-major order and propagate support before the first observation. Maintain an
in-queue flag; append a changed cell only if it is not already queued, clearing
the flag when popped. Observation draws are indexed by cell, and an observation
never triggers backtracking.

Brace-range steps may contain any signed decimal magnitude that fits within the
64-byte pattern. Native parsers saturate the internal magnitude at 10,000,
which exceeds the maximum endpoint gap of 9,999 and therefore preserves the
single-start-term result for oversized directed steps. Equal endpoints emit
one term for either sign of any explicit nonzero step.

**In progress — [`straddling_checkerboard_transducer`](s/straddling_checkerboard_transducer/README.md):** package owner `roscode_title_audit`; root owns suite and catalog wiring. Exact bounded contract: ABI `i64_array_bytes_output`; input `[mode,board[30],length,text[length]]`, with mode `0` for encoding or `1` for decoding, `0<=length<=64`, and exact frame length `32+length` (96 valid words maximum; 97 is the trailing-value probe). The board is three rows of ten bytes. The first row has exactly two zero-valued holes; each hole's column digit is the row indicator for the corresponding second or third row. The other eight top-row cells and all twenty lower-row cells contain distinct printable ASCII bytes `32..126`. Encoding maps a top-row symbol to its column digit and a lower-row symbol to its row-indicator digit followed by its column digit. Decoding scans decimal ASCII digits from left to right; a digit naming a nonempty top-row cell emits that symbol, while a digit naming a top-row hole consumes one following decimal digit and emits the lower-row symbol. Empty lower cells and duplicate board symbols are invalid. Encoding input bytes must occur in the board; decoding input bytes must be `0..9`. Output is the raw byte stream, at most 128 bytes for encoding and 64 for decoding. Malformed input or board returns `-1`; null or undersized output returns `-2`, with validation before capacity checks and no partial writes. The profile measures key/table lookup and variable-length prefix decoding, distinct from local fixed monoalphabetic, A1Z26, and one-time-pad methods. Method context: Esslinger (ed.), *Learning and Experiencing Cryptography with CrypTool and SageMath*, edition 12 (2018), §2.2.1, pp. 33–34, [CrypTool Book PDF](https://www.csd.uoc.gr/~hy458/2022/resources/files/CrypTool-Book-en-v12-May18.pdf). Its front matter permits free distribution with author/title/CrypTool-site attribution and additionally licenses the book under GNU FDL 1.3-or-later. Only the algorithm idea is used; no book text, code, examples, or exercise data and no Rosetta task content are reused.

### Implemented, unverified: `hashiwokakero_small_solver`

The exact package contract, method, independent exhaustive reference, bounded
search argument, rights note, and ten-language implementation plan are recorded
in [`RESERVATION.md`](h/hashiwokakero_small_solver/RESERVATION.md). In brief,
`i64_array_scalar` input is `[n,(x,y,demand)*n]`, with `2<=n<=6`, distinct
integer coordinates in `0..7`, and demands in `1..8`. Candidate bridges join
consecutive row/column islands and take multiplicity 0, 1, or 2. Exact vertex
degree totals, no crossings, and global connectivity are required. Return the
lexicographically smallest valid bridge vector, or `-2` if no arrangement
exists; malformed input returns `-1`. For `r` occupied rows and `c` occupied
columns, visibility yields at most `E<=2n-r-c` candidate edges; with `n<=6`
the maximum is seven (a 2-by-3 arrangement), so exhaustive verification checks
at most `3^7` assignments. The primary uses residual-degree backtracking and
safe feasibility pruning; the independent reference validates complete
multiplicity vectors from scratch in lexicographic order. Rule context
comes from [Nikoli's official Hashiwokakero rules](https://www.nikoli.co.jp/en/puzzles/hashiwokakero/);
solver context comes from the [published branch-and-cut study](https://arxiv.org/abs/1905.00973).
Only the Codewars title/tag is discovery input. No puzzle content, text, code,
example, or test is reused. All ten language ports, package-local references,
fixtures, rights notes, and static inventory are present. The root statically
reviewed the shared edge order, tie, crossing, connectivity, and packed-result
semantics; scalar-suite registration and README/catalog entries are integrated.
No programs, tests, scripts, checkers, builds, compilers, profilers, or
benchmarks were run.

## Algorithm Archive quantum spectral energy expectation (2026-11-20)

The completed 49-chapter body-method crosswalk is recorded in
[`ALGORITHM_ARCHIVE_CHAPTER_BODY_AUDIT_2026-11-20.md`](ALGORITHM_ARCHIVE_CHAPTER_BODY_AUDIT_2026-11-20.md).
Its sole confirmed missing operation is `quantum_spectral_energy_expectation`;
it is distinct from [`split_operator_imaginary_time`](s/split_operator_imaginary_time/README.md),
which evolves a state, and from the classical scalar energy formula packages.
The [Quantum Systems chapter](https://www.algorithm-archive.org/contents/quantum_systems/quantum_systems.html)
describes the Hamiltonian expectation as a Fourier-domain kinetic operator
combined with a pointwise potential term. The Archive states that its sample
code is MIT licensed and its chapter text is CC BY-SA 4.0. Only the method
idea was consulted; no code, prose, examples, fixtures, or tests are reused.

**Implemented, unverified:** ABI `i64_array_float64`;
input `[N,V_q[0..N),psi_re_q[0..N),psi_im_q[0..N)]`, with `N` a power of two
in `2..32`, exact frame length `1+3N` (97 valid words maximum and 98
parseable). Each payload uses signed Q8 scaling by 256. Treat the samples as a
periodic grid over unit length, so `dx=1/N`, and require exact normalization
`sum(psi_re_q^2+psi_im_q^2)=256^2*N`; bound potential samples to `[-2048,2048]`
and wavefunction components to `[-2048,2048]`. The signed frequency bins are
`f_j=j` for `j<=N/2` and `f_j=j-N` otherwise, with `k_j=2*pi*f_j`.
Compute `T psi = IFFT((k_j^2/2)*FFT(psi))`, using an unnormalized forward
transform and inverse normalized by `N`, then return
`E=(1/N)*sum_j Re(conj(psi_j)*(T psi_j + V_j*psi_j))`. The primary uses a
radix-2 FFT in `O(N log N)` time and `O(N)` scratch; the independent reference
uses direct DFT sums in `O(N^2)` time. The scalar binary64 result uses absolute
and relative tolerances of `1e-9` and `1e-10`. Rights/provenance, all ten
language ports, package inventory, fixtures, and suite registration are still
complete in [`q/quantum_spectral_energy_expectation/`](q/quantum_spectral_energy_expectation/)
and registered in both the float64-array runner and verifier. Ten native ports,
the radix-2 primary, direct-DFT independent reference, bounded fixtures,
workload checker, static inventory, README, and rights note are present. The
contract, fixture vectors, frequency convention, and suite dispatch were
reviewed statically. Static formula review also corrected the N=4 single-site
fixture to exact discrete normalization and its matching analytic energy. No
project execution has been performed.
